Oṃ, salutation to the Self that is Being-Consciousness-Bliss.
Now begins the *Śivasūtravimarśinī*.
First Unmeṣa.

The Group of Rudras and Kṣetrajñas: [The Rudras are the forms of the Lord who effect the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe consisting of subject and object. The Kṣetrajñas are the bound souls (paśus), beginning with Brahmā.
From whom it arises and wherein it finds rest—
That reality from which this entire universe has flashed forth as such, and of which this universe consists—
that supreme principle of vibration (*spanda-tattva*), consisting of nectar surging from the multitude of blisses of absolute freedom (*svācchandyānanda*),
[wherein "absolute freedom" means sovereignty, and the "multitude of blisses" is that which is the cause of all powers].

Having stated the qualifier in the form of *vimarśa* (reflective awareness) by means of a *bahuvrīhi* compound—"from which the rays [of phonemes] beginning with 'a' and ending with 'kṣa' emerge (*ucchalat*), that is, issue forth in an exceeding manner, as a collection consisting solely of power"—he states the qualifier in the form of *prakāśa* (light): "Amṛta" (Nectar). And he is of such a nature of bliss.

Victorious is that Consciousness, whose essence is reality and whose nature is a slight vibration— the primordial cause of all causes, which is both unsurpassed and inexpressible. [This is stated by way of elucidating the meaning of the *Spandakārikās*.]
Victory to that consciousness of Śaṅkara, which, though non-dual in essence, appears as the entirety of duality [in reality,
this is the implied sense].
Having observed the inconsistency of the commentaries on these [Śiva-sūtras] here in reality,
I shall explain the Śiva-sūtra according to the tradition of the Guru.

"From *vigāna*—that is, from the contradiction (*vigāna*) of the Guru’s statement; or alternatively, *vigāna* is knowledge (*jñāna*) that is contradictory, or *vigāna* is censure (*nindā*), according to the lexicon which states that it means 'the state of being blameworthy. Therefore, the connection is:
'from that very [contradiction], there is inconsistency. For this very reason, I shall explain this. Although one should have said 'in speech' (*vacane'),..."
The mention of "tradition" (āmnāya) is for the purpose of establishing its authority.
p. 2) Here, someone—
by the phrase "someone" is meant one who has attained a state of greatness through a particular grace of Maheśvara, and for that very reason, he is unprecedented.
Through the excellence of his devotion to Maheśvara, which was awakened by the descent of power (*śaktipāta*),
he did not accept the teachings of the lower systems such as those of Nāgabodhi and other Buddhist masters;
instead, devoted to the worship of Śiva, he followed the instructions of the Siddhas of the Supreme Lord (*pārameśvara*).

There was once a venerable teacher named Vasugupta, a great Mahāmaheśvara whose heart was purified by the authentic tradition (satsampradāya) on the mountain of Śrī Mahādeva; he was "great" because of his contemplation of the identity with the Lord (Īśa).
At that time, in a world of living beings that was for the most part permeated by dualistic views, the secret tradition (rahasyasampradāya) [was nearly lost].
For tradition (*saṃpradāya*) is instruction handed down through a lineage; that too follows the maxim of "from ear to ear," and for this very reason, let it not be interrupted.
With the intention "let it not be interrupted," Paramaśiva, intent on bestowing grace, favored [the author] in a dream.
"With his intuition awakened" [the phrase "his intuition awakened in a dream" is connected with the word "by Agniveśa.
It was done so that, having discovered the secret which exists here upon this great rocky surface of the mountain...].
"Reveal it to those who are worthy of grace.
(p. 3) And having been awakened, he, searching for that great stone, turned it over by the mere touch of his hand.

Having made these Śiva-sūtras— which are a compendium of the Śiva-upaniṣads [or a compendium of the Śivarahaṃsya-āgama scriptures]— as if they were a dream verified by experience [or a dream established as authoritative], he then obtained them; and so says the Vārttika:
Long ago, on the glorious Mahādeva mountain, the Śiva-sūtras indeed appeared to that teacher Vasugupta by means of a perfected instruction (siddhādeśa).

Thus [he says]. And having correctly mastered these, he revealed them to the excellent disciples beginning with Bhaṭṭa Śrī Kallaṭa and summarized them in the Spandakārikās. From that [Vasugupta], they were received according to their respective traditions through the lineage of gurus.
The Spanda-sūtras have been thoroughly determined by us in the Spandanirṇaya; now, however, the Śiva-sūtras are being determined.

In this regard, first, as a counter-position to those who propound the distinction between the individual soul and the Lord— arguing that the self is one thing and the Lord is another— he teaches that, from the perspective of ultimate reality, Śiva alone is the Self of the universe by virtue of his supreme consciousness.
p. 4) Consciousness is the self. [On this point, the Vārttika states:
"Consciousness is established as the nature of the self, consisting of the essence of knowledge and action."
Since its nature is unobscured, by whom can its state of Śiva-hood be prevented? Thus [ends the verse]. || 1 ||

In this context, that which is unperceived (*acetita*)—meaning unmanifested—is a non-entity because it lacks existence for anyone. Since the act of consciousness (*citikriyā*), being a universal form, exists everywhere, that which perceives is the conscious (*cetana*), which is independent in all cognitive activities; its state is consciousness (*caitanya*).

[Consciousness (*caitanya*), the act of cognizing (*citi*), the cognizer (*cetana*), and the Self (*ātman*)—these are conceptual distinctions, like the expression "the head of Rāhu"; in reality, everything is one.
The activity of consciousness (*citikriyā*) is the touch of light (*prakāśābhimarśa*); its state is autonomy (*svātantrya*).
It consists of the connection with all cognitive and active functions [i.e., it consists of the connection with the activity of consciousness]. Of this connection...

Because consciousness is perceived as resting upon its correlates, it is manifested as consisting of the connection with the act of cognition (*citikriyā*); thus, it is extracted [from its latent state].

This is called perfect sovereignty (*paripūrṇa-svātantrya*). And that belongs only to the Blessed Lord Paramaśiva; it does not belong to those beginning with Anāśrita and ending with Śiva-tattva, such as Sakala and the others.

The Śiva-tattva, which is being emanated as actually inferior to that [Ātman], is designated as Anāśrita (the Unsupported), possessing qualities such as being indivisible, unmoistenable, and undryable; this is because its existence is dependent upon that [Ātman]. And although it consists of infinite attributes such as eternity, omnipresence, and incorporeality, nevertheless, regarding these [attributes like] eternity...

Since independence— which is impossible elsewhere, such as in the case of space, atoms, and so forth— is conceivable even in other instances, this is merely a demonstration of the exaltation of that very independence.
Thus, by means of the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*), consciousness (*caitanya*) is shown as the exclusion of other attributes;
"thus" (*ittham*) indicates the manifestation of the full assertion of autonomy. And so says the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta:

"The word *caitanya* (consciousness), ending in an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*), expresses in the ancient Sūtra nothing but absolute freedom (*svātantryamātra*), without implying any specific attributes.
He explains the meaning of the word *mātra* by saying "without implying" (*anākṣipta*). For a word ending in an abstract suffix...
It expresses precisely the exclusion of other concomitant properties; as they say:
"The two [types of negation] differ according to whether or not there is an exclusion of other properties."
The basis for the distinction between conventions is in accordance with the desire of the cognizer;
this very distinction exists everywhere between those [words] that denote substances and those that denote states.
Thus:
"Cognition (citi) is of the nature of reflective awareness (pratyavamarśātman)...
as stated in the *Śrī-Pratyabhijñā*. In the phrase "it cognizes" (cetayate), cognition (citi) refers to the act of cognizing (citikriyā); its reflective awareness is [the subject].

The Self (*ātman*) is one's own nature (*svabhāva*), characterized by the wonder (*camatkāra*) of its own essence. For instance, a jar does not produce wonder within itself; its own essence is not reflected upon, it is not manifested within itself, and it is not perceived as being undivided. Therefore, it is said that [the jar] is not cognized. By Caitra, however, [his own essence is perceived] as "I" within himself.
Through the conjunction of the power of impetuous exertion and creative effulgence, one's own Self is wondrously stirred, reflected upon within itself,
and manifested as "this," which is the act of discernment;
by means of this very nature, through its differentiation from what is other, [it perceives] blue, yellow, pleasure, pain, and so forth.
Thus it is said: this very consciousness (*caitanya*) is sovereignty itself, which is the Self (*ātman*); the Self is not, however, anything else as it is conceived by the proponents of dualism.

[It would be] of diverse and distinct natures. Because that [diverse and distinct nature], being insentient due to its inertness, lacks selfhood; and because if it were of the nature of consciousness (*cidātman*), diversity would be untenable—since consciousness cannot be differentiated by space, time, or form, and thus, by not being perceived apart from consciousness (i.e., by not being manifested), it would be non-existent.

However, because they are being perceived as objects by those whose nature is consciousness—and since there is no difference [between them] due to their non-distinction from consciousness—it is impossible to establish a distinction [the genitive case *bhedasya* is used in the sense of the object;
in the phrase "to establish a distinction," the meaning is "to create a distinction"]. For if the selves were pure consciousness, there could be no difference in their essential nature.

The meaning is that because of the impossibility of [such] occurrence— according to the logic to be explained [since the persistence of impurity is observable, and once the suspicion of difference has arisen, it will be explained that it is non-distinct], there is no persistence of difference;
for even through the connection with a non-distinct impurity, difference is untenable prior to liberation.

[Previously: Even though impurity (*mala*) exists, because it is quiescent at the stage of liberation, the doctrine of a plurality of selves (*anātmavāda*) cannot be asserted; or, even if there were a possibility of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of impurity [or, despite the cessation of impurity], how could there be any diminution [or deficiency] from the beginningless Śiva at the stage of liberation?

Or rather, such a deficiency arising from impure residual impressions (*malasaṃskāra*) ought not to exist; for if that were admitted, there would be no liberation at all, but only continued transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). Or else, those who are liberated Śivas would themselves become transmigrating beings.
As it has been said:
By stating, "Consciousness alone is the one Self" (p.
7), the untenability of the doctrine of multiple selves is indicated; that is, it is asserted that there is no distinction between selves.

Moreover, worldly people accept the body as the self; the Cārvākas and Vaidikas accept the vital breath (prāṇa); the Yogācāras among the Buddhists accept consciousness (buddhi); and the Mādhyamikas accept emptiness (śūnya) as the self.
In order to refute their views, the author teaches by means of a question beginning with "atha" (now/then), for those who desire to know: "What is it? (kaḥ).

In order to awaken those who are to be instructed, it is not the body, the vital breath, the intellect, or the void—entities accepted by the worldly Cārvākas, the Vedic [Mīmāṃsakas], the Yogācāras, the Mādhyamikas, and others—that is the Self;
rather, as has been stated, consciousness alone is the Self (the word "Self" being understood). Of that very [consciousness], the body and so forth [are the instruments].
[And the body and so forth are apprehended precisely as being manifest.

Even in the state of the imagined subject (*kalpitapramātṛ*), there is a manifestation as the true subject (*satyapramātṛ*) consisting of the non-imagined reflective awareness of "I" (*akalpitāhaṃvimarśamaya*). This has been stated in the venerable *Mṛtyujidbhaṭṭāraka*:
The nature of the Supreme Self, however, is consciousness devoid of all limiting adjuncts (upādhis) belonging to the self that possesses a body and so forth. As it is said in the *Yogavāsiṣṭha*:
"Having abandoned through reasoning whatever object of knowledge this may be..."
Having attained the remaining pure consciousness alone, contemplate: "I am He, I am He."
And in the *Aṣṭāvakra-gītā*:
"The light is my own form; I am not distinct from it.
When the universe shines forth, then I am indeed that very radiance. This is the nature [of the Self] taught in all the scriptures.
It is recited.
Thus, it is said; and in the *Śrīvijñānabhairava* (p. 8) as well:
"The Self is the attribute of consciousness (*ciddharma*). The distinction (*viśeṣa*)—that is, the differentiation—is in all bodies."
It does not exist anywhere;
therefore, a person seeking liberation should contemplate everything as being composed of that.
Thus it is said. Since this very group of instruments [is as follows]...
having summarized this with two verses, [the author] addresses those to be instructed with a sign of recognition: "This indeed is the Cit..."
"It vibrates within all bodies"—thus it is said with direct experiential knowledge (*sābhijñāna*) in the *Śrī Spanda*, as taught by the Guru.

Furthermore, that which has been called consciousness (*caitanya*) is itself the Self (*ātman*), the essential nature (*svabhāva*); for no specific distinction has been enjoined [regarding it], since no such distinction as "this alone is the Self" has been stated [in the case of the universe]. (Because no specific distinction has been enjoined—i.e., because no distinction such as "this alone is the Self" has been stated—[it belongs] to the universe.)

[It is said: of the universe, which consists of existence and non-existence, nothing whatsoever belongs to anyone if it is not being cognized—[the term "not being cognized" (acetyamānaḥ) is connected with the word "nature" (svabhāva);
"not being cognized" means not being manifested; for that which is not reflected upon might as well not exist].

At times it possesses a nature; however, when being perceived, because it has become one with self-luminous consciousness (*cit*), its very essence is consciousness itself—its nature is nothing other than the nature of consciousness.
As it is said in the venerable *Ucchuṣmabhairava*:
"As long as these are not the knower, how can they be the object of knowledge, O beloved?
For the knower and the object of knowledge are one; therefore, there is no impurity. (From this very reason.
This is precisely that.
(9) Because the individual soul (jīva) consists of all things...
[this] is summarized by these two verses.
Since consciousness is the very nature of the universe, for that reason alone, the miserable means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and so forth are useless for its realization. [As it is said:
"That which is called manifestation shines everywhere."
Since it cannot be denied, what is the use of postulating means of knowledge for it?
Thus, because the non-establishment of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has been taught by the venerable Abhinavagupta in the *Tantrāloka*: "Even for that wretched means of valid cognition,
there are indeed other means of valid cognition which extend the very life of all things."
Even for them, the supreme soul is that very same Supreme Lord.
Thus, by the venerable Abhinavagupta, it has been pointed out that accomplishment (siddhi) is dependent solely upon consciousness.

This is because accomplishment depends on self-luminous consciousness, and because consciousness—due to the reasoning already stated—cannot be obscured by anything, and thus shines forth eternally. As it is said in the *Śrītrikahṛdaya*:
Just as one who desires to step over the shadow of his own head finds that the head cannot exist at the location of the feet, so it is with this Bindu-kalā.

Thus: the connection here is that this [power] is such that for one who attempts to leap over it, just as the head would not be in the region of the feet, so it is. With this very intention, [it is said] in the *Spanda* (p.
"Wherein it is situated... and so forth, beginning thus... "...that exists in the ultimate sense."

By this extensive passage, it has been established through valid means that consciousness—which is of the nature of the *spanda* reality consisting of Śaṅkara—is eternally self-luminous and exists as the ultimate reality. || 1 ||
If the very nature of the universe—consisting of both the living and the insentient—is indeed consciousness in the form of Paramaśiva, then how can this bondage exist?

To pacify such a doubt, the *saṃhitā* (the conjunction) is employed; otherwise, according to the rule that "close proximity [of sounds] is *saṃhitā*," through the application of a phonetic junction (*śliṣṭasaṃdhi*), consciousness itself, when there is ignorance of the Self, is bondage.

By reading with the elision (*praśleṣa*) of the letter *i*, there is one single sūtra; otherwise, by means of two separate sūtras due to the non-elision of the letter *a*, there is an absence of conjunction. Thus, according to the sequence of ascent and descent, here [is described] impurity (*mala*), which consists of the conceit of self (*ātmābhimāna*) in what is not-self (*anātman*) and the conceit of self in what is not-self.

This has been demonstrated by the reading [of the two terms] as either separated or conjoined. And so, the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta stated in the two aphorisms, "The Self is consciousness" and "Knowledge is bondage":
"This meaning is shown through both their conjunction and their separation."
In the ancient aphorism, the word *caitanya* (consciousness), ending in a nominal suffix, expresses mere sovereignty (*svātantrya*) alone,
without implying any specific attributes.
But by the second sutra, which speaks of either action or the instrument,
duality is asserted for that [Self] whose nature is pure consciousness alone.
The manifestation of duality is ignorance of that [Reality]; because of its insubstantiality, it is called bondage.
For this very reason, it must be completely eradicated—this is established through repetition.
Thus, by reading the sūtra with and without the elision of the vowel *a*, he states:
"Knowledge is bondage" (jñānaṃ bandhaḥ). || 2 ||

Since, according to the reasoning stated here, nothing whatsoever is established as distinct from the light of consciousness, [this statement follows the view of the proponent of non-duality regarding the opponent who maintains the doctrine of difference: what is the existence of impurity (mala), or of what nature is its power to obstruct [namely,
its quality of veiling or obscuring the very nature of consciousness]?

The proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin) speaks by avoiding the method of objection stated according to the system of the proponent of difference (bhedavādin), and specifically by avoiding that very method of objection stated in accordance with the tenet propounded by the proponent of difference.

They maintain that impurity is ignorance (*ajñāna*). "Impurity" refers to that which is characterized by the concealment of one's true nature, manifested solely through the sovereign freedom of the Supreme Lord; it is a state of incomplete knowledge whose essence consists in the erroneous identification of the self with the non-self. This is the *āṇava* impurity.

Regarding "in *saṃsāra*": according to the principle that "the sprout of *saṃsāra* is karma, which is the cause of *saṃsāra*—namely, the impurity (*mala*) consisting of *māyā*, whose nature has been described in such passages as 'herein alone occurs the manifestation of diverse objects of cognition called *māyā*'"—the sprout is the cause, which is the impurity of action (*kārmamala*), and its [further] cause is the impurity of *māyā*. Thus, the impurity of action belongs to that which consists of *māyā*.

And its cause is atomic (*aṇava*); this is the intended meaning. Although ignorance is twofold—consisting of both the personal (*pauruṣa*) and the intellectual (*bauddha*)—only the personal is intended here, not the other; this is indicated by the qualification "the cause of the sprout of transmigratory existence" (*saṃsārāṅkurakāraṇa*). Thus, the venerable teacher Abhinavaguptapāda has said:

"By means of this qualification, having excluded the possibility that [liberation] exists in something residing in the intellect that occurs subsequent to saṃsāra, he declared liberation to exist in its absence.
Thus, [it is] the cause of the sprout of saṃsāra.
Thus, the world is bound by ignorance; from that [ignorance] proceed both creation and dissolution.
Thus, according to the position stated in the *Śrīmālinīvijaya* and the *Śrīsarvācāra* (p.
that which [is performed] by the Supreme Lord through His power of absolute freedom (*svātantrya-śakti*), which consists in the concealment of His own manifested nature;
"By the power of Mahāmāyā"—according to the tradition of the *Āmnāya*, "Mahāmāyā above Māyā" means that Māyā has pervaded everywhere, excluding only the single Śiva-tattva;
otherwise, since it would exist above Māyā, how could there be a distinction of states? This is the opinion of Bhaṭṭotpala.

Within one's own self, there is a similarity to space due to its transparency; yet, because it is not contracted by the veil of the clouds of *māyā*, the contraction— from the level of *anāśrita-śiva* down to the *māyā-pramātṛ*— is manifested as that very [contraction].

Bondage consists in the non-manifestation (*akhyāti*)— that is, the failure to appear— of non-difference from Śiva, which takes the form of a loss of autonomy. Furthermore, we have [already] demonstrated how it is logically untenable for impurity (*mala*) to exist as something distinct [from consciousness].
This has been demonstrated in detail during the discussion on initiation at the end of the fifth chapter of the *Śrī-svacchandoddyota*:
"And this is the meaning of the aphorism for one who is incapable [of purification] due to his own impurity..."

Thus it is summarized by this portion of the *kārikā*. In this way, within the Self—that is, within the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) in the manner already described—there is the concealment of one's true nature (*svarūpagopanā*), which consists in the erroneous cognition (*akhyāti*) characterized by the conceit of non-selfhood [and the loss of the autonomy of consciousness, as stated in the passage: "the loss of the autonomy of consciousness..."].
This concealment of one's true nature has been explained in the *Pratyabhijñā* with respect to the *vijñānākala* subjects.

13) Knowledge is not merely bondage; rather, it is the ignorance rooted in the conceit of selfhood (*ātmatābhimāna*) directed toward that which is not the Self, such as the body, and likewise the lack of awareness regarding even one's own sovereignty (*svātantrya*) within the conceit of sovereignty. Thus...
Form [is bondage]; knowledge, too, is indeed bondage. And this has been summarized by the verse beginning with "the departure from the supreme nectar-essence... and so forth.

Thus, whatever form is denoted by the word "consciousness" (caitanya), which consists of autonomy— even within that conscious self— there exists, as in the case of the Vijñānākala, a state consisting merely of the sense of incompleteness due to the non-manifestation of autonomy;
and even within that autonomy, there is a lack of awareness regarding the autonomy found in the body and so forth.

The two-fold *āṇava-mala* (the impurity of atomicity), consisting in the form of the conceit of selfhood (*ātmatābhimāna*) with respect to that which is not-self, is summarized by this aphorism. As it is stated in the *Śrī-Pratyabhijñā*:
"The loss of sovereignty of consciousness, and the lack of consciousness regarding sovereignty itself."
This impurity consists of two kinds of atoms, due to the loss of one's own true nature.
Thus [ends the second section].
Is bondage merely of the nature of this individual impurity (*āṇavamala*)? No; he says:
"The group of wombs" [the group of wombs consists of the impurity of *māyā*, limited agency (*kalā*), and the impurity of action (*kārmamala*); these constitute the body of limited agency].
The term *bandha* (bondage) continues [from the previous context]. This group, which belongs to *māyā*— the womb that is the cause of the universe—
is the direct or indirect cause of that [universe], initiating the body, the worlds, and so forth.
The collection of principles beginning with *kalā* and ending with *kṣiti*, whose nature consists of limited agency (*kiñcitkartṛtā*) and so forth, is that very form [which is rooted in *māyā*;

thus it is the bond of impurity (*malabandha*)]. That which belongs to *māyā* (*māyīya*) "impels" (*kalayati*)—that is, it impels [the soul] toward its own essential nature and causes it to enter into it; because it delimits each respective object through the entry into its own essential nature, it is called *kalā*.
[In each respective object or subject, *kalā* is simply one's own limited capacity.
That whose activity, body, and essential nature are *kalā* is "that which has *kalā* as its body"; the meaning is that even the *kārma* impurity (*mala*) is a bond.
This too belongs to one who, being incapable due to innate impurity, yet desires to act toward what ought to be done.

This is already included by this very [statement]. How this is so should be understood from our *Spandakārikā-nirṇaya*. And among these principles beginning with *kalā*—[wherein by "the first," *vidyā*, *kāla*, *rāga*, *niyati*, and so forth are included]—there is the characteristic of limited agency (*kiñcitkartṛtva*) and the rest.

The innate impurity (*āṇavamala*), which is fixed upon its own foundational wall [meaning that, in reality, it alone is the root of the other two impurities], is established as such by virtue of being the obscuring factor for individual souls;
the intention is that the categories beginning with *kalā* are themselves impurities.
As it is said in the venerable *Svacchanda* (p.
"The consciousness that is obscured by impurity is the loss of the autonomy of awareness."
By means of the *āṇavamala* (the impurity of finitude) characterized by the aforementioned description, the contraction of consciousness first arises.
[It is] dependent upon *kalā* and *vidyā*;
its self is colored by *rāga* (attachment); it is delimited by *kāla* (time)—[that is, limited]; it is constrained.

It is thus restricted: by means of the state of being male (*puṃbhāva*), that is, by the principle of the Person (*puruṣatattva*); by the "qualities" (*guṇa*), that is, by the division of the three qualities (*guṇatraya*); by "intellect and action," that is, by the organs of perception and the organs of action; by the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) such as sound and the rest; and by the gross elements beginning with earth. Thus it is.
Furthermore, it is restrained by necessity (niyati), augmented by the state of being a person (puṃbhāva),
endowed with the disposition of primordial matter (pradhāna), and possessed of the three qualities (guṇatraya).
Seated within the principle of intellect (buddhi-tattva) and enveloped by the ego (ahaṃkāra), [the Self is associated] with the mind,
the intellect, the organs of action, the sense organs, the subtle elements (tanmātras), and the gross elements.

Thus, with the intention that only the two impurities— the *kārmamala* and the *āṇava-māyīyamala*— have been mentioned up to this point, he says "the *kārmamala*" because: "For him whose own greatness is concealed, who has forgotten his true self through delusion..."
That very contraction is called his *āṇava-mala* (the atomic impurity).
Then, that state which exists within the body of the elements for one whose own station has been obscured by the pervasion of the six coverings is called the impurity of Māyā.
That which, dependent on the internal organ, engages externally through the organs of action and so forth initiated by karma— this is considered its "karmic impurity" (kārma-mala).

Thus, according to the Adhyātmanaya: "The obscuring nature of impurity (*mala*)— as well as the two-fold obscuration of karma (*kārmamāvaraṇa*), namely 'I am a performer of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice and shall go to heaven' and 'I am a doer of evil and shall go to hell'—
is demonstrated in the Śrīmālinīvijaya."
"Action, consisting of merit and demerit, is characterized by pleasure, pain, and so forth.
This [is] both the impurity of Māyā and the impurity of Karma. (p.

Right here [in the individual state], the manifestation of differentiated objects of cognition is called *māyā*, which bestows birth and experience; and when there is non-awareness regarding the agent, there is also *kārma* (the karma-born state).
Thus, in the *Śrī Pratyabhijñā*, it is stated that the impurity of limited agency (*āṇavamala*) has as its very foundation the state of contracted and specific cognition;
for all impurities consist precisely of contracted and specific cognition. (3)
Now, he explains how this threefold impurity—consisting of ignorance, the source of knowledge, the group of powers, and the body—functions as a bond:
"The support of knowledge is Mātṛkā. (4)

This threefold nature of impurity—consisting of the sense of incompleteness (*apūrṇamanyatā*), the manifestation of objects as distinct from oneself (*bhinnavedyaprathā*), and the state of being an object of cognition (*vedyatā*)—is the unmanifested Mother (*mātṛkā*), whose form extends from the letter *a* to *kṣa*.
When unknown, she is the Mother; what proof is there for her being unknown? She alone is the binder when unknown, but when known, she brings about accomplishment (*siddhi*).
The Mother of the Universe [is the source] of that knowledge which consists of the manifestation of various contracted objects of cognition;
[through such expressions as] "I am incomplete," "I am incomplete," etc., the impurities of finitude (āṇava), illusion (māyīya), and action (kārmika) are illustrated.
[One thinks: "I am emaciated," "I am stout," or "I am a performer of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice."

Thus, [of that knowledge which consists of the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of various non-conceptual and conceptual appearances (or, consisting of the reflective awareness of gross and subtle words).

By way of being permeated by the sound of words— according to the principle that "there is no cognition in the world that is devoid of the accompaniment of words"— cognition, being thus intermingled with words,
assumes the form of sorrow, pride, joy, passion, and so forth.
The consciousness that resides within the space of the aperture of the heart—the sky of consciousness—is itself situated in the center of that;

it is indeed of the nature of the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*). In reality, the bond of Brahmā (*brahmapāśa*) is a difficult knot because of its indivisibility. The [powers] beginning with Brāhmī are most terrible, for they hang from the bond of Brahmā.
The most terrible mistresses of the seats cause delusion again and again.
Thus, according to the method taught in the *Śrītimirodghāṭa*, there are eight groups (*varga*) and the [eight] *kalās* beginning with *nivṛtti*.
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*) are included.
She is the Mother (*Ambā*) and the Eldest (*Jyeṣṭhā*), who brings forth the arrangement of the sequence of scripts as established in the *Śrīsarvavīra* and other scriptures.

The meaning is that she is the power of the *mātṛkā*. She is the presiding power (*adhiṣṭhātrī*); for it is precisely because of her presiding that [the state] lacks the internal contemplation of non-duality—that is, it is devoid of that internal contemplation of non-duality which is the reflective awareness of the identity with consciousness within the fullness of the "I" (*pūrṇāhaṃtā*). Not even for a moment...
Since cognitions that have not attained rest are directed exclusively toward the external, it is entirely appropriate to describe these cognitions as being binding. And this...
"...of that which arises from the mass of sounds..."—
by this verse [it is shown that] its powers, which conceal its own nature, are perpetually active.
And this has been summarized by the following verse: || 4 ||
Now, he teaches this reality of resting in the goal, which is the means for the pacification of bondage—[this reality, along with its ultimate truth]:
"Bhairava is exertion. (5)
This very reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), which is of the nature of bliss, belonging to consciousness that is both the all-pervading expansion of the universe and transcendent to the universe—
this reflective awareness, which is the unfolding of one's own essential nature (*svarūpavikāsa*) and constitutes the "unfolding" (*unmeṣa*) of the Absolute (*anuttara*)—
arises instantaneously from consciousness that consists of reflective awareness.

[By the power of the descent of grace (*śaktipāta*), there is a sudden, ever-new unfolding of one’s own nature, which consists of a vibration characterized by the emergence of the reflection of the other that is of the nature of surging forth. That very [unfolding] is *udyama* (the upward effort),
through its embrace as a state of identity by bringing about a state of aesthetic relish (*samarasatā*) via the equilibrium of all powers.

Like the fluid within a peacock’s egg; because it sustains the entire universe without exception and because it consists of the devouring of the potter that is all conceptual construction—even for that which remains as residual impression (*saṃskāra*)—it is Bhairava.
[Just as in the expression "clarified butter is life,"] because exertion (*udyama*) is the cause for the manifestation of the nature of Bhairava, exertion itself is [Bhairava].
Regarding "Bhairava": Bhairava is so called because his nature consists of supporting (*bharaṇa*), protecting (*vaṇana*), and vomiting out (*vamana*).

According to the etymology "the fearlessness of the fearful" (*bhīruṇām abhayam*), he is the bestower of fearlessness upon those in transmigratory existence. *Bhī* is fear—the terror of saṃsāra; the cry (*rava*) produced by that is *bhīrava*.
He is born from that, manifesting for those who utter such cries; [he is] this very Bhīrava.

This is the awakener of the contemplation on the fear of *saṃsāra* by virtue of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*). Time (*kāla*) is "bhīraḥ" because it sets the stars (*bhāni*, i.e., the lunar mansions) in motion; those who blow upon that time are the "bhīravāḥ"—the yogins who delight in the meditative absorption of devouring time (*kālagrāsasamādhi*).
This is their innermost nature. It is a "ravaḥ," a roar, for the sake of fear—that is, to terrify the fettered folk (*paśu*).

Bhairava is the Lord of those goddesses of consciousness, such as Khecarī and others, who possess the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the *kalās* beginning with *Ākāra*, which arise from the totality of sounds (*śabdarāśi*). Furthermore, he is called Bhairava because he is terrifying (*bhīṣaṇa*), being intent upon shattering the course of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāravṛtta*); for thus he is etymologically defined in the scriptures by the venerable Bṛhaspati-pāda.
And because its essential nature has been explained according to its etymological meaning in the *Śivatanu*, it serves for the manifestation of one's own true nature, which consists of Bhairava.
It is thus taught that [this state] arises for those who possess devotion and whose wealth consists of inward-turned attention to this very reality.
And it has been said in the *Śrīmālinīvijaya*: "For one who thinks of nothing at all... [as the venerable teacher Abhinavaguptapāda has stated].
"For one who thinks of nothing" indicates the uselessness of conceptual constructions;
and thus, the instantaneous absorption into the object of knowledge is described.
He explains how that occurs: "By means of an exceedingly weighty Guru, through an awakening directed toward the object of knowledge, characterized by its sudden and full growth."

The suffix *tasi* is explained as having the sense of the third case (*tṛtīyārthe*), or alternatively, it is understood through grammatical non-co-referentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇyataḥ*). Furthermore, "possession" (*āveśa*) occurs for that which is not independent, due to the submergence of its own nature within that [other].
The primordial nature of Śambhu consists of that which is distinct from the object of cognition;
therefore, the meaning of the statement here is to be understood as follows: that which is to be known unfolds by itself.

"Without certainty, [the reflection] does not immediately remain— disregarding the Mother who is mirrored in the mirror of the Mother and displaying its own glory— until there is an excellence of purity in the heart, according to its degree. Thus, it is through being awakened by the Guru.
The immersion that arises is declared to be the Śāmbhava [state].

Thus [it is said]. For here, regarding the phrase "from awakening by the Guru" (*guruṇā pratibodhataḥ*), the meaning "from awakening by the Guru himself" (*gurutaḥ svasmāt pratibodhataḥ*) has been taught by the Gurus. This is also stated in the *Śrī-svacchanda*:
It has been said that the person who meditates upon the Bhairava form of the Self remains as nothing but that very essence, according to the analogy of the bhrāmara-kiṭa (the bee-worm).
His mantras become successful, O beautiful one, for him who is constantly disciplined.
Thus, for "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*) here means precisely the reflective awareness (*vimarśana*) of the state of the emergent subjectivity (*udyantṛtā*).
[The "being" of the emergent is "emergence"; its "state" is the agency of exertion.
And this occurs because, for one who is intent upon a single thought, there arises the emergence of another.
That, however, should be known as the opening of the eyes; one should perceive it by oneself.
This is what is included by this [verse]. || 5 ||

Thus, having demonstrated the absorption into Bhairava— which is the means for supporting the sudden emergence of the manifestation of the Other and which is the sole cause for the pacification of the bondage of ignorance— even the state of emergence (vyutthāna) possesses a tranquil appearance of duality due to the excellence of this reflective awareness [i.e., through the firmness of practice regarding the manifestation of the Other].
He says that it occurs thus:
"In the unification with the wheel of powers (śakticakra), there is the dissolution of the universe. (6)

This Bhairava, who has been described as having the nature of arising through the emergence of another's consciousness and being the self-rising subject—of Him alone, by virtue of His being both the internal object of focus and the external gaze, there is that which transcends the sequence and non-sequence of the entire wheel of powers (*śakticakra*).
Here, "sequence" (*krama*) refers to the nature of the manifestation and interruption of emission, maintenance, and withdrawal; "non-sequence" (*akrama*) is its transcendence.
The manifestation of these occurs simultaneously; thus, it pervades both sequence and non-sequence, being "that which pervades sequence and non-sequence.
As it is said in the *Jñānagarbha*:
"That which, through the interplay of its reliance upon the three sequences, is continuous..."

I place within my heart that supreme, divine Consciousness, which shines forth loftily while transcending the three sequences; she who, being the very embodiment of sequence, yet excels as the manifestation of the non-sequential.

The meaning is that although she manifests herself as the threefold sequence of emanation and so forth, by transcending that very sequence she shines forth; thus, the supreme, ineffable, and sovereign consciousness of the Lord, whose nature is both sequential and non-sequential, is here grasped. [She transcends...]

Even when described as being neither sequential nor non-sequential, nor possessing the nature of both, nor being empty, nor full— [that is, having the form of both the diminished and the complete]— she is of a different nature than these, the unsurpassed Supreme (Parā).

There exists a certain power of absolute freedom (*svātantrya-śakti*), by which— from the initial manifestation of the earth upon its own ground up to the final repose in the supreme subject— there occurs the expansion of the wheel of powers such as Emanation (*sṛṣṭi*) and the rest;
[the meaning is that this wheel of powers, beginning with Emanation, is in fact the very nature of the Supreme Power].
This play has been demonstrated. When there is that unification of this manifested wheel of powers (*śakticakra*)— according to the method taught in the secret traditions—

which consists of reflective awareness (*vimarśana*) in its appropriate sequence [wherein the sequence itself is contained within light and reflective awareness], there occurs the withdrawal of the universe, from the Fire of Time (*kālāgni*) up to the final digit (*kalā*).

The meaning is that even for that which exists as the body-self and as the external, there occurs its reduction to the fire of supreme consciousness (*parasaṃvid*). And it has been said in the *Śrībhargaśikhā*:
"Death, time, and the entire collection of creative powers (*kalākalāpa*),"
The web of transformations is the naturalization of practice.
22) It is the collection of conceptual constructions regarding unity and multiplicity—[the unity of distinct selves].
Then he swallows everything whole.
Thus it is said; and also in the *Śrīmad-vīrāvalī*:

"Wherein all the accumulations of principles (*tattvasaṃcaya*)—even as mere residual impressions (*saṃskāraśeṣatayā*)—dissolve; [the consciousness (*citi*) is the great cremation ground (*mahāśmaśāna*); therein the accumulations of principles go to dissolution and are consumed by fire]."
Behold that funeral pyre situated within the body, possessing a brilliance equal to the fire of time.
Thus it is said. Also in the *Śrīmanmālinīvijaya*:

"One should contemplate the reality devoid of utterance"—that is, the reality whose nature is the Supreme Speech (*parāvāk*), and for this very reason, it is beyond utterance; for the locus of utterance is indeed the *vaikharī* speech.
"Contemplating" means reflecting instantaneously, immediately after the manifestation of the object of experience within the wheel of powers (*śakticakra*).

The meaning is that the reflective awareness of such an object of knowledge is itself the Śākta means. [As it is said: "That immersion which one attains by contemplating with the mind alone is here designated as the Śākta."
By saying this, the very same point has been described through a different turn of phrase.

And this [knowledge], having reached the heart through the service of the feet of a true guru— as it has been said by someone that even the state of being knowable is attained— does not fail to take root there.
Are the words of instruction effective for those whose minds are utterly deluded?
Do the torrents of rain from the sky, even when clinging closely and without interval, impart any moisture to the petals of a lotus?

Therefore, this means reaches manifestation only through the service of a true guru; enough with this prolixity, which only yields exhaustion. By the phrase "reaches manifestation," nothing further has been disclosed [the meaning is that the contemplation of the wheel of powers (*śakticakra*) has not been revealed in greater detail].
23) This very [reality] is that which,
through its opening and closing...
Thus, when [the mind] is firmly established in one place...
This is summarized by the first and the last verses. (6)
For one who has thus withdrawn the universe, there is no distinction whatsoever between the emergence from and the state of meditative absorption; thus he says:
"The enjoyment of the Fourth State (turya) arises within the distinctions of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep. (7)

Regarding the fourth state (*turya*), which is characterized as "Bhairava is the exertion (*udyama*) within the manifold difference and distinct appearance of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep about to be examined immediately hereafter"— [that is, when its definition has been reflected upon]— and which consists of the vibration (*sphurattā*) that permeates all states:

The meaning is that for one who is joined with the aforementioned great yoga, the arising of whatever mental application (*ābhoga*) or wonder (*camatkāra*) occurs is always of the nature of the wonder of the Fourth State (*turya*). Some read "consciousness" (*saṃvit*) instead of "arising" (*saṃbhava*) here as "the consciousness of the application of the Fourth State" (*turyābhoga-saṃvit*), and they read *saṃvit* for the sake of clarity. And this...

Just as the moon— whether it resides in Avīci hell or in the abode of Śiva— suffers no interruption of its radiance and bliss because it consists of the enjoyment of the Fourth State (turyābhoga); and just as the moon gladdens the world through both its void and non-void aspects by gladdening all things with equanimity, so too does it gladden the world like the external moon.
The intended meaning here is simply this: [it is] clearly of the nature of the manifestation of its own essential form;
resembling a flower, it shines forth on all sides and, through a multitude of delights, gladdens the world in an instant.
In the same way, O Goddess, when the great yogin wanders the earth,
he illuminates the entire variegated universe with all the rays of the moon of knowledge.
"By means of this [practice], one should gladden everything all around, from Avīci up to Śiva," and so forth;

by such passages in the *Śrīcandrajñāna*, the state of being composed of the enjoyment of the Fourth State (*turyābhogamayatva*) for the great yogi at the beginning of the waking state and other stages is shown.
However, in the *Spanda*:
"Even amidst the distinctions of waking and so forth..."—
this is summarized by the verse [Kārikā 7].
He defines this triad beginning with waking by means of three aphorisms:
"Knowledge is waking. (8)
Dreams are conceptual constructions. || 9 ||
Non-discrimination is the state of deep sleep characterized by illusion. || 10 ||
The objects of all common experience are the domains of consciousness;

the state of waking and dreaming consists in a single jar becoming the object of valid cognition through both non-conceptual and conceptual awareness, while the state of deep sleep consists in the lack of recognition of its own nature regarding that very same object. But elsewhere...
The apprehension of objects by men through the senses is called waking;

that which consists of the recollection of objects by the mind without those [senses] is designated as dreaming; where neither the object nor the recollection exists, that is declared to be deep sleep.
Thus: for the world, cognition born of the external sense-faculties is the waking state (*jāgarāvasthā*). But those [cognitions] which are mental alone— (p.

The conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) whose objects are the unique meanings of the waking state—that itself is "dream" (*svapna*), the dream-state, because it is characterized primarily by such conceptual constructions. However, that which is non-discrimination (*aviveka*), the absence of discernment (*vivecanābhāva*), or non-apprehension (*akhyāti*)—this alone is the nature of *māyā*, consisting of delusion (*mohamaya*), namely the state of deep sleep (*sauṣupta*). This is mentioned incidentally while defining the state of deep sleep.
The essential nature of even this illusion (māyā) that is to be cut away has been stated: "But the essential nature of illusion is everywhere defined primarily as consisting of delusion.
And thus, by this definition, even in all three states beginning with waking, [it is present].

It has been shown that the three-fold nature [of valid cognition] exists. Thus, in this context, whatever non-conceptual (*avikalpaka*) cognition is appropriate for the state of dreaming is "waking"; however, those conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) therein are "dreaming.
Non-discrimination of reality is the "deep sleep" (*sauṣupta*) state. Although conceptual constructions are not consciously perceived in deep sleep, nevertheless—
When there is a desire to enter that state— that is, the desire to enter the state of deep sleep—

immediately thereafter, there exists a corresponding dream consisting of mental constructs and conceptualizations fashioned from latent impressions (saṃskāras), just as there is the appropriate waking cognition.

Furthermore, according to the intention of the *yogya*, first there is knowledge (*jñāna*) in the form of various *dhāraṇās*—that is, a stream of cognitions such as "I am air," "I am space," and so forth; this occurs during the waking state. Following that, there are conceptual constructions (*vikalpas*) in the form of a stream of those very cognitions.

26) Dream, as well as meditative absorption (*samādhi*) characterized by the lack of conscious awareness of the distinction between subject and object, is also shown by this method of expression to be the state of deep sleep (*sauṣupta*). For this very reason, in the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra*, [the nature] of waking and the other states...

The threefold nature [of each state] is produced by mutual interpenetration—there is the threefold nature in waking, the threefold nature in dreaming, and the threefold nature in deep sleep. This is the interpenetration: just as waking, dreaming, and deep sleep exist even within waking, so too do waking, dreaming, and deep sleep exist within dreaming, and waking, dreaming, and deep sleep exist within deep sleep; however—

The meaning is that they do not transcend the state of deep sleep (*suṣupta*); [this is said] even with reference to the capacity [of the senses]. "Awakened, and indeed awakened; fully awakened, and thoroughly awakened..."

By these and other verses beginning with "unawakened" (*abuddha*), the states of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the fourth (*turya*) are described; thus, their distinction has been defined. (8, 9, 10)
Thus, when the triad beginning with the waking state has been explained in accordance with worldly convention,

he for whom the nature of the fourth state (*turya*)— consisting of the enjoyment of that state and characterized by non-dual pervasion— shines forth through the withdrawal of the universe by means of the union with the wheel of powers (*śakticakra*), [proceeds] by ascending that stream.
Entering the previously mentioned consciousness that transcends the fourth (turyātīta), he is the Lord of Heroes (vīreśa), the enjoyer of the triad. || 11 ||

He who, through the method of contemplating the wheel of powers (*śakticakra*), perceives these three states— waking and the rest— as permeated by the bliss of the fourth (*turyānanda*), and who, by the excellence of his entry into that supreme awareness, sees them as consisting solely of a flow of the essence of bliss with the latent impressions of duality dissolved, is the enjoyer and the one who experiences wonder regarding this triad.
p.
27) For that very reason, he who perceives the dyad of the grasped and the grasper within the three states, such as waking and the rest—

The meaning is that even one who is devoted to enjoyments is not smeared by karmas, like a lotus leaf situated in water. That person who knows both that which is proclaimed as the object of enjoyment and the enjoyer among the abodes, is not smeared while experiencing [those objects].

According to this principle, he— this Lord and Master of the senses of the heroes who are intent on devouring the distinctions of phenomenal existence, who possesses an empire over himself free from rivals, and who is filled with supreme bliss—
having entered the reality of the venerable Manthānabhairava, churns each and every object of knowledge so that it is dissolved within his own self.
Having formed [the mass] and having gathered it together, he causes it to arise; thus, the one designated as *manthāna* (the churner) is *Svacchandabhairava*.

This is what is stated in the *Mahāmnāyas*. However, he who is not of such a nature is merely a worldly *paśu* (bound soul), being experienced through states such as waking and so forth. Even a *yogin*, in this regard...
It has been stated that Vīreśvara did not ascend the *dhārāmaṇḍala*, but was indeed a fool; as they say:
"If liberation for a person were to occur through the power of departing the body (*utkrānti*) without the experience of one's own true nature (*svabhāva*)," [it would be so].
Even in this view, one might object: "Surely that deluded person who commits suicide by hanging would be a partaker of liberation?"
Likewise,
even those in the Videha state are bound at the time of dissolution due to being perfumed by the qualities;
yet embodied beings are liberated by taking refuge in pure knowledge.

Through the immersion in the cultivation of these two types of meditative concentration— either that "this entire world resides within me, who am the womb of gnosis," or that "I reside everywhere"— [one attains stability].
"By worshipping you, men whose afflictions and calamities have been shattered shall before long attain the status of lords over the three worlds. Thus it is said.
And this the yogin [performs] by means of the yoga of free will (*svacchanda-yoga*), which moves with a free course [and consists in abiding in the activity of the supreme reality,
being established in one's own self through a movement of free will].

He who necessarily moves as this Great Yoga, which is denoted by the term *Svacchanda* because it consists of the realization of identity with the Supreme Reality— being joined to and absorbed in the station, the abode of Śrī Svacchandabhairava— he attains equality with Him.
Engaged in the state of Svachchanda, he shall attain equality with Svachchanda.

This has been demonstrated in detail in the *Śrī-svacchanda* and other scriptures by such passages as these. In the *Spanda* [Kārikā] as well, there is the perception of that [reality]—that is, the knowledge of that reality—which is constant across all states, as stated in the *Jñānagarbha*: [text follows].
O Mother Caṇḍikā, whichever of the fourteen paths one may travel— whether it be the external organs, the intellect, the ego, the mind, or the suṣumnā—
that particular portion of the Self (kalā) becomes of such a nature as to reach the abode of Śiva.
Ah, she who arises tenfold is difficult to find in the world, even by the gods!

Thus: "The abode of Śiva" means the dwelling place or support of Śiva, who is the object of knowledge (*vedya*). It is "constantly non-deviating from the three states," meaning that it does not deviate from its nature as the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*) throughout the three states of waking and so forth;
however, in the fourth state (*turya*), it is indeed free from error. And it has been said:
"There is no state whatsoever in which consciousness does not exist;
therefore, yogis worship you as the very mass of consciousness (*ciddhana*).
This is summarized by the verse. (11)

29) Are there for this great yogin certain stages (*bhūmikā*) of ascent toward reality (*tattva*), which are the stations (*sthāna*) by means of which the station situated above the thirty-six principles (*tattva*) is characterized?

[This is the meaning of the sentence: Are there stages (*bhūmikā*)? By which stages is the level situated above reality (*tattva*) indicated? He says: "There are; the stages of yoga are marvelous. (12)

Just as someone experiences wonder upon seeing an object of extraordinary excellence, so it is for this great yogin during his constant engagement with the manifestation and reflective awareness of various objects of knowledge— that is, during the savoring of these very forms and his resting in the universal I-consciousness.

For one whose entire wheel of the senses is smilingly serene and blossomed through the power of immersion into one’s own Self— which is a mass of consciousness consisting of ever-new wonders and unsurpassed excellence—
the wonder that arises within the Self, which is uninterrupted bliss, is characterized as "smilingly serene" (meaning: motionless with astonishment).

The state of being repeatedly filled with wonder due to a lack of satiety constitutes those very stages (*bhūmikās*) pertaining to yoga—the identity with the supreme reality (*paratattva*). These are limited stages that indicate the ascent toward and rest within that [reality], and not the functional experiences of the *kanda*, *bindu*, and so forth. [The *kanda* is the *mūlādhāra*.]
The *bindu* is the location between the eyebrows. As it is said in the *Śrīkulayukti* (p.
"When the Self is known by the practitioners through the Self..."
Then, indeed, one perceives wonder within oneself by means of the self alone.
Thus,
for one who observes that very nature as being the presiding subject and remains,
as it were, smiling, from where could such a false construction arise?
Thus it is summarized by this verse. || 12 ||
For this yogin who has attained such a stage of yoga— [for the yogin who has reached such a stage]—
the power of will is Umā Kumārī. || 13 ||
The will of the yogin who has attained the state of Supreme Bhairava is that very power,

Umā, who is the supreme consort of the Lord (Pārameśvarī) and whose nature is absolute freedom (svātantrya). She is the Virgin (Kumārī), intent on the play of the emanation and reabsorption of the universe,
according to the reading "kumāra krīḍāyām" [she plays with the youth].

Moreover, she is of a nature that slays the ground of illusion (*māyābhūmi*) which gives rise to duality, rendering its expansion unmanifest; and she is a maiden (*kumārī*), not yet enjoyed by others, throbbing with the intention: "When shall I obtain a husband through my own agency as an enjoyer? (*bhoktrikātmyena*).

Or else, just as Umā—the daughter of the mountain, Pārvatī—is a maiden who has abandoned all attachments and is constantly engaged in the practice and worship for the sake of attaining identity with Maheśvara. (p. 31)

In the same way, our teachers have seen and explained the reading exactly as "tathaiva asyecchā" (and her will is likewise). Others, however, having read "śaktitamā" [the power of will is the supreme power; she is the maiden], have explained that this excellence belongs to the power of will in relation to knowledge and action.

Thus, unlike worldly beings, this yogin’s will is not gross, but is indeed the supreme power (*parā-śakti*) itself, unimpeded everywhere. As it is said in the venerable *Svacchanda*: "That Māyā which arises from yoga through identity with the supreme reality—that which conceals its own nature—is veiled by that [power]."

The meaning is that she remains with her supreme form concealed by the manifold expansion of names and forms belonging to all the goddesses. Furthermore, having descended into the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), this power of the Lord (bhagavacchakti) remains assuming the state of a maiden (kumārītva), because she is not to be enjoyed by others; and such is she.

She nurtures the worlds and brings them to fruition with their desired fruits; the Goddess exists through the names and forms of all goddesses, concealed by her yogic power (yogamāyā), a maiden who brings the worlds into being.
Thus, in the *Śrīmṛtyuñjayabhaṭṭāraka* as well, it is said:

"That supreme power of mine, which is my will, is inseparable. This means that this aforementioned vitality (*vīrya*) which has become such is my own supreme power, having attained the nature of will; what kind of power is it? It is "born of its own nature" (*svabhāvajā*).

"Co-emergent" (*sahajā*) means endowed with power (*śaktiyuktā*), which is to say, it is the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) that is non-different from all the powers of the universe contained within it;

by the word "inherent" (*svabhāvajā*), he clarifies this, and by "of fire" (*vahneḥ*) and "endowed with power," he makes it manifest. By the word "of all" (*sarvasya*), he indicates that it is the causal, creative power belonging to itself—connected to its own nature of consciousness-bliss—and not [something else].

"They are distinct," says Kṣemarāja; having cited alternative readings such as "endowed with power" (*śaktiyuktā*) and "her own power" (*svā śaktiḥ*), he explains [the verse]. [It is] born of its own nature.
It should be understood as being like the heat of fire, or like the rays of the sun.
"Or rather, that power which is causal in nature belongs to the entire world. This [power],
however, does not function as an impeller by means of a desire to move.
Moreover, through contact with the power of the Self, a person may become equal to that.
Thus it has been demonstrated by means of this verse in its particular manner. || 13 ||
For such a great-souled yogin—[the meaning is that for the yogin of great aspiration]—the visible body is [his own body, which is like his own limb]. || 14 ||
Whatever is perceived, whether external or internal, all that he perceives as "I am this"—

the universe as if it were his own limb— since, according to the principle to be stated later, "The universe is the accumulation of his own power," it is not distinct from his own essential nature. [Thus, for him, nothing else] shines forth.
By way of distinction:

the body—consisting of the physical form, intellect, vital breath, and the void—is an object of perception like blue and other such objects; it does not appear as a perceiver, as in the case of a bound soul (paśu). [The sense of "I" in the body is not true subjectivity.]
Thus, both within the body and externally, his realization is everywhere undivided, like the fluid of a peacock's egg.
As it is said in the *Śrīvijñānabhairava* (p. 33): [Realization is knowledge.]

Just as waves belong to water and the flickering of flames to fire, so too the universe—which is like a wave belonging to the Lord, the conscious Self who is like the ocean—appears as if divided though it is non-different from Him; one should meditate that it undergoes its rise and fall right there within Him. This is the implied sense. The radiance belongs to the sun.
These various manifestations of the universe have emerged from me alone, Bhairava.
Thus it is said.

And this very [consciousness] exists always and everywhere as the object of enjoyment (*bhogya*) for the subject (*bhoktṛ*). For that which is called the "object of enjoyment" is termed the "object of knowledge" (*prameya*); and since the object of knowledge exists as a subordinate element to the subject, it does not exceed the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). And that...

An object of enjoyment (*bhogya*) of this kind cannot, in reality, exist apart from the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*), because all things ultimately rest within the subject alone; therefore, the essential point is that the enjoyer alone manifests in the form of both [the subject and the object].
This is what is included by this [verse]. || 14 ||

As for this statement that the manifestation of everything visible is of a single nature—both as the body of all that is seen and as the visibility of the void—that is not difficult to establish; rather:
"Through the friction of the mind within the heart, there is the vision of the visible world as one's own self. (15)

Because it is the locus of the foundation of the universe, the light of consciousness (*citprakāśa*) is the heart (*hṛdaya*). Therein, due to the "clashing" (*saṃghaṭṭa*) of the mind—that is, the "clashing on all sides" (*samantād ghaṭanāt*), which is the cultivation of one-pointedness of the moving mind—consciousness itself, when possessed of contraction, is designated by the word "mind" (*citta*). Having completely set aside the multitude of objects within that light of consciousness, [one should remain].

The meaning of the sentence is "the state of complete absorption. Through the cultivation of one-pointedness toward that very [object], there occurs the sleep of the visible object—which consists of the blue body, the vital breath, and the intellect—as it moves and moves.
Furthermore, this vision of emptiness— which is of the nature of the absence [of blue and so forth]—
is a manifestation that accords with reality as it is, appearing as if it were one's own limb, by means of having abandoned the distinction between subject and object.
For the mind, when it becomes absorbed in the luminosity of consciousness (*cit*), perceives the entire universe as permeated by that very luminosity.

This has been stated in the *Śrīvijñānabhairava*: "When the object of knowledge is the consciousness-principle (*cit-tattva*) within the space of the heart, one whose senses and intellect are held steady, standing between the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the object of knowledge (*prameya*), attains sovereignty (*svātantrya*), which is the meaning of 'good fortune' (*saubhāgya*). Alternatively:

Having entered through meditative cultivation into the center of the union of the upper and lower lotuses, his senses are dissolved; thus, he is one whose eyes and the entire circle of other sense organs have merged into the space of the heart by means of that [central channel].
He is "one with dissolved senses," situated within the center of the lotus-casket.
With a mind focused on nothing else, O fortunate one, he shall attain supreme good fortune.

Thus it is said. For here, the supreme good fortune is the attainment of the state of the Lord of the Universe (*Viśveśvara*). With reference to the great yogin who has entered into the activity of the true reality (*tattva-vṛtti*), it is also stated in the venerable *Svacchanda-tantra*:
"And he—[meaning] he alone who has attained supreme *sāmarasya*—[perceives] the immobile, the insentient, and the mobile..."

And "with consciousness"—thus, in brief, it exists in two ways, pervading the sixfold path (adhvan). For the path consists of six aspects in the form of the signified (vācya) and the signifier (vācaka), existing within all fourteen categories of beings, such as the divine origins;
within all entities, such as the qualities (dharma) and so forth; within principles (tattva), such as the earth and so forth; and within the instruments of experience, such as jars and so forth.
Abiding in a state of aesthetic identity (*sāmarasya*) within the instruments of action, one remains with the immersion into Supreme Bhairava (*parabhairava-samāpatti*) undiminished in all states.
This very state, consisting of samādhi without emergence, is the great secret. [It exists] in all beings, in the categories of existence, and in the senses.
Whatever exists, whether stationary or moving, sentient or insentient.
"Pervading the entire path, he abides in a state of equilibrium.
35) Thus, here is the observed proof:

"Just as a person perceives the itching of his own body, so too does he who is of the nature of the Supreme Brahman perceive the activity of the entire universe. [Thus it is said. In the *Spanda*, however, it is stated that by presiding over one's own self, this will occur everywhere in such a manner.
By this very [statement], this has been included. || 15 ||
Right here, he states another means:
"Or, through union with the pure reality (śuddhatattva), the power [of the soul] becomes non-bound (apaśu). (16)
"Pure" (*śuddha*): according to the perspective of the secret tradition (*rahasyāmnāya*), "above *māyā* is *mahāmāyā*";

thus, because the power of *māyā* has pervaded everywhere, the pure reality (*tattva*) is indeed that which is called Paramaśiva. In this context, the designation of the reality is made with respect to those who are to be instructed. The reality (*tattva*).

When he contemplates the universe there as being called Paramaśiva— [reflecting that "this universe is indeed composed of Śiva"] and realizes "this is identical with Him"— then, being one whose binding power known as *paśutva* (the state of being a bound soul) no longer exists, he becomes the Lord of the entire world, just like Sadāśiva.
Thus it has been stated in the venerable *Lakṣmīkaulārṇava* regarding the perfection of initiation: "The signs (*pratyaya*) that have been described as preceded by *stobha*—
where 'signs' refers to the cognitions of objects obstructed by distance, such as location, and 'stobha' refers to the veiling of the principle of consciousness (*cittattva*).”

O Goddess, even a sixteenth part of *saṃdhāna*— which is the discernment of the pure reality— is not equal to the manifestation of sovereignty, because that [latter state] is beset by obstacles to its stages;
indeed, O Goddess, they do not merit even a sixteenth part of *saṃdhāna* itself.
Thus it is said. In the *Śrīvijñānabhairava*, however,
it is stated that "everything— from the soles of the feet to the tips of the hair, the entire body part by part— is simultaneously of the nature of consciousness alone."
One should contemplate that the world, whether manifesting sequentially or through the pervasion of the wonder of consciousness, shines both internally and externally as nothing other than Light;

for according to the principle that "otherwise, its status as an object of cognition would be untenable," it is Light itself that shines. Indeed, one should contemplate the body as consisting of consciousness, or the world as such.
The supreme arising occurs simultaneously through the non-conceptual mind.
Thus:
"He whose consciousness perceives this entire world as a play—seeing it thus and being constantly disciplined—he is liberated while living; of this there is no doubt."
Thus it is summarized by this verse. || 16 ||
For this yogin whose nature is such knowledge, vitarka is self-knowledge. || 17 ||

The reflective inquiry (*vitarka*) and discernment (*vicāra*) that "I am indeed Śiva, the soul of all"—this alone is his knowledge of the Self (*ātmajñāna*). As it is said in the venerable *Vijñānabhairava*: "The Supreme Lord is omniscient, the creator of all, and all-pervasive."

"By the firm conviction, 'I am that very one who possesses the Śaiva dharma,' one becomes Śiva. [The Śaiva dharma belongs to Śiva; it consists of pure autonomy and so forth. By contemplating with certainty, 'I am that very one, and that very one is I,' this state of Śiva-hood is the ground of Śakti. "
Thus, in the *Spanda* as well...
this very [is] the grasping of the Self. (p.
By this, the following is stated: for in that context, "graha" (seizing) refers to the grasping of the Self, which is knowledge;
and this very meaning—that non-difference from Śiva, who is the Self of the universe—is also intended here. || 17 ||
Furthermore, for him, the bliss of concentration is the joy of the world. || 18 ||
That which is perceived is the "world" (*loka*), namely the collection of objects; and that which perceives is also the "world," namely the class of subjects.

While this [world]—the collection of subject and object imagined by the common world—manifests, the bliss of the yogin, arising from the absence of conceptual constructions such as "I" and "this," is itself the bliss of meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
Since both sides are unchanging and identical to the plumage of a blue jay,
how can there be the conceptualization that "the yogi is inward-facing" or "he is outward-facing"?

The meaning is: when there exists the object which is one's own essential nature, free from the modifications of the "I" and "this" portions, there occurs for all embodied beings a common perception of the grasped and the grasper;
however, this is the distinction for yogins regarding that connection—[for all embodied beings, that is, for all subjects].
The cognition of the object, the subject, and the act of cognition is without distinction; however, for yogins,

there is in that state a state of composure (*samādhānatā*), which consists in not forgetting the true nature of the cognizer (*pramātṛ*) as it penetrates the initial, middle, and final stages— this is attentiveness (*sāvadhānatā*).

Thus, according to the principle established by the venerable Vijñānabhaṭṭāraka, that bliss which consists of aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*)— culminating in the attentive repose within the state of the subject (*pramātṛpada*)— is precisely his "bliss of samādhi" (*samādhisukha*). This has been stated in that very same work:

One should contemplate everything as filled with one's own bliss—that is, everything as filled with the nectar of one's own bliss and full of the joy of one's own consciousness, having abandoned the self-bliss derived from sense objects. In this regard, the manifestation of the world—even though it consists of the congealed essence of consciousness—is more conducive to the practice than other forms of concentration (*dhāraṇā*). Thus, one should contemplate either the world or one's own body.
One should remember [the deity] filled with one's own bliss;
simultaneously, by means of that very nectar of one's own, one becomes composed of supreme bliss.
p. 38) Thus it is said. And this very thing is the attainment of immortality (amṛtaprāpti). ... [omission] ... .
This is what is summarized by this [verse].

Furthermore, that very bliss of meditative absorption (samādhisukha) belonging to him who delights in his own self— that same bliss of absorption consisting of one's own bliss (svānandamaya), which is the object of the yogi’s own experience— is of such a nature.

For those worlds who behold it, by means of the method of the transmission of bliss, it results in the manifestation of their own bliss; that is to say, it causes them to reach their conclusion (paryavasyati), it brings them to rest, and it impels them toward that state.
The meaning is that it grants repose in the manifestation of their own bliss for them. This too—
This is in perfect agreement with the previously cited *Śrīcandrajñānagrantha* (p. 23, sūtra 7). 18.

Now, he demonstrates the yoga of power (*vibhūtiyoga*)—the capacity of such a yogin to accomplish various desired manifestations through powers such as *aṇimā* and so forth: "Upon the concentration of power, there is the production of a body. (19)

When he firmly contemplates that very power of his which was described by the aphorism "Desire, Power, Umā, Kumārī" (1-13)— [which is a synonym for Rudra’s power]— and becomes one with it, then, by virtue of that, [he attains the state of Rudra].
A body arises for him according to his desire. As it is said in the venerable *Mṛtyuñjayabhaṭṭāraka*:
"From that, power proceeds—devoid of an object [or devoid of an object of cognition], free from the knowable, consisting of supreme vibration."

The Supreme Power (Parāśakti), who is the Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā) from whom all great illusions arise, is she from whom disease has departed. From that very abode of the End of the Twelve (Dvādaśānta), she proceeds and unfolds as Will (Icchā)—
for that Will is taught to be of the nature of Knowledge (Jñāna) and the essence of Action (Kriyā).
Having begun thus:
"That womb (yoni) of all the gods and also of the powers (śaktis) is manifold;
the womb consists of Agni and Soma, and within it [resides] that [state] of the yogi who has attained non-difference from the supreme reality..."

That Supreme Power (parāśakti) is said to be "unfolding" (unmiṣantī), because she is the womb consisting of fire and moon for all the deities— Anāśrita, Sadāśiva, Īśvara, Ananta, Rudra, and the rest— as well as for their powers such as Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and the others, and for Brāhmī and the rest; it is from her alone that they arise.

Since everything proceeds from her who is primarily characterized by *soma*, for that very reason the universe—whose primordial nature consists of *agni* and *soma*—is as if composed of *agni* and *soma*. Thus, those who know the truth say that even fire gladdens and even snow burns; in this way, the power (*śakti*) is shown to possess the capacity for creation, maintenance, and destruction. [It] proceeds.
Thus [it is said]. Regarding the greatness of the concentration of power (*śakti-saṃdhāna*), it is stated in the *Lakṣmīkaulārṇava*:

"Even if the production of a body according to one's desire is observed through mantras and other means, nevertheless, it is not natural because it is subject to deviation due to its artificiality. Therefore, only the concentration [of power] is [the cause] for the production of another body."
[The meaning is "the cause. Without the *saṃdhāna*, there is no initiation (*dīkṣā*), nor is there the accomplishment of the supernatural powers (*siddhi*);
likewise, there is no mantra, no application of mantras, and no attraction through yoga.
This has been established by such passages as:
"And thus, the Creator, when requested according to one's desire, [bestows] objects that reside in the heart of the waking person" (p. 40).
Having brought about the rising of the moon and the sun, he brings about [liberation] for embodied beings [those possessing identification with the body].

This is what is summarized by the following: For the embodied yogi who has not yet abandoned the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the body, the Sustainer, Maheśvara, reveals the objects residing within his heart— objects consisting of various unprecedented creations and so forth— by means of the unfolding of the vehicle of the forms of the Moon and Sun, which is the nature of Light and Bliss [through the expansion of *prāṇa* and *apāna*].

The meaning of this is as follows: having brought about the emergence of Power— which consists of the state of equilibrium between the Moon and the Sun, and which is of an equal energy, consisting of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and pervading the body— one attains it by means of its outward flow and thereby accomplishes the goal.
"Likewise, even in a dream, [one attains] desired objects..."—
I have demonstrated in the *Spandanirṇaya* that this independence of the dream state, as set forth in this verse, has been applied as an illustrative example. 19.
He states that other accomplishments (siddhis) desired by him also come to pass through this very majesty:
"The conjunction of beings, the separation of beings, and the union with the universe. (20)

The *bhūtas* consist of the body, the vital breaths, the states of being, and so forth; their "reconnection" (*saṃdhāna*)— that is, their nourishment (*paripoṣaṇa*)— occurs in certain instances, such as during replenishment, or during the subsiding of diseases and the like.
