Separation (*pṛthaktvam*) is the disjunction of the body and so forth from afflictions such as disease; and [the sense is that] because of the presence of His penetration (*āveśa*)— He being eternal, all-pervading, and independent— nothing whatsoever is obstructed by space, time, or other such distances for the entire universe.
The "impact" (*saṃghaṭṭa*)—consisting of being made an object of knowledge and so forth—arises when there is the aforementioned conjunction of powers (*śakti*).
This is present in all the scriptures within the sections on spiritual practice (*sādhana*). That very same [impact] is described in the *Spanda* [Kārikās]:
even one who is weak—that is, one whose vital constituents (*dhātu*) are diminished—even for such a person, the cessation of hunger is that reality of *spanda*.

The meaning is that it is reckoned among the supernatural powers (siddhis). Since, having mastered that, one proceeds to action, one should likewise conceal one's hunger, even if one is extremely hungry.
Thus:

"Languor (glāni) is that which robs the body; its course proceeds from ignorance (ajñāna). That ignorance is destroyed by the unfolding of that [consciousness]; for languor is that [state], and ignorance is indeed its cause. And therefore:
For yogins, there is an absence of wrinkles, gray hair, and so forth, as well as firmness of the body. [The root text reads: "Lassitude is a destroyer of the body.
If that were so, from what could it arise if it were causeless?
Thus:
for just as an object that was seen indistinctly, even when the mind was attentive,
shines forth with even greater clarity when cultivated by the exertion of its own power.
The exertion of the power of consciousness.

p. 42) Likewise, by that power of consciousness and effort [expressed as "so be it"], whatever object exists in its own specific form, characterized by particular place and time— that object, for a person who relies upon the power of consciousness, [is realized] quickly.

"It occurs to me. Therefore, the sense here is that it is not difficult for an object separated by space and time to become an object of cognition. Whatever exists in its ultimate reality, by whatever means, in whatever place, and in whatever manner—that very thing proceeds forth without delay, having overcome [all obstacles] through power.
By these and other such statements, the manifestation of power (*vibhūti*) has been demonstrated along with its logical justification in the *Spanda* [Kārikās]. || 20 ||

But when, not desiring limited accomplishment, he desires the manifestation of the universal Self, then for him—due to the arising of Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā)—there is the attainment of mastery over the wheel (cakreśatva). || 21 ||

When, out of a desire for the manifestation of his universal self-nature (*vaiśvātmya*), he concentrates his power (*śakti*), then, through the arising of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*)— in the form of "I am indeed all"— his sovereignty (*māheśvarya*) is accomplished, consisting in his lordship over the wheel of his own powers which constitute the universe. As it is said in the *Svacchanda*:

Therefore, that supreme knowledge (parā vidyā), which exists above the reality of the Self (ātmatattva) that culminates in Māyā, does not exist as something other than this [knowledge], because by means of this very [knowledge] the entire universe is encompassed. This is the meaning of the term "other" (anyā)— that it is not "other" (aparā) in such a manner.

For here, the best of yogis simultaneously attains the supreme qualities such as omniscience; since he attains these [supreme qualities]—meaning omniscience and so forth in their non-dual form—simultaneously here in the *unmanā* state, this is the *parā* (supreme) Vidyā, according to the meaning of the verbal root *vid*, "to obtain. As they say:
O knowers of the ritual, the omniscience, contentment, beginningless awakening, sovereignty, eternal undiminished power, and infinite power belong to the All-pervading Lord.
"They say there are six limbs of Maheśvara. Thus [it is said].
p.
43) Regarding the "feeling" (*vedanā*) of the beginningless reality (*anādidharma*): its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is the essence of independent power (*svātantrya-śakti*).
Its "feeling" is the investigation (*vicāraṇā*), which is the awakening to that which belongs to the self—namely, its state as the Supreme Self (*paramātmatva*), which is the form of Śiva.
Precisely for this reason, since it is not the non-Self and does not have that as its object, this exclusion is established;

therefore, because it conforms to the meanings of the verbal roots *vida* (to investigate) and *vida* (to know), this is called "knowledge" (*vidyā*), according to the venerable Kṣemarāja. It is the awakening to the state of the Supreme Self.
Because it consists in the supreme self through the avoidance [of the unreal], it is therefore called "knowledge" (vidyā).
Abiding there— in that state known as *unmanā*, which is the Vidyā— one should manifest, unveil,

and recognize one's own light (*tejas*), the consciousness-light (*cij-jyotiḥ*) that is supreme, uncontracted, the ultimate cause, and the very nature of Paramaśiva; and thus one shall attain the state of Śiva, reaching identity with Him.
The venerable Kṣemarāja says: One should manifest the supreme light, the ultimate cause;
when that supreme light is manifested, one abiding therein attains the state of Śiva.
Thus,
when it remains pervading all objects as if out of a desire to see them, then what is the use of much speaking? One will understand it by oneself.
This is included by this very [statement]. || 21 ||
But when he desires only the state of delighting in his own self—[he who delights completely (ā) within his own self (svātman) is "one who delights in his own self" (svātmārāmaḥ)]—then for him:
From the continuous connection with the great lake, there is the experience of the potency of the mantra. || 22 ||
The supreme Bhaṭṭārikā is Consciousness (*saṃvit*), who emits the entire universe—beginning with the power of Will (*icchāśakti*) and extending to the gross objects of knowledge (*sthūlameya*).
She is characterized by her role as the initiator of the flow of all things, such as the *khecarīcakra*, and by her transparency and non-obstruction;
for she initiates the flow of the entire movement of the *khecarī*, *gocarī*, and other powers, and possesses the capacity to sustain the reflection of the universe.
Because it is transparent, capable of receiving reflections, unobstructed by the universe, and profound due to its difficulty of being perceived,

consciousness is compared to a great lake. By means of its continuous contemplation— through inward-turnedness and the constant reflective awareness of identity with that [consciousness]— of what is about to be described...
Of that which consists of the reflective awareness of the supreme I-consciousness (parāhaṃtā), whose nature is the expansion of the mass of sounds—
[where "mass" refers to the causal state, the undivided nature of those gross sounds divided into the forms of words, sentences, and so forth;
and "expansion" means the agency of manifestation upon its own ground in the form of various reflective awarenesses].

"the desire to manifest the state of universal form. This is the experience of the potency of mantra—the manifestation as the nature of one's own self of the Great Mantra, which constitutes the potency of all mantras, namely the Full I-consciousness (*pūrṇāhaṃtā*).
For this very reason, it is stated in the *Śrīmālinīvijaya*:
Beginning with the words, "That power of the Creator of the World...
[it continues] by way of the fiftyfold forms headed by Will (icchā) and so forth [in the form of the fifty phonemes from A to Kṣa].
p.

45) The Supreme Power (parāśakti), which is undisturbed and not distinct from that [Supreme Subject] because it is inseparable from the nature of Mātṛkā and Mālinī, remains unknown to bound souls (paśus) as the source of all mantras and vidyās.

She is called *mātṛkā*. When agitated within the wombs of the seed-syllables (*bīja*) through the state of mutual fusion resulting from their reciprocal friction, she—consisting of the forms from *na* to *pha*—is designated as *Mālinī*. This means she "bears" (*malate*) the universe like a mirror within herself;

thus, her meaning is that she possesses the nature of the entire universe. Having thus demonstrated that [the alphabet] consists of the entirety of the universe, [the author proceeds] from that very source...

The extraction of the mantra has been shown; thus, the Supreme Śakti herself is the Great Lake (*mahāhrada*). From that, through its contemplation—[contemplation being reflective awareness (*vimarśana*)]—the Mātṛkā arises. Having seized her power, the mantras... [proceed].
This has been established through such figurative expressions as those cited above.

Thus, beginning with the statement "Consciousness is the Self" (1.1), it is shown that [the world] consists of the non-manifestation of that [Self], which is itself composed of the non-manifestation of consciousness, as manifested by its own sovereignty.

The meaning is that it is the very nature of the *āṇavamala* (the impurity of individuality). The realization of Bhairava, which consists of the aforementioned effort (*udyama*), pacifies every form of bondage and transforms the entire universe into the nectar of its own bliss; furthermore, it bestows all supernatural powers (*siddhis*), up to and including the penetration of the potency of mantras.

Thus, this first unfolding (unmeṣa) has been described as consisting of the manifestation of the Śāmbhava means—[Śāmbhava being that which arises in Śambhu, whose nature is light, or that which comes from Him]. Here, however, the nature of Śakti is described in the middle; that belongs to the form of the Śāmbhava.
With the intention of demonstrating the possession of power— [the possession of power is the essence of sovereignty]— thus says Śiva: || 22 ||
Thus ends the first unfolding (unmeṣa) of the [work] titled [the name of the work], by the disciple of the venerable Mahāmāheśvara Ācārya Abhinavaguptapāda’s lotus feet. 1.
Śivasūtravimarśinī | Now begins the second unfolding (unmeṣa).

Now the *śāktopāya* (the means of power) is demonstrated. In this regard, *śakti* is the supreme power of consciousness (*parā saṃvicchakti*), which is the fullness of the I-consciousness (*pūrṇāhantā*) and whose nature is the agency of the manifestation of the universe. Having first analyzed its essential nature—which was sown as a thread within the final *unmeṣa* (opening) of the first chapter as being "the expansion of the potency of mantra" (*mantravīryasphārarūpā*)—we shall now begin another *unmeṣa*.
The mind is the mantra. || 1 ||
It is called *citta* because by means of it the supreme reality (*paraṃ tattvam*) is perceived (*cetita*) and reflected upon (*vimṛśyate*).
It is defined as such through its etymological derivation from the two roots *cit*, meaning "to protect" (*pālane*), and *trai*, meaning "to protect.
It is called *mantra* because the nature of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvararūpa*) is protected (*gupta*) and reflected upon within (*antar*) without differentiation by means of it.

For this very reason, its nature is defined as consisting of the act of reflection (*manana*), which is essentially the vibration of the Supreme, and its nature is also defined as protection (*trāṇa*), which consists in the pacification of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) composed of duality.
Furthermore, by virtue of being intent upon the contemplation (*vimarśa*) of the deity of the mantra, it has attained that [state].

p. 48) *Marasyam* [is the attainment of oneness with the presiding deities of the mantras]. The mantra is indeed the mind of the worshipper itself, and not merely a collection of various phonemes. As it has been said:
In the illustrious Sarvajñānottara,
those who do not recognize the mantras as they are being recited are deluded gods and Gandharvas, arrogant due to their false knowledge.
Thus, it is stated in the *Śrītantrasadbhāva* as well:

"That which is remembered as the imperishable power (*śakti*) that constitutes the very life of mantras is consciousness-power (*saṃvit-śakti*), whose nature is the reflective awareness of the full 'I' (*pūrṇāhaṃ-vimarśana*)."
Deprived of her, O lady of beautiful hips, they are as fruitless as autumn clouds.
Thus [it is said]. However, in the *Śrī-Śrīkaṇṭhīya-saṃhitā*, it is stated: "A separate mantra and a separate practitioner never achieve success;
all this has its root in knowledge, otherwise it is not successful at all."

Due to the metaphorical identification of the signified and the signifier, the mantra is the deity of the mantra. Thus, regarding the practitioner, the mantra, and the deity, a cognition that perceives them as distinct—as the worshipped and the worshipper—does not attain accomplishment.
However, because they possess the nature of protecting through contemplation (*manana-trāṇa*), mantras abide within the power of gnosis (*jñāna-śakti*).

The meaning is that, having attained the great heroism consisting of the power of knowledge, they become bestowers of all accomplishments (siddhis) and capable of accomplishing their respective specific tasks.
Thus it has been said. And this is stated in the *Spanda*: "Together with the mind of the worshipper, these possess the nature of Śiva.
This means that those mantras possess the quality (*dharma*) of Śiva—the Supreme Lord—which consists of attributes such as omniscience that are not shared by others.
The meaning is that they consist of the nature of reflection and protection, and their essential form is non-different from Śiva.
Thus it has been demonstrated by way of this figurative expression. || 1 ||
And for this [cognition], effort is the means of accomplishment. (2)

49) Of the mantra of the aforementioned form, that which consists of the effort to sustain the first unfolding of the desire to synthesize (*anusaṃdhitsā*)—[wherein "the desire to synthesize" (*anusaṃdhitsā*) is the wish to synthesize; of that, the first [moment] occurs when the supreme manifestation emerges]...

Cessation (*nirodha*) therein has the nature of exertion (*prayatana*). That exertion which is uncreated (*akṛtaka*) is itself the means of accomplishment (*sādhaka*), bestowing upon the practitioner identity with the deity of the mantra. As it is said in the *Śrītantrasadbhāva*:
"O Dear One, just as a bird perched on its own body perceives its prey..."
One should attract it swiftly, indeed with innate speed.

In that very same way, the lord of yogis should draw back both the mind and the *bindu*. (The verb "should draw back" is a transitive action word. The *bindu* is the nature of undivided light. As it has been said:
"When the power of action has arisen in the abode of the Moon, Sun, and Fire...")
"That light which is indivisible is indeed our supreme *bindu*.
Just as an arrow resting upon a bow flies forth when struck with effort, so too does [the soul].
Likewise, O lady of excellent hips, the drop (bindu) runs forth by means of the upward movement alone.
Thus it is said. Elsewhere also, the apprehension of that [is the very essence of the mantra; the meaning is that it is the power of the mantra].
The essence of the mantra is... [the very knowledge of that].

Thus it is said. For here, by the power of his own uncreated effort (*akṛtaka-nijodyoga-bala*), the lord of yogins (*yogīndra*) should draw forth the mind, the action, and the *bindu*—he should cause them to attain the nature of supreme luminosity (*paraprakāśātmatā*). Likewise, the *bindu* (p.
The supreme illuminator [is realized] through the utterance that consists of uncreated agency, which is the nature of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*),
and not through the utterance of seed-syllables (*bījākṣara*) consisting of places of articulation, producing organs, and effort,
because the latter culminates in the means of the individual soul (*āṇavopāya*); this is for the sake of resting in the supreme subject.
"It flashes forth by means of the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) whose nature is the agency of the innate arising"—this means that it runs, that is, it expands. And this is stated in the *Spanda*:
"This alone is the arising of that object of meditation within the mind of the meditator."

The "attainment of identity with that" (*tadātmatā-samāpatti*) refers to the attainment of identity with the deity of the mantra for the practitioner who so desires. This is the intended meaning here: during the state of reciting the mantra—on account of the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and other such practices—the practitioner’s mind [is focused] upon the form of another deity who has been constrained by the mantra.

That state of non-differentiation which is accomplished spontaneously without effort is itself the primary manifestation (*udaya*)— in the form of direct perception— of the deity to be worshipped for the meditator whose consciousness is capable of such reflective awareness; it is not, however, a state where the form is perceived as distinct [from the self], according to this very consciousness.
[This is because] the injunction "having become Śiva through attaining the nature of Śiva, one should worship Śiva" has fulfilled its purpose.
This has been stated by this [verse]. || 2 ||
He characterizes the potency of such a mantra, whose practitioner and goal have been previously introduced:
"The reality of the body of the Vidyā is the secret of the mantra. (3)

Vidyā is the manifestation of supreme non-duality; that which has this as its body and essential nature is the Lord Śabdarāśi, whose being (*sattā*)—consisting of the creative awareness (*vimarśana*) of the full "I" (*pūrṇāhaṃ*), which is composed of the non-difference of the entire universe—is the radiance (*sphurattā*). That is the secret (*rahasya*) of the mantras, meaning their vitality (*vīrya*), their *upaniṣad*.
As it is said in the *Śrītantrasadbhāva*: "O Dear One, all mantras consist of phonemes (*varṇa*), and they, in turn, consist of power (*śakti*)."
Power (śakti) should be known as Mātṛkā, and she should be known as having Śiva as her essence.
Thus, in that very [Śrītantrasadbhāva], this meaning— though extremely secret— is clearly elucidated in detail by means of the scripture to be cited hereafter: "And likewise,
they do not know the Guru as God, nor the observances (samayas) declared in the scriptures."
Devoted to deceit and crookedness, their sole purpose is fickleness— [fickleness being the tasting of flavors by that which is fickle, i.e., the tongue;
thus they are those for whom the tasting of flavors is the only goal, meaning they are addicted to the relish of sense objects such as sound and the rest]— and they are devoid of spiritual practice.
For this reason, O Goddess, my virility was concealed by me;
because it was concealed, the remaining castes alone were preserved for you.

Having thus performed the binding of the pedestal— the "binding of the pedestal" being the "root-binding" consisting of a brief statement of the connection and so forth at the beginning of the scripture—
that Mātṛkā, O Goddess, is endowed with supreme splendor (where "supreme splendor" refers to the supreme I-consciousness).
This entire universe, from Anāśrita Śiva down to the end of the Brahma-world [or, from Anāśrita Śiva down to the limit of gross objects of cognition], is pervaded by her.

O Goddess, worshipped by the gods, when that supreme radiance situated there— [“situated there” means situated in the *mātṛkā*; “situated in the letter *a* (avarṇa)” means established in the Unsurpassed (*anuttara*)]— is pervaded, O Beloved, it remains all-pervading like the letter *a*, which is established as the phoneme (*varṇa*).
"Thus I shall explain clearly to you for the sake of a definitive conclusion," beginning thus— (p. 52) — and so forth.
That supreme, subtle power which is proclaimed as "beyond conduct" (nirācārā),
having coiled within like a sleeping serpent around the bindu of the heart— the power of the Absolute (anuttara-śakti)—
by its own sovereignty, effects the delimitation of the measure of the entire collection of states consisting of the grasped and the grasper.

By concealing her own nature and resorting to self-limitation, she manifests herself as the *bindu* (the point), even while remaining established in a state of universal activity. She is called *bindu* because she "knows" (*vindati*); she is the independent subject in the act of knowing, whose nature is non-dual luminosity (*prakāśa*). Thus, she is essentially of that very nature, and for this reason, she is the supreme consciousness (*parā saṃvit*).

Subtle, consisting of the nature of vital breath, and having emerged from ritual conduct such as meditation and worship characterized by a restricted self— thus being beyond ritual conduct (*nirācārā*)— she reaches the *bindu* of the heart, which resides within the circle of the heart-lotus; due to the predominance of its contracted nature,
it has attained its growth in the state of duality as an external form, appearing as the *bindu* whose essence is the human (*nara*).
Having wrapped [the universe] within and caused it to dissolve into its own self, it takes the form of a serpent in deep sleep;

the meaning is that, because it is devoid of any inclination toward external existence, it rests solely in its own self. This is the intended sense here: the *bindu*, whose nature is supreme light, desiring to manifest the universe through its sovereignty...
Through the different modes of resting in the locations characterized by the *dvādaśānta*, the space between the eyebrows, and the heart,

one should understand that [the self] consists of the nature of Man, Śakti, and Śiva; here, within the triad of abodes consisting of Will and so forth, there is that which is pure luminosity (*prakāśamātra*) while the three abodes remain present.
"It is stated in the scripture that, in the form of the *bindu*, this is considered the *śivabindu*.
Therein, O illustrious Umā, she is asleep and perceives nothing at all."

The fourteen worlds, along with the moon, fire, sun, and stars, having been brought under its own control by means of its power and measure, become as if deluded by poison; the meaning is that they come to exist without even knowing their own self.
But that goddess, having been cast into his belly, became as if stupefied by poison.
Awakened by that resonance (*nādāna*), she— desiring to manifest the state of various reflective awarenesses (*parāmarśatā*) as the *vindu* itself—
vibrates in the form of sound whose essence is resonance (*nādātmaka-śabda-rūpatayā*). Thus, she makes all things audible and reflects upon the universe as non-different from herself.

Sound (*śabda*) is reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) in the form of the supreme speech (*parāvāk*); it resounds as that very [awareness], manifesting as the vital essence (*jīvakalā*) of all beings, and is thus "of the nature of resonance" (*nādātmā*). As it has been said:
"That sound which consists of resonance (*nādātmaka*), abiding in all living beings," [by the Supreme One].
O lady of excellent complexion, it was churned by the Bindu residing within the belly, which is of the nature of gnosis.
Indeed, while the churning was proceeding with the force of that whirling within the body of Śakti,
drops of exceeding luster were first produced from its breaking apart.

The supreme, subtle Kuṇḍalinī energy, whose form is the *amākalā*, having arisen and attained a union with Śiva consisting of the state of the churner and the churned— which is the nature of mutual aesthetic integration (*sāmarasya*)— and having thus arisen,
assumes the forms of will, knowledge, and action, manifesting the state of Raudrī.
Assuming the form of a *śṛṅgāṭaka* (triangular node), she abides as Ambikā;

assuming the form of the crescent moon consisting of the syllable *U*, she presides as Jyeṣṭhā; and assuming the form of a distinct line resting upon the bindu consisting of the letter *Ra*—which is the nature of Kālāgni arising from the *Śiva-bindu*—she manifests as Raudrī.
The essential meaning of these five verses ending with "ekaivetham" has been explained. However, when that subtle *kalā*, namely Kuṇḍalinī—
the Lord who consists of four *kalās* and resides within the womb of Śakti— is present...
O Dear One, through the application of churning and rubbing, straightness is produced;
that is known as the Jyeṣṭhā-śakti, situated in the middle of the two bindus.
The line alone, when agitated by the *bindu*, is Amṛtakuṇḍalī;
she is to be known as Rekhiṇī, between whom both *bindus* reside.
She is declared to be the three-pathed one and is sung of by the name Raudrī;
she is designated as Rodhinī because she obstructs the path to liberation.

Ambikā, shaped like a crescent moon and possessing the luster of the half-moon, is indeed this single Supreme Power (*parā śakti*) which, though one, thus arises as threefold— [in the forms of *anuttara*, *icchā*, and *unmeṣa*]. It is she who is born.
From these [vowels], both joined and unjoined, the group of nine is produced;
it is remembered as ninefold, characterized by that group of nine.
O Goddess, O leader of the gods, she who resides within the five mantras—namely Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Īśāna, Tatpuruṣa, and Aghora—is declared to be fivefold; thus she should be known.
O Goddess, you who traverse the twelve musical notes are declared to abide in twelve places;
you exist in fiftyfold divisions, beginning with the letter 'a' and ending with the letter 'kṣa'.

Residing in the heart is the Supreme Goddess, whose nature is the Supreme Word (*parāvāk*). For the supremacy of the reflective awareness of the "I-self" (*ahamātman*), which is of the nature of the Supreme Word, is independent of anything else; thus, desiring to manifest external form through her own sovereignty, she remains the Supreme Goddess in the form of the Supreme Word alone—because the sequence of signifier and signified has not yet arisen, because division is indistinct, and because the light of consciousness (*cijjyotis*) alone is predominant.

In its nature as the seer (*draṣṭṛ*), it is designated by the term *paśyantī*. Subsequently, although the sequence of signifier and signified (*vācya-vācaka*) has its divisions merely outlined, because it resides solely within the intellect (*buddhi*) in a state that is neither clearly manifest nor unmanifest,
and because vision (*darśana*) is predominant, it is denoted by the term *madhyamā*, existing as the intermediate state between the seer and the seen.

Furthermore, due to the power of the places of articulation (*sthāna*), the organs of pronunciation (*karaṇa*), and the effort (*prayatna*), and because of the sequential apprehension of each respective phoneme, as well as the clarity of the distinction (*vibhāga*) and the predominance of that which is perceptible, it exists within the manifest body (*vaikhara-śarīra*) and is therefore designated by the term *vaikharī*. Thus, in the manifestation of the universal form (*viśvarūpatā*), there is a threefold division according to the states of the supreme (*para*), the subtle (*sūkṣma*), and the gross (*sthūla*).

The essential meaning of these two verses beginning with "hṛtstha" has been explained as follows: The first *aṇavā* is said to be at the throat; the second is said to be there; but the third *aṇavā*, which should always be known to reside at the root of the tongue, is [the third].
The production of phonemes occurs at the tip of the tongue; of this there is no doubt.
In this way, sound is produced, and the world of moving and non-moving beings is pervaded by sound.
By means of this and other passages, [it is shown that] the Mātṛkā consists of the supreme power of speech (parāvāk) belonging to Parabhairava; for this very reason, she is Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, and Ambā.
Since it has been stated that the emergence of all phonemes occurs through the manifold variety of the differentiation of the expansion of the power of consciousness (*khyāti-śakti*),
it has been demonstrated that for mantras whose bodies are formed by the conjunction of phonemes, that very Goddess— whose nature has been explained—
is the secret reality of the body of *vidyā*. And this is so according to every scripture.
This is precisely the intention behind explaining the extraction of mantras preceded by the *mātṛkā-mālinī-prastāra*.

Since the *Śivasūtras* consist of a compendium of the essence of the secret Āgamas, we have placed our emphasis on their corroboration with those scriptures; therefore, one should not be envious of us. Even so, if [the matter] is thus corroborated in the Āgama...
The secret meaning is not understood; therefore, service to a true guru must be performed. And this is the meaning of the aphorism:

"Having ascended that" (*tadākramya*)—that is, having presided over the power of the unconditioned nature of consciousness—the mantras proceed toward their own specific functions, such as bestowing grace upon embodied beings, just as the sense organs proceed toward their own respective domains. However, for those whose function has ceased...

Through the dissolution of those [powers] into the sky of one's own essential nature (*svasvabhāvavyoman*) along with the mind of the worshipper, there occurs the attainment of the state of Śiva-nature (*śivadharmitā-samāpatti*), due to the absence of the impurity of illusion (*māyākāluṣya*). This is shown in the *Spanda* by these two verses beginning with "The powers, the mantras... (3).
However, for those for whom this aforementioned power of mantra—

which is also conducive to the realization of the great lake— is not brought to heart through the will of the Supreme Lord alone, but rather [is concerned] only with the secondary [powers] produced by the digits (*kalā*) such as *bindu* and *nāda*;
The mind of those who have attained limited accomplishments grows toward them; within the womb, there is an expansion of consciousness that is like a dream of extraordinary knowledge. || 4 ||

The embryo is non-manifestation (*akhyāti*), which is Mahāmāyā; therein, within that very essence, there is the expansion of the mind toward the manifold of limited mantra-attainments. Satisfaction with that much of a manifold is precisely this unqualified *vidyā*, which is of a nature common to all people and consists in limited knowledge (*kiñcijjñatva*); it is impure *vidyā*, and that itself is the dream.
Delusion is manifold, consisting of conceptual construction, and culminates in differentiation. Thus it is stated in the *Pātañjala* [Yoga Sūtra]:
"Those [powers] such as intuitive insight (*prātibha*), when arising for one whose mind is in a state of meditative absorption (*samāhita*), are called 'obstacles' (*upasarga*);
however, when arising for one whose mind has emerged from that state (*vyutthita*), they are inferred to be 'accomplishments' (*siddhi*) because they are contrary to that [state of] vision."

In that regard, from the mind, ear, skin, eyes, and tongue aided by the dharma born of yoga, there arises knowledge of the subtle, the concealed, the distant, the past, and the future; from the sense of hearing, knowledge of divine sounds;
from the sense of touch, the attainment of divine touch; from the sense of sight, the vision of divine forms; and from the sense of taste—
From the supernormal power of divine taste comes the knowledge of divine smells. This is the purpose [of the discussion] here in both the Sūtra and the Bhāṣya.
For one whose mind is distracted (vyutthitacitta) conceives of these perfections as his own, like a man in poverty who regards even a tiny bit of wealth as a vast fortune.
But by a yogi whose mind is concentrated (samāhitacitta), there should be detachment even toward those [perfections] that have approached him.
The supreme human goal consists in the cessation of the arising of the threefold suffering;

indeed, one should become dispassionate toward those accomplishments (*siddhis*) which are contrary to that [goal]. Thus, these are obstacles (*upasargas*) in *samādhi* and accomplishments (*siddhis*) in the state of emergence (*vyutthāna*).
This is so.

Therefore, *bindu* refers to that particular radiance (*tejoviśeṣa*), which is an ever-increasing clarity resulting from the intensification of the practice of meditation in locations such as the space between the eyebrows.

Through the practice of piercing the *bindu*, it becomes manifest to those who meditate on the *dharātattva* (the earth-element). Likewise, the *nāda* (sound) begins with a resonance as dense as the roar of a swift river or a thundercloud,
and as it gradually becomes subtle, it manifests as an imitation of the humming of bees intoxicated by honey.

It is a particular sound uttered by oneself which those who practice the principle of space (vyomatattva) hear; likewise, it is a form—the perception of the shapes of various visible objects—which is observed by those whose minds are fixed upon the principle of fire (tejastattva), even when there is an obscuration such as deep darkness; and similarly, it is a taste, even in the absence of any tangible object to be tasted.

The taste of nectar (*amṛta*) in the mouth, which is experienced by those intent on the *dhāraṇās* such as *lolāgra* and *lambikā* while meditating on the water-element (*aptattva*), should be understood as follows: even the specific pleasure of touch for those meditating on the air-element (*pavanatattva*) proceeds from this very [source]. One who practices the yoga of *unmeṣa* should not find satisfaction in this alone.
Because it constitutes an obstacle to ascending to the unsurpassed state, sound (*nāda*), form (*rūpa*), and from this, taste (*rasa*),
arise very quickly as agitators for embodied beings.
This has been demonstrated by this [verse]. || 4 ||
But when the yogi, having set aside even the limited accomplishment that has arrived, takes hold of the supreme state alone,
then—
upon the natural arising of Vidyā— there is Khecarī.
The state of Śiva. || 5 ||

When the Vidyā whose true nature was previously described arises spontaneously—fashioned solely by the will of the Supreme Lord, natural, and emerging while submerging limited accomplishments—it moves in the "void" (khe), that is, in the sky of consciousness; thus, the Khecarī Mudrā is manifested. Of what kind is it?
(58) Khecarī is the state belonging to Śiva, the Lord of Consciousness, who abides [as such]; it consists of the surging forth of one's own bliss. But not...

Having assumed the lotus posture (*padmāsana*), the yogi should place the Lord of the Eye (the *akṣeśvara*) at the navel. He should then lead that [energy], which is rod-like in form, up as far as the three voids (*kha-traya*). [The three voids are: the head (*ke*), the three voids (*kha-traya*) [which is the power (*śakti*)], and the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*) situated there. Having fixed the mind there by means of the three voids, [he should proceed].
One should impel [the breath] for the sake of ascending.
Having restrained [the breath] there, the great yogi should quickly impel it through the three apertures;
having bound this, he attains movement in the sky.
Thus, although they consist of following specific configurations (*saṃsthāna*), nevertheless...
[they] attain the supreme state through the nature of the object by means of the *kula*-path (the meaning of *kula*-path is by way of the door of the *akṣa*-family).
Constantly.
It moves within all living beings and is known as *khecarī*.

Thus, its nature is defined by the supreme consciousness (*parasaṃvitti*) described in the *Śrītantrasadbhāva*. In this way, through the pacification of all agitation belonging to *māyā*, which is characterized by duality, it consists solely in the emergence of one's own true nature, which is of the essence of consciousness.
The potency of mantra and the potency of mudrā have been taught. As it is said in the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*:
"The single seed-syllable consisting of emanation—[the seed-syllable consisting of emanation is the form of the potency of mantra;
the seed-syllable is 'I']—and the mudrā are one: the mudrā is Khecarī, whose nature is that of Supreme Bhairava."
He in whom these two arise abides in the state of supreme tranquility.
Thus [it is said].
In the *Spanda*, however, the potency of the *mudrās* is subsumed precisely through the determination of the essential nature of the potency of the *mantras*.
"When agitation is dissolved, then there shall be the supreme state."
By the latter half [of the verse], which refers to something else, the nature of the *khecarī* as described in the *Cūḍāmaṇi* is indicated through a figurative turn of phrase. || 5 ||
Therefore, even in this attainment of the power of mudrā and mantra, the guru is the means. || 6 ||
A *guru* is one who proclaims and teaches the ultimate reality (*tāttvika-artha*); in this context, he is the means (*upāya*) by virtue of demonstrating pervasion (*vyāpti*).
Here, pervasion consists of the essential nature of the power of the *mudrā* and the power of the mantra. As it is said in the *Śrīmālinīvijaya*:

"That guru is declared to be equal to Me, the revealer of the potency of mantra. In the *Spanda*, however, because such things are well-known— meaning, because the status of the guru and so forth is established— it is likewise stated elsewhere:
"He who is the Guru is declared to be Śiva; he who is Śiva is remembered as the Guru.
There is no difference between the two, neither of the Guru nor of Śiva. [This verse] has not been included.
[It is] the boat for crossing the unfathomable ocean of doubt.
I pay homage to that wonderful speech of the Guru, which is variegated with words of manifold meanings.
By this concluding statement, even this is indeed included:
the Guru, or the grace-bestowing power of the Supreme Lord (pārameśvarī anugrāhikā śaktiḥ). As it has been stated in the venerable *Mālinīvijaya*:
"That very [reality] is called the wheel of power (śakticakra), and it is called the mouth of the Guru. Thus it is said;
and in the venerable *Triśirobhairava* as well:
"The power that is even more powerful than the Guru resides within the mouth of the Guru."
Thus, that very [emptiness], providing an opportunity, is the means. || 6 ||
Therefore, from a gracious guru comes the awakening to the wheel of the Mātṛkās. || 7 ||

The phrase "it belongs to the disciple" is the ellipsis to be supplied. According to the method taught in the *Śrī Parātriṃśikā* and other texts, the first digit of the reflective awareness of "I" (*ahaṃvimarśa*)—which is indeed the supreme reality, the ultimate Light itself, consisting of the ineffable reflective awareness (*anākhyaparāmarśa*), the unsurpassed (*anuttara*), and incapable of being designated by specific terms such as Śiva or Śakti—is that very [reality]. It is he alone.
And because He desires to manifest the universe through His sovereignty, He manifests within Himself the nature of Śiva and Śakti;

for that reality characterized as Śiva, there exists a Śakti whose essence is the perfect I-consciousness (*pūrṇāhaṃtā*), which is His unchanging nature, supreme (*anuttarā*), and whose form is Kula. Thus, Kula—characterized by the letter *A*—is His body.

The first letter has been explained. Being of the nature of Anuttara-kula, she flows forth as the nature of bliss [in the form of the letter Ā]. Being thus, preceded by the manifestation of the stages of will (*icchā*) and sovereignty (*īśana*), [she takes the forms of *i* and *ī*. First, the limit of will (*icchānta*) is the very self-reflective awareness (*ahaṃ-vimarśa*) itself, meaning it is the form of the first *kalā*.]

The stage of unfolding (*unmeṣadaśā*), which is of the nature of knowledge, is characterized by an abundance of the threading together of the manifestations of the objects of knowledge; and the stage of contraction (*ūnatā*)—the stage of unfolding in the form of the letter *u*, and the stage of contraction in the form of the letter *ū*.

Having thus demonstrated that desire itself is twofold—just as its manifestation is a slight increase of that very [desire], so too that same desire, having attained the state of the syllable *ṛ*, is like a flash of lightning; both its manifestation and its slight increase are denoted by *ṛ*. Furthermore, the phoneme *ra* is the seed-syllable of fire (*vahnibīja*), whose nature is light (*tejas*). Thus...

Desire (*icchā*) is indeed like lightning; *ḷ* is its flash-like manifestation. Because it is slightly more intense than *la*, and because desire is characterized by passion (*rañjitatva*), the four neuter vowels possess efficacy only in the two cases—either in the sound *ra*, which is the nature of pure light (*tejomātra*), or in the sound *la*, which is the nature of stability—but not elsewhere.

Having thus elaborated upon it through its fourfold nature known as the "eunuch seeds" (*ṣaṇḍhabīja*), which consists of: (1) being colored by the object of desire (*eṣaṇīya*) due to its stability as a mere form of light resembling a flash of lightning; (2) being colored by the manifestation of the object of cognition (*meyābhāsa*) as a mere form of nectar; and (3–4) the inability to produce further seeds.

The seed-syllable of the triangle (*trikoṇabīja*)— which is the letter *e* and is indeed the seed-syllable of the womb (*yonibīja*)— is proclaimed through the friction of the desire for unsurpassed bliss (*anuttarānande-cchā*). And through the conjunction with the unfolding of unsurpassed bliss (*anuttarānandonmeṣa*), it takes the form of the letter *o*, which is the nature of the attainment of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) [and the acceptance of the power of emanation (*nirmāṇaśakti*)].

By the union of these two aforementioned seed-syllables [the pair *e* and *o*], there is the hexagon and the trident-seed [meaning the trident-seed consisting of *ai* and *au*], because it is primarily characterized by the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) which is full and pervaded by the powers of will (*icchā-śakti*) and knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*).

Having demonstrated that which consists of the union of the three powers (*śaktitrayasaṃghaṭṭana*), and having unveiled the *bindu*, which is the singular consciousness of the universe up to this limit;
Simultaneously manifesting the ground of emission (*visarga-bhūmi*), which consists of the two *bindus* that release [the energies] both internally and externally,
she thereby demonstrates through internal reflection (*antar-vimarśana*) that this entire universe rests within the Absolute (*anuttara*) itself;
whereas through external reflection (*bahir-vimarśana*), she reveals the five groups of five, from *ka* to *ma*, as well as *a-i-u-ṛ-ḷ*.
The meaning is that they manifest as the arrangement of phonemes (*varṇa*). He elaborates on the entire [universe] up to the individual soul (*puruṣa*).
Each individual power possesses five powers; thus, from each one, there arises a pentad.
It is from these very powers—meaning those beginning with consciousness (*cit*) mentioned above, which are the root of all phonemes—that [the universe emerges].
According to the terminology taught in the *Śikṣā* [following the sequence taught in the *Śikṣā*,

such as grammar], those who perceive the designation "inner-staying" (*antaḥstha*) because they abide within the ground of the cognizer (*pramātṛbhūmi*) due to [the categories] such as *niyati*, *kalā*, *vidyā*, and *rāga*— namely, *ya*, *ra*, *la*, and *va*— [are so designated].

Because they abide within the internal male ground as the sheaths (kañcuka) beginning with Niyati; because they are called "intermediate" (antastha) since they sustain the universe by sustaining the levels of the subjects; because they are designated by the term "dhāraṇā" in the scriptures;
and because they have blossomed through the dissolution of duality and the attainment of non-duality beyond that.

She has illuminated the four classes of phonemes known as the *ūṣman*s. Herein—[that is, within these *ūṣman* letters, such as *śa*, etc.]—the form of the object of knowledge (*meyarūpa*), which is the object of enjoyment (*bhogya*), is the complete nectar-like phoneme.
Having demonstrated that, at its conclusion, the demonstration of the seed-syllable of the vital breath (*prāṇabīja*) is made;
it consists of the unstruck sound (*anāhata*) nourished by the power of the Absolute (*anuttaraśakti*), being of the nature of the phoneme *ha*.
It possesses this much form of both the signified and the signifier—the signifier consisting of mantras, phonemes, words, and the sacrificial paths (*adhvan*).

This is to make known that the universe consists of the expansion of the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan), whose forms are speech, the arts (kalā), the principles (tattva), the worlds (bhuvana), and the sacrificial tracks (adhvan). For this very reason, by means of the method of contraction (pratyāhāra),
it is contained within— and is essentially identical with— Śiva and Śakti themselves, namely the Absolute (anuttara) and the Unstruck Sound (anāhata).
"Viśva" (the universe) is the reality of the reflective awareness of "I," which is the very essence of the potency of the Great Mantra.
As it has been stated by our supreme preceptor, the venerable Utpaladeva:
"The repose of Light within itself is indeed proclaimed to be the state of 'I-ness' (ahambhāva)."
And that very state is called rest, because of the cessation of all dependence.
"Autonomy, agency, and supreme lordship as well. Thus,

that which is the reality of Mātṛkā up to this point is precisely the letter *ka*— [the letter *ka* consisting of the Absolute (*anuttara*), the letter *sa* consisting of the emission (*visarga*), and the peak-syllable (*kūṭavarṇa*) *kṣa* consisting of their union].
It is shown at the end by means of the *sakāra*-pratyāhāra, which is the essence of the union with the unsurpassed visarga, [and] by the *kūṭa*-seed-syllable;
enough, therefore, with revealing this secret. Of such a kind...
there is no Vidyā higher than Mātṛkā.

Of the wheel belonging to the Mātṛkā, whose power is indicated by the sacred tradition (āmnāya), and which consists of the aforementioned collection of powers such as Anuttara, Ānanda, and Icchā. (p. 64)

Perfect awakening consists of immersion into one’s own essential nature, which is a mass of consciousness and bliss. This has been indicated here merely by way of direction (*diṅmātreṇa*). Thus, this is the clear determination of the phonemes (*varṇa*) in this context: *a* is the first digit of the Absolute (*anuttara*), the nature of *Akula*, the fullness of I-consciousness (*pūrṇāhantā*). *Ā*— *Note: The text fragment ends with "ā-", indicating the beginning of the next phoneme.*

*Ī*: She herself, being the sovereign (*īśitrī*), is as if resting within her own self; for this very reason, she takes the form of the junction between two *i*-sounds. *U*: When there is an outward orientation of will (*icchā*), she is the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) whose nature is the unfolding of the universe. *Ū*: When that [power] is non-distinct from the object of knowledge—like a city in a mirror—due to the predominance of the object of knowledge, she is the principle of consciousness (*saṃvittattva*).

The state of appearing deficient (*ūnatāvabhāsitva*). Indeed, because the two-fold desire (*icchā*), resting upon the plane of the void (*śūnyabhūmi*), is touched by light through the assistance of the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), it is *ṛ*. Because [the same desire], spreading further into the extreme void, is somewhat lacking the power of knowledge, it is *ṝ*.

Because the hearing of the letter *la* assumes a state like that of wood or stone, its manifestation is like a flash of lightning due to its nature as stability; for this very reason, because it rests solely within itself and lacks outward orientation,
these [letters] possess the nature of nectar (*amṛta*), being incapable of producing other seeds.

The designation "neuter" [is applied] as follows: *e* is the seed-syllable of the triangle because, when the Will (*icchā*) of both the Absolute (*anuttara*) and Bliss (*ānanda*) expands, the Absolute predominates and the Will, Knowledge, and Action are in equilibrium. *Ai* is the lengthening of those same two [syllables] due to the excess of the measure (*mātrā*), resulting from the extreme expansion of the Will and the Sovereign (*īśitrī*).

*O*—this is the form of expansion within the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) during the state of universal unfolding (*viśvonmeṣa*), arising from the desire of the two supreme blisses (*anuttarānanda*) to manifest externally. *Au*—because of its extreme length, this very [syllable] constitutes the seed-syllable of the trident (*triśūlabīja*), due to the clear manifestation of will, knowledge, and action. *Aṃ*—this is...

Thus, because the universe up to this limit consists of the nature of consciousness (*vedana*), there is first the reflective awareness of the possessor of power (*śaktimat*) as the *bindu*. Then, "aḥ" is the reflective awareness of the predominance of power, in the form of the *visarga*, which is none other than the previously mentioned Absolute (*anuttara*) inseparable from the power of bliss (*ānandaśakti*).

The powers of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*) are five; each one of these powers is further joined with a pentad (*pañcaka*). Thus, there arises from the Absolute (*anuttara*) the *ka*-group; from the Will (*icchā*), abiding in its own essential nature, the *ca*-group; and from the Will—which is of two kinds, namely the non-greedy and the greedy—the *ṭa*-group and the *ta*-group.
From the opening [of the eyes], the fivefold nature of the *pa*-group arises. Among them, Brāhmī is the presiding deity of the *a*-group;
Māheśvarī is the presiding deity of the *ka*-group, which possesses the nature of the five elements—earth, water, fire, air, and ether—and Kaumārī is the presiding deity of the *ca*-group.

The fivefold nature of the organs of action consists of the anus, genitals, feet, hands, and speech; and Cāmuṇḍā is the presiding deity of the *tavarga* (the dental class of consonants). Furthermore, there is a fivefold nature consisting of the sense organs—the nose, tongue, eyes, skin, and ears—and the principles of mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṃkāra*), primordial nature (*prakṛti*), and the individual soul (*puruṣa*).
And: the four principles of *niyati*, *rāga*, *kalā*, and *vidyā* belong to the semi-vowels (*antasthā*);
*māyā* and *kāla* are included within these very [principles]. The letters *śa*, *ṣa*, and *sa* belong to *īśvara*.
Thus, through the *pratyāhāra* (phonetic contraction) of the vowels *a* and the letter *ha*, the entirety of the signified (*vācya*) and the signifier (*vācaka*) is [contained].

To demonstrate that the entire universe, which consists of the sixfold path (*ṣaḍadhva*), rests in the Absolute (*anuttara*) alone, the letter *ka*, whose essence is the Absolute, and the letter *sa*, which consists of power (*śakti*), are shown at the end as a "peak-seed" (*kūṭabīja*) in the form of their union; such is the determination of the phonemes. As for the extensive [explanation]: [The text continues: *vitataṃ tu*... [the rest of the passage follows].
This has been elucidated by our venerable masters in the *Śrīparātriṃśikāvivaraṇa*, the *Tantrāloka*, and other works. And it is said in the *Śrīsiddhāmṛta*:

In this context, that very power of emission (visarga-śakti) belonging to the Supreme Lord— which consists of pure consciousness alone and is designated by the term *kuṇḍalinī* because it contains the entire universe within its womb— is, in the form of the vowel-less digit (*anacka-kalā*),
the seed of all this universe consisting of the signified and the signifier; for the existence of ignorance and other such factors as its cause has been cast far away.

The sense is that, even in reality, since all established orders are grounded in consciousness, nothing whatsoever could manifest without consciousness as their life-force. And from such a consciousness, there arose the threefold reflective awareness known as Anuttara (the Absolute), Icchā (Will), and Jñāna (Knowledge); and from those three reflective awarenesses—
According to the principle already stated, there arises the emergence of all other reflective awarenesses. Kuṇḍalinī, who is the life-force of the seed-syllables, consists of consciousness;
from her arises the triad known as the Fixed (dhruva), Will (icchā), and Expansion (unmeṣa), and from that, in turn, the phonemes.

66) Regarding the passage beginning with "ā from the vowel 'a'": the word *ekaḥ* (one) refers to its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), while the other [instance] indicates a manner (*prakāra*).
Thus, just as bliss (*ānanda*) arises from the Absolute (*anuttara*), so too from Will (*icchā*) arises the Sovereign (*īśitrī*), and from Expansion (*unmeṣa*) arises Deficiency (*ūnatā*), and so on.

The meaning is that the phonemic collection (*varṇajāta*) has arisen in its entirety as the emission-power (*vaisargikī kalā*) consisting of the letter *ha*, which begins with *ka* and ends with *sa*. Although it should have been stated as "ending with *ma*," it was stated as "beginning with *ka*" in order to indicate its birth from [the letter] *ha*. For [the sūtra] states: "The throat is the place of articulation for *a*, *ku*, *ha*, and the visarga."

According to this principle, the *k*-group, the letter *ha*, and the *visarjanīya* arise from the letter *a* alone. By the general statement "the power belonging to the *visarga*," the *visarga* whose nature is both transcendent (*parā*) and immanent (*aparā*) is indicated. The meaning of all this is that everything produced from the *visarga* is in fact the *visarga* itself, manifesting as the reflective awareness (*āmarśa*) of each respective [phoneme]. For it is that very [visarga] which...
By encompassing the entire universe within its single form as the supreme subject, it flashes forth as the nature of the letter *Ha* (anuttara-hakāra);
thus, through its internal and external aspect, it manifests itself as the essence of Nara, Śakti, and Śiva. Therefore, he says: "And that is fivefold.
The word "and" (*ca*) indicates the reason: because that very emission (*visarga*), which is the point (*bindu*), is the autonomous subject in the act of knowing.
In its external form it is in the heart, and in its human form, even while existing externally, it rests solely within its internal form.
As *nāda* (sound), it exists as *śakti* (power) in its internal form; as *śiva*, it flashes forth in the supreme state at the *dvādaśānta*.
Thus, it is fivefold. For this very reason, even within the body, from the heart to the crown of the head—namely, the heart, throat, *lalanā*, *rasanā*, and *suṣumnā*—[it resides].

Even though he consists of five elements, in reality his essence culminates in only three forms; therefore, one should not suspect any contradiction between what precedes and what follows. Now, one might ask: "How can this single entity reside in the heart and other locations? To this, he says: "For he is all-pervasive. This is the meaning of the two verses beginning with "ā" (the letter *a*).
It has been taught: up to the *kalā* of emission (*vaisargikī*).
And that [emission] is fivefold, from the letter *ka* to the letter *sa*, ending with the visarga.
It exists externally and internally, in the heart, in the resonance (nāda), and in the supreme state;
it is the bindu within the self, extending from the heart to the crown of the head, for it is all-pervasive.

"But those devoid of the first and the last"—this means that not only is there futility for the *mātṛkā* when its nature as the supreme potency of mantra (*mantravīrya*) is unknown, but there is futility even for mantras whose nature consists of "reflection" (*manana*) and "protection" (*trāṇa*). Thus he says "those devoid of the first and the last.
The word "but" (*tu*) has the sense of "and" (*ca*). The "first" is the letter *A*, the "last" is the letter *Ha*; by these, [he refers to] mantras.

The meaning is that [if] they were devoid of the final stage consisting of the ego-reflection (*ahaṃparāmarśa*) and its forms, and were not recognized as being of that nature, they would be like autumn clouds—utterly ineffective. On the other hand, however, [if they possess that nature], they would perform their respective functions; this is the intended sense. Thus, they would be *mantras*.
Like an autumn cloud. (p.
67) This much is the characteristic of the Guru: the knowledge of the beginning and the end is indeed the primary quality of the Guru.

He states the characteristic [of the Guru] with the words "of the Guru. Thus, by virtue of being endowed with such qualities as omniscience (*jñānitva*), he whose nature is luminosity and who fills the universe is worthy of worship by all, just like me; this is the statement of the Blessed One. And he should cause [the disciple] to realize this.
Such a knower is to be worshipped like me; he is Bhairava, whose very nature is the deity.
A teacher of this kind—not only knows the mantras which consist of the vibrating power and vitality of supreme consciousness, but knows whatever is even mundane, through verses, songs, and the like.

Regarding the phrase "the verse and so forth," he says "verse" (*śloka*). Indeed, that Guru, by virtue of that unsurpassed yoga of knowledge, perceives everything whatsoever—whether external, such as a verse, or internal—as being essentially the nature of the *mantra*, through the act of self-reflective awareness (*ahaṃ-parāmarśa*). Thus, [he acts] as one who possesses the nature of knowing all things, the nature of contemplation (*manana*), and the nature of bestowing grace upon transmigrating beings.
The meaning is that [the world] consists precisely of the nature of the self-appropriation (*ahaṃparāmarśa*).
The point is that nothing whatsoever could manifest apart from the state of being the supreme subject whose essence is light. For whatever exists is joined with a beginning and an end.
"Therefore, knowing thus, one perceives everything as being nothing but mantra.
And this [is stated] in the *Spanda* [Kārikās]:
"This power belongs only to those yogins who possess thorough knowledge of the reality of the *mātṛkā*."

It bestows the accomplishment (*siddhi*) characterized by enjoyment (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*); otherwise, by means of being permeated by the respective denotations [of those objects], it assumes the form of joy, sorrow, and so forth, and thus merely causes bondage for bound souls (*paśu*). Therefore, because it would be devoid of the fruit characterized by enjoyment and liberation, it would be entirely fruitless—this is the summary meaning. [It is] of the nature of action (*kriyātmikā*).
The power of Śiva residing within bound souls is a binder; established in its own path, when known, it brings about accomplishment.
This very point has been indicated by this very manner of expression. || 7 ||
For such a person as this, who possesses the awakening to the wheel of the *mātṛkās*,
the body is the oblation. (8)
That body, which consists of gross, subtle, and other forms and is consecrated as the subject by all [beings], is the oblation being offered into the supreme fire of consciousness by the great yogi;
for, through the pacification of the state of being a subject limited to the body, he is always established in the state of being the pure subject of consciousness (*cinmātṛtā*). As it has been said:
In the *Śrīvijñānabhairava*,
within the fire that is the abode of the Great Void (*mahāśūnya*), the elements, the senses,
and their objects are offered together with the mind; that is the oblation (*homa*), and consciousness is the sacrificial ladle (*sruk*) of the Great Void.
Wherein— the fire that is the supreme reality— is the dissolution (*laya*) on all sides (*ā samantāt*) of the state of void and absolute void;
therein, the world consisting of the elements, senses, objects, worlds, and principles,
together with the mind which is the cause for the conceptualization of its divisions, and consciousness itself as the power that synthesizes the universe, is the sacrificial ladle (*sruk*).

That by which [the offering] is sacrificed is *homa*; the meaning is the offering of oblation (*havis*) into the fire. This is because of such scriptural passages as: "Consciousness is the ladle (*sruk*); thought is the clarified butter (*ājya*)," and so forth.
Thus it is said. Also, in the *Śrītimirodghāṭa*:

"O Goddess, he who is dear, he who is a friend or kinsman, he who is a donor, and he who is most beloved—by consuming his body, [one attains] that which is favorable for one's own self among those things that serve as its support. "Dear" refers to those who are affectionate.
The meaning is that by consuming [it], through the pacification of that egoism and so forth, the yogi enjoys the creation of mental constructs;
indeed, he would fly up into the courtyard of the sky.
Thus, for here the essential meaning (*piṇḍārtha*) is precisely the pacification of the state of being a subject identified with the body. Also in the *Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā* (p.
"Others [offer] all the functions of the senses and the functions of the vital breaths..."
They offer all the activities of the senses,

as well as the mental functions and the vital airs such as those exiting through the mouth and nose, into the fire of self-restraint; that is, they cast them into the fire named yoga— which has self-control of the mind as its cause and is fully illuminated by right knowledge.
The intended meaning is that they perceive the object being grasped and being conceptualized with a mind that, through one-pointedness alone, has abandoned all other activities.
Thus [it is said]. In the *Spanda*, however, this is summarized by the very statement:

"When agitation (*kṣobha*) is dissolved, then the supreme state arises. For in its commentary (*vṛtti*), it is stated that "agitation consists of the sense of 'I' directed toward the body and so forth."
The venerable Bhaṭṭa Kallaṭa. || 8 ||
And for this [being], knowledge is food. || 9 ||

That which was previously stated to be "bondage" (1.2)— namely, knowledge— is the "food" for yogins because it is being consumed and swallowed [by them]. This refers to that which was previously described as death, time, and the entire collection of constituent parts (kalā).
The collection of transformations becomes the natural state of practice;
then, he swallows all that arises from the discursive thoughts of unity and diversity.
Thus [it is said]. Now, regarding the subject matter already stated, he indicates another point: and that knowledge which consists of the reflective awareness of its own nature—
p. 70) His food, by virtue of producing complete satisfaction, is the cause for resting in one's own self. As it has been said in the *Śrīvijñānabhairava*:

In this context, the meaning is that "satisfaction" (tṛpti) refers to that state of Bhairava, whose self pervades the universe, which arises day after day for the yogi whose mind is concentrated upon any one of the stages (bhūmikās) among the one hundred and twelve stages established by any one of the methods.
In this context, satisfaction consists in having a full appearance; it is a state of absolute plenitude.
Thus, since the three means known as Śāmbhava, Śākta, and Āṇava are taught as distinct, reasoning (*yukti*) consists of the cognitive states pertaining to these specific number of stages (*bhūmikā*).
In that regard, it consists precisely of the knowledge of one hundred and twelve stages. And this is stated in the *Spanda*:
The awakened one—meaning, one whose power of absolute freedom (*svātantrya-śakti*) is uncontracted—should remain at all times...
This is summarized by this *kārikā*. || 9 ||

But when he is not thus constantly attentive, then, even for one who possesses knowledge, due to the pride of his attentiveness, there occurs the vision of dreams arising from that [state] during the withdrawal of consciousness (vidyā). || 10 ||

When there is a submergence—that is, a dissolution—of Śuddhavidyā, whose nature is the expansion of the aforementioned knowledge, then there occurs the clear emergence of the dream-state arising from that [submergence]; a state consisting of duality, having the form of a proliferation of conceptual constructions, in which the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of Vidyā have been progressively suppressed. Thus it has been said:
And this is not taught by Śaṅkara unless he is pleased (Śrīmālinīvijaya, p. 71).
Even when instructed in some way, the latent impression does not arise at all.
Having begun thus:
"Even when one has attained the mere acquisition of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), if he does not remain vigilant,
the Vināyakas— the various divine hosts— join him to impermanent enjoyments."

Seeing the purity of being in the Brahmin who possesses truth-bearing wisdom (*ṛtambharā-prajñā*), those in various celestial realms invite him, saying: "O, please sit here! This enjoyment is delightful; this beloved woman is desirable;
this elixir wards off old age and death; this vehicle travels through the air; these [are the celestial nymphs]."
The wish-fulfilling trees, the auspicious Mandākinī, the perfected great seers, the most excellent and favorable Apsarases,

divine hearing and sight, and a body like a diamond— all this has been acquired by you, O Long-lived One, through your own virtues. May you attain this imperishable, ageless, and immortal station, beloved by the gods.

By means of proclaiming the qualities of divine objects and displaying them with humility and respect according to the method taught in the *Pātañjala-darśana*, they entice the yogin toward impermanent enjoyments.
Therefore, the underlying sense is that one should become dispassionate toward enjoyments because they constitute obstacles to the attainment of supreme perfection (*parasiddhi*).
Thus it is said:
"Otherwise, however, creation would be independent because it possesses that nature,
just as for an ordinary person in the two states of waking and dreaming, so too for the one independent Supreme Lord."

For the yogin, by abandoning the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) in his own essential nature as consciousness which sustains the universe— namely, "this entire universe is mine"— there remains the creation of the variety of manifold existents, capable of producing diverse delusions through the expansion of the powers of vision and action (*dṛk-kriyā*) within the two states [of waking and dreaming]. This has a flow as difficult to restrain as that of a bound soul (*paśu*).

The meaning is that by the very creation of blue, pleasure, and so forth, this [consciousness] is brought under its own control. However, for one whose mind is concentrated (*samāhitacetas*), the supreme power of the Lord (*pārameśvarī śaktiḥ*), which manifests there in the form of both knowledge and the object of knowledge, is not capable of obstructing the covering of its own conscious nature; such is the sense.

By this, it is summarized in the *Spanda*. Therefore, it is taught that the yogin must always remain intent upon the reflective awareness (*vimarśana*) of pure knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*). As it has been said (p.
"Therefore, one should not form attachment to those [objects] out of a desire for the supreme. Thus it is said in the *Śrīpūrva* (Mālinīvijayottara-tantra). Also in the *Śrīspanda*:
"Therefore, one should be constantly diligent in discerning the reality of Spanda."

Remaining awake, one attains one's own true nature without delay; [striving constantly for the manifestation of the essential nature of the Śākta-tattva, one experiences even in the waking state the ultimate reality of Bhairava, who is a dense mass of the essence of unobscured consciousness.]
Thus, from the statement "In this way, the mind is the mantra" (2-1) onwards, regarding the potency of the mantra:
one should contemplate the reality devoid of vocal utterance by means of the mind alone, making it the object of investigation through firm one-pointedness.
The immersion that one attains therein is designated as the Śākta.

Having thus analyzed the Śāktopāya as it is traditionally taught, [the following is stated] by means of the aphorism (2-10): "For one who is anointed with attentiveness, there is the vision of dreams arising from that during the withdrawal of the Vidyā. This is mentioned in connection with the incidental question: "What is the means for the submergence of the vision of the manifold expansion consisting of duality?"
Thus, the opportunity for the exposition of the individual means (āṇavopāya) has been granted. May there be auspiciousness! 10.
