*Śivasūtravimarśinī*: Now begins the third unfolding (*unmeṣa*).
At this point, the means of the individual (*āṇavopāya*)—which is the operation of the fetters (*pāśavyāpāra*)—is introduced. When, however, those two...

When conceptual thought (*vikalpa*) requires another means for its own refinement, it then assumes limited forms such as the intellect (*buddhi*) and the vital breath (*prāṇa*) as its instruments; having attained a state of atomicity (*aṇutva*), it brings forth the *āṇava* knowledge. For that [knowledge] consists essentially in the repose of the mind (*cittaviśrānti*). As it has been said:
"Having previously cast all that is to be done into the fire of emptiness—
this is proclaimed as the individual (āṇava) state known as the 'resting of the mind'. Desiring to explain this, he first demonstrates the nature of the individual soul (aṇu):
The self is the mind. || 1 ||

That which, because it is permeated by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of objects, constantly takes the form of intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṅkṛt*), and mind (*manas*) through its activities such as determination and so forth—that is the *citta*. It is that very [citta] which pervades (*atati*) those objects [through their ascertainment, conceit, and conceptualization]. [At-]...

[This is based on the reading *sātatyagamane*. Due to the non-manifestation of one's own nature, which consists of consciousness (*cidātmaka*), and by relying upon the functions (*vṛtti*) of *sattva* and the other *guṇas*, there occurs— by means of the functioning that depends upon the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, such as illumination, mobility, and obscuration— the activity of illumination (*prakāśa*), which is the operation of the intellect (*buddhi*), and mobility (*cāñcalya*).

The meaning is that the Self is atomic (*aṇu*) because it "migrates through the wombs" due to the obscuration of the mind and ego; however, for this [Self], which is of the singular nature of consciousness, there is no expansion, for in reality...
The meaning is that there is no movement of the Self—which is by nature eternal, omnipresent, and conscious—to any other location or state.

For this very reason, it has been stated that "the Self is pure consciousness" (1.1); however, this is not contradicted here, as we are currently dealing with the state of *aṇava* (atomic limitation), which is characterized primarily by the manifestation of contraction within that consciousness.
Inconsistency between what precedes and what follows. || 1 ||
For this very nature of consciousness, which is of the nature of the atom (aṇvātman), knowledge is bondage. || 2 ||

Bondage is that cognition which consists of the manifestation of distinctions appropriate to itself, taking the form of mental activities such as determination (*adhyavasāya*—which means certainty—and by "etcetera," conceptualization, self-conceit, and so forth), all of which are composed of pleasure, pain, and delusion. Indeed, it is precisely because he is fettered by this that he transmigrates. As it has been said:
In the *Śrītantrasadbhāva*,
it is said: "Established in *sattva*, established in *rajas*, and established in *tamas*— thus perceiving the qualities (*guṇas*)—
the embodied soul wanders, going from one place to another."

Thus, this very [consciousness] manifests in the form of the emergence of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*); that is, by the will of the Lord alone, the subtle [elements] such as sound and so forth— which serve as the causal basis for the gross elements— manifest, and their emergence is what is meant.

Manifestation occurs through the transformation of space and the other elements into the state of the gross body; thus, whatever is a cavity such as the channels (*nāḍī*) is space (*ākāśa*), the emergence of the subtle element of sound (*śabda-tanmātra*). Whatever is active, such as the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), is air (*vāyu*), the emergence of the subtle element of touch (*sparśa-tanmātra*). Whatever has the nature of heat, luminosity, and so forth, such as fire (*agni*), is fire (*tejas*).

The emergence of the subtle element of form (*rūpa-tanmātra*); whatever has a liquid nature, such as blood and so forth, those are water, the emergence of the subtle element of taste (*rasa-tanmātra*);

whatever is solid, such as flesh, bone, and sinew, that is earth, the emergence of the subtle element of smell (*gandha-tanmātra*). Thus, by that [body] whose form and configuration consist of the emergence of the subtle elements, which resides within the mind, ego, and intellect, and which is being experienced—

The attainment of selfhood and experience reside within the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). Thus, when *rajas* arises in the mind (*manas*), *tamas* arises in the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), and *sattva* arises in the intellect (*buddhi*), that which has its activity or functioning in such a manner exists within the city— the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*)— consisting of the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*) and the three qualities (*guṇa*).
The eightfold group (*aṣṭaka*) which constitutes the cause of the gross body (*sthūla-śarīra*) and is situated there is the primary "city of eight" (*puryaṣṭaka*).

Because the gross body is its effect, the [individual soul] is confined by it; identifying itself as the self merely to that extent, it becomes bound through the power of its own capacity—such as its universal nature—which has been forgotten. Therefore...

Thus, being entirely dependent on another and distinct from the nature of all-pervasive power, [the self] experiences the bondage of the body— arisen from the *puryaṣṭaka* (the eightfold subtle body) produced in accordance with the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of its own beginningless karma, which are manifested by *māyā*— due to the emergence of causal conditions for the fulfillment of experience.
Since this bound soul (*paśu*) consumes— that is, experiences— the arising of knowledge regarding its own restricted objects,
because the state of enjoyment exists through the production of the notion of being a consumer of only its own objects; therefore,
as long as there is no awakening and [the cycle] is not severed due to the continued existence of that eightfold city of the self consisting of gross and subtle elements, it shall transmigrate.

[One would experience the incessant whirling of the wheel of karma—the latent impressions of various bodies and enjoyments—until the dawning of awakening, [driven] by that which resides within the mind, ego, and intellect.
Constrained by the city of eight, he experiences that which arises from the resulting cognitions.
"He experiences enjoyment under the control of another; because of that state, he wanders in saṃsāra...
This has been restated by this [verse].
... Therefore:

We shall now declare the cause of this dissolution of saṃsāra—[that is, the cause for the destruction of this beast-like saṃsāra]; thus, the two genitive cases should be explained as being in grammatical apposition (vaiyadhikaraṇya).
This is for the purpose of refuting that [notion], namely, for the sake of dispelling the cause of transmigratory existence—the egoistic conceit of being an enjoyer—in the Spandaśāstra. (2)
(76) But surely,
in the world, cognition is illuminating, and the self alone is also illuminating.
Because these two are not separate, the knower shines forth within knowledge. [Regarding the word "knowledge":
because of the determination (*adhyavasāya*) that perceives blue and so forth, it is the knower—the self whose nature is light—who manifests.
This is because these two, the knower and knowledge, possess a single nature. As it has been said:
That which is manifest is not separate from manifestation,
and that manifestation is not separate from reflective awareness;
nor is there any reflective awareness other than the essential nature of "I."
"I am of the nature of the Self, whose sole form is consciousness.
And again: "When the sun of ultimate reality shines forth, the entire darkness of ignorance perishes."
"Then even the wise, though possessing stainless vision, do not perceive anything of the phenomenal expansion of existence (bhavaprapañca).
Thus: "Knowledge is not different from you; the object of knowledge is certainly not separate from knowledge."
Therefore, nothing else whatsoever is different from that; thus, the distinction is not real. And so it is said.
Thus, according to the perspective stated in the *Śrī-Vijñānabhairava*, even knowledge is indeed of the nature of light (*prakāśamaya*).
When this is recognized through *pratyabhijñā* (recognition), yet such reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) does not occur due to the power of *māyā*,
then there is a lack of discrimination regarding the principles (*tattvas*) beginning with *kalā*.
Illusion. || 3 ||

The non-discrimination of the principles (tattvas) beginning with *kalā*— which consist of limited agency and so forth, extending down to the earth (*kṣiti*)— and including the coverings (*kañcukas*), the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*), and the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), is that which has the nature of obscuring one's own ultimate essential reality.

The realization of those very things considered to be distinct as being of a non-distinct nature—that is *māyā*, the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) consisting of the non-recognition of reality (*tattvākhyāti*). As it is said in the *Śrītantrasadbhāva*:
"Consciousness, intensified by *kalā*—[that is, by the *kalā*-principle characterized by limited agency (*kiṃcitkartṛtva*)]"...

He is one whose consciousness, characterized by universal agency, has been stirred up and rendered incomplete. By *vidyā*—that is, by the principle of *vidyā* consisting of limited knowledge—the objects of the senses (*gocarāḥ*) have been revealed, brought to the state of being objects of cognition (*prameya-bhūmikā*) through their attractiveness. By *rāga*, that is, by the principle of *rāga*, he is colored.

The bondage of that beast (paśu), whose self has been rendered full of longing for sense-objects, consists of a subtle form of limited egoity—the nature of which is the impurity (mala) pertaining to Māyā. "Having that as its locus" means having the bondage of Māyā as its basis;
it is by nature the latent impressions (vāsanā) of auspicious and inauspicious karma. It is precisely within that twofold impurity that he is bound.
This is the meaning: [the soul] has its range of experience shown by *vidyā*;
its self is colored by *rāga*, and it is joined with the instruments such as the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth.

Thus, bondage has been described as consisting of Māyā; its [subordinate] nature consists of the subtle elements (tanmātras). Briefly stated, merit (dharma) and demerit (adharma) are qualities that serve as its substratum.
"There he remains bound by the noose; thus he stays bound by them.
However, in the *Spanda*, it is said:
"But these [beings] of unawakened intellect... [meaning they are unawakened due to the absence of the supreme Lord's supreme grace].
Those whose intellects have not shed the deep sleep of ignorance, and who— being the outpourings of the vibration of qualities and so forth—

are intent upon immediately covering, that is, obscuring, that firm foundation which arises from non-conceptual realization and consists of abiding within one's own supreme Self, whose sole activity is the mere universal vibration.

Because there is an absence of awakening, which serves as their antidote, and because they have gained the upper hand, they are thus metaphorically described as casting [beings] down onto the path of the continuous succession of birth and so forth—a path that is terrible and difficult to traverse; this is how the sentence connects with what follows. This is the underlying intention:
just as, for example, certain kings and others, due to the presence of states such as negligence, even though [the means of protection] exist...

Enemies who look for vulnerabilities, failing to perceive one's own power— such as that of an army— and remaining intent on ousting one from one's position, cast one into great calamity until they themselves recognize the existence of that power. In the same way, [the false doctrines] cast the unawakened person into a great calamity until they recognize their own nature, characterized by universal agency and so forth.
For one who does not realize their own majesty— which exists in the form of a universal vibration—

and instead perceives as the self only the creation of the body and so forth, which is dependent on all effects, these streams of cognition consisting primarily of qualities such as "I am happy" and so on, having gained full sway, [obscure] the state of abiding in the true Self.

"Having obstructed [the truth], they reach only saṃsāra until the attainment of awakening; thus, only those who are awakened are the subjects of this teaching, not those who are unawakened. By the phrase "striving to conceal their own abiding state," this has been stated by way of a figurative expression. (3)
And therefore, for the sake of the pacification of this— [“this” meaning for the cessation of the bondage of *māyā*]—
there is the withdrawal of the *kalās* within the body. (4)

Regarding the gross, subtle, and supreme bodies—which consist of the great elements, take the form of the *puryaṣṭaka*, and extend up to *samanā*—the dissolution (*saṃhāra*) of those portions (*kalā*) which are the constituent principles (*tattva*) beginning with earth and ending with Śiva occurs through the contemplation of their absorption into their own causes, as stated in the Upaniṣad: "Therefore... [and so forth].

"From this Self, space was produced; from space, air; from air, fire; from fire, water; from water, earth; from earth, the person. The person indeed is all this"—thus they arise in due order according to their respective causes. Such is the sequence of the principles (tattvas). Now, [the following concerns] the reverse order of these principles:

The dissolution of the elements beginning with earth and ending with Śiva into their own respective causes is to be meditated upon according to the order of ascent; or else, it is to be contemplated— this is the implied meaning— by means of the method of visualizing the cremation and so forth, through the agency of Kālāgnirudra, whose body is formed by the fire raised up from one's own left big toe through the power of visualization.
As it is stated in the venerable *Vijñānabhairava* (p.
"In the form of the path of the worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*) and so forth, or by way of the states of difference, difference-and-non-difference, and non-difference."

By means of the persistence of the worlds, the principles (*tattva*), and the limited powers (*kalā*) within the path (*adhvan*), "at the end" refers to the repose in the state beyond conceptual thought at the conclusion of contemplative cultivation (*bhāvanā*). This is the individual means (*āṇavopāya*) known as meditation (*dhyāna*);
one should contemplate everything in its proper sequence.
Through the persistence of the gross, the subtle, and the supreme, until finally there is the dissolution of the mind.
Thus,
by the fire of time (kālāgni) arising from the station of time— from the big toe of the right foot— [the "city" is the body;
"appearance" is the cognition of limited objects of knowledge and so forth], one's own city [is dissolved].
At the end, one should contemplate it as consumed by fire; then a state of peaceful radiance arises.

Thus it is said; and such passages exist in all the Āgamas. For this very reason, [the text speaks of] "utterance, instrument, meditation, color, and the arrangement of locations. Here, utterance (*uccāra*) refers to the activity of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) in both its gross and subtle forms; the instrument (*karaṇa*) consists of the specific configuration of the body.

The activity of *mudrā* and so forth is the activity of the intellect; *dhyāna* is the contemplation within the awakening of one's own heart of that very supreme reality (*paratattva*), which is self-luminous and included within all principles (*tattva*). *Varṇa* is the sound, mostly resembling an unmanifest imitation, vibrating during the subtle utterance of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
The seed-syllables of creation and withdrawal, whose locus is the triangle, the kanda, the heart, and so forth— through the practice of these,
the attainment of supreme consciousness occurs;
that which arises is called the perfect *āṇava* immersion (*samāveśa*).

Thus, in the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra*, meditation (*dhyāna*) and other such practices are described as being of the nature of the *āṇava* means. However, because this is gross, it has not been included in the *Spandaśāstra*, which consists of the illumination of the *śākta* means. That which is here [in the *Spandaśāstra*] is presented by way of its ultimate conclusion: [when one gazes toward the most vivid state of non-conceptuality through the purification of conceptual thought...]

The meaning is that within the means of power (*śāktopāya*), which is characterized by the awakening of consciousness (*cittasaṃbodha*), there is the culmination of the individual means (*āṇavopāya*), which is characterized by the repose of consciousness (*cittaviśrānti*).
That [state] beginning with the means of power exists for us.
In this regard as well, some points will be corroborated and will be corroborated further from the Spanda treatise. || 4 ||

Having thus demonstrated the means known as meditation (*dhyāna*), which shares the same security (*yogakṣema*)— wherein "yoga" is the attainment of what has not been attained and "security" (*kṣema*) is the preservation of what has been attained— he taught the following: breath control (*prāṇāyāma*),
withdrawal of the channels (*nāḍī-saṃhāra*), mastery over the elements (*bhūta-jaya*), and isolation from the elements (*bhūta-kaivalya*).
The distinctness of the primary elements. || 5 ||

The ellipsis is to be supplied as "are to be meditated upon by the yogin. The "withdrawal" (*saṃhāra*) of the channels (*nāḍī*), which carry the *prāṇa*, *apāna*, and so forth— that is, the hollow tubes—

is their unification through the technique of *prāṇa* and *apāna* (by means of practicing *pūraka* and the other breath-controls), such that their nature of flowing externally and internally is abandoned, and they are merged into one place within the nature of the *udāna* fire.

The attainment of dissolution within the central channel (madhyamā-nāḍī) means that through long-term practice of breath-retention (kumbhaka), the vital breath (prāṇa-vāyu), which was previously circulating through all the channels, dissolves into the upward-moving breath (udāna); because it flows through them, the withdrawal of those channels is figuratively designated as such. As it is said in the venerable *Svacchanda*:

One should perform exhalation (*recaka*) by means of the *apasavya*— that is, through the left nostril— and inhalation (*pūraka*) by means of the *apasavya*, that is, the left, thereby filling the air. When this is performed continuously in this manner, it effects the purification of the channels (*nāḍī*),
the path of the way of liberation, or the central abode (*madhyadhāman*), and brings about the pacification of the vital wind (*māruta*).
One should exhale with the left [nostril] and fill [the breath] with the right;
for this is the purification of the channels and the path to the way of liberation.

81) Through exhaling, filling, and retention, the breath-controls (prāṇāyāmas) are threefold.
[Prāṇāyāma is the bringing of the vital breath under one's own control by conquering its natural flow. These are the three types of prāṇāyāma.]
These are remembered as common and external, being produced in sequence within the path of the nose for the sake of universal [perception]. However, these three are also internal.
By means of the internal [middle path], there should be illumination at the *dvādaśānta* and filling in the heart;

this is the "unwavering *kumbhaka*," meaning the effortless and perfectly tranquil *kumbhaka*, which are to be performed—that is, brought to completion. It should be exhaled and filled by means of the internal [path].
Having performed a motionless kumbhaka, three internal [breaths] should be performed.
Thus: the "conquest" (*jaya*) of the elements (*bhūta*), such as earth and the rest, is their mastery through the concentrations (*dhāraṇā*). As it has been stated in that very same work:

"Because of the presence of the wind at the region of the feet due to its horizontal movement, of the digestive fire in the navel, of the earth at the station of stability in the throat, of the fluid in the uvula, and likewise of space in the aperture of Brahma (*brahmarandhra*). And so forth.
The *dhāraṇās* have been described. Here, the object of meditation for *dhāraṇā* consists of the nature of the phonemes, the mandalas, the insignia (*lāñchana*), and the syllables.

First, having established the earthly *dhāraṇā* at the throat, one should pierce the fivefold earthly principle (*tattva*) from the heart by means of five upward thrusts (*udghāta*). Then, by this same sequence—

From the heart itself, by means of four upward thrusts (*udghāta*), one draws the fourfold *asattva* from there; then from the heart itself, by three [thrusts], the threefold fire into the field of the navel; immediately after, from the heart itself, by two [thrusts], the wind located in the big toes; and from those toes as well, by means of the method of contraction.

Having awakened the vital energy (*prāṇa-śakti*) upward from the heart itself by means of the technique of a single *udghāta*, one pierces the single-stringed "space-knot" (*vyoma-granthi*) located at the aperture of Brahmā (*brahma-randhra*), like an arrow; thus, all supernatural powers (*siddhi*) arise at the "twelve-finger limit" (*dvādaśānta*).
[The fire-element concentration (*dhāraṇā*) is on the thumb; from the center of the navel...]
The Māheyī [vow] is located in the region of the throat, while the Vāruṇī is situated at the uvula.
"The concentration on space at the crown of the head is remembered as that which brings about all accomplishments.
Thus [it is said]. From the elements comes the isolation (*kaivalya*) of the mind; from that, its withdrawal [is achieved]. As it has been stated in that very same place (p.

Having restrained the breath at the navel itself by means of the technique of gradually moving it downward from the heart after the unshakable *kumbhaka*, and likewise having restrained the mind at the navel itself by means of the technique of withdrawing it from the range of the senses, one [should then restrain] the breath preceded by the restraint of the mind.
For the yogi who restrains [the breath] at the navel, the breath-control becomes perfectly tranquil;

thereafter, in order to remove the agitation of the obstructed vital air, one should exhale very gently through the left nostril from the navel—this is the intended meaning. [From the movement in the heart, and from the range of the mind and senses...]
The fourth, however, is prāṇāyāma, which is remembered as "well-pacified."

Thus [it is said]. The meaning is that by moving the vital breath (*prāṇa*) from the heart to the navel, and likewise the mind (*manas*) from its objects to that very place. Separateness from the elements (*bhūtebhyaḥ pṛthaktvam*) means the state of being a pure, autonomous conscious self (*cidātmatā*) uncolored by them. As it has been stated in that very same [text]:

Having pierced all the centers, beginning with the heart and throat, from which the mind has emerged— thus reaching the state beyond mind (unmanā) by means of the previously mentioned characteristics described in the section on the five *praṇavas*— and having then abandoned all this,
one attains absolute freedom (*svacchandatā*) through the excellence of resting in the state of intense, profound *unmanā*.

The meaning is that, by attaining the state beyond the fourth (turyātītadaśā), the lord of yogis experiences immersion into the Supreme Bhairava, who is a mass of consciousness and bliss. O Goddess, having gradually abandoned all states up to the Transmental (unmanā) through the previously mentioned characteristics, one shall attain absolute freedom (svacchandatā).

Thus: "The unification of the elements, the separation of the elements, and the conjunction of the universe" (1.20)—what was previously stated occurs without effort for one who is immersed in the *śāmbhava-upāya*. However, this [present practice] is to be accomplished through the exertion of the *āṇava-upāya*; this is the distinction. || 5 ||

Thus, the purification of the body (*dehaśuddhi*)—that is, the cleansing of the body through the meditation on its dissolution into its own cause, or through the meditation on the body and so forth being consumed by the fire of time (*kālāgni*)—has been explained. (p. 83) [This is followed by] the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*).

He states that the attainment of perfection in the form of various respective principles (*tattva*) through retention (*dhāraṇā*), meditation (*dhyāna*), and concentration (*samādhi*) arises from the veil of delusion (*mohāvaraṇa*) and not from the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*):
"Perfection [arises] from the veil of delusion" (6).

"Moha" means delusion or *māyā*; from the obscuration caused by that, there arises the attainment (*siddhi*) consisting of the enjoyment of various levels of reality (*tattva*), which is acquired through the sequence beginning with the aforementioned concentration (*dhāraṇā*)—[the word "beginning" includes meditation (*dhyāna*) and absorption (*samādhi*)]. However, it is not the manifestation of the supreme reality (*paratattva*). As it is said in the venerable *Lakṣmīkaulārṇava*:
The Self-Existent Lord, the Divine—the Blessed One who, because he does not look toward anything else, is endowed with the power of self-sovereignty;

the Blessed One whose nature consists in the play of the emergence and dissolution of the universe and so forth, and whose true essence is luminosity and the like; the Divine, the Mass of Consciousness, the Supreme Lord.
Thus, by his own will and not out of dependence on any other purpose,
he is of the nature of manifesting through the infinite variety of forms of subjects such as the various Rudras and kṣetrajñas;
shining forth, he brings forth the state of being a subject under māyā, having forgotten his own essential nature as the dense mass of independent consciousness.

Devoid of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) and tendencies (*vāsanā*) arising from births as various animals, birds, humans, reptiles, and so forth; having been brought under [his] control and rendered dependent; and for that very reason deluded and defiled by the bond of *māyā*, which consists in the manifestation of differentiated objects of knowledge—he [is the state] of all living beings.

The meaning of the sentence is that, because existence and manifestation are impossible without the light of Śiva, perception does not see its own self— which is of the nature of the light of consciousness— nor does it reflect upon it;
[it is] devoid of birth and mental impressions (*saṃskāra*).
The supreme abode is free from conceptual construction, without beginning or end, and auspicious.
"Though it is directly perceptible to all beings, one who is deluded does not see it. But for one whose delusion has dissolved...
The middle [form of *udāna*] is the form of the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*).

Because the state of being a living being (*prāṇīyatva*) of *udāna* is submerged through the emergence of the pervasion of consciousness (*cid-vyāpti*), it possesses the nature of the power of knowledge. One should not be deluded by the thought: "In the absence of the intellect (*buddhi*), how can there be knowledge? For that [power of knowledge] is eternally manifest. As they say:

When diverse objects manifest through non-apprehension (*akhyāti*), they are called "intellect" (*buddhi*); when there is non-duality within the pure consciousness (*cinmaya*), it is called "awakening" (*bodha*).
The venerable Somānanda also said:
"Without intellect, how could there be awakening? That intellect is born of primordial nature (*prakṛti*)."
And if it is argued that there is no connection between that [object] and the cognition when the object is situated elsewhere;
That intellect, moreover, which is subtle and established in all directions—
that knowledge consisting of pure consciousness— is eternally innate to that Śiva.

Thus, by taking recourse to that power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), which is consciousness (*saṃvit*) in the form of emerging and vibrating radiance, the yogi obtains the very seat situated therein; seated upon his own power of knowledge, he becomes the Great Lord of Consciousness (*cinmaheśvara*).
Having taken recourse to the vital breath (*prāṇa*) within the interval between the paths of *prāṇa* and *apāna*.
And by taking hold of the power of knowledge and that very seat situated therein, one obtains the posture.

Having abandoned the gross state of the vital breaths— that is, the gross nature consisting of exhalation, inhalation, and so forth, which resides within the *prāṇa*, *apāna*, and *samāna*— then, following this gross *prāṇāyāma*, one proceeds by the middle path to the subtle, internal [practice].

Since that [supreme state] is obtained even when one has abandoned even the subtle vibration— which consists of the manifestation of non-consciousness and is beyond the vital breaths and so forth— taking the form of emission, inhalation, and the like; therefore, that alone is the supreme vibration,
which is the very regulation (*āyāma*) of the vital breaths that possess the distinction between gross and subtle.
The *niyama* (observance), whose nature is the manifestation of the primary state of tranquility, has been indicated and defined as preeminent.
This is because, having attained this *prāṇāyāma*, one does not fall back again; that is, one never abandons the state of being the conscious subject (*citpramātṛmayatā*).
[But] having abandoned the subtle, and then the internal...
For from that, the supreme vibration is obtained, which transcends even the subtle.
That is designated as *prāṇāyāma*, from which one does not fall away again.

Having disregarded and cast aside whatever state or activity of the qualities— such as sound, touch, and so forth, which consist of *sattva* and the other *guṇas*— is experienced by the mind through consciousness.
For indeed, by means of one's own mind alone—through the reflective awareness of non-conceptual consciousness (avikalpasaṃvit)—there is entry into the abode of supreme consciousness (paraciddhāma).

This is because withdrawal (pratyāhāra) consists in bringing back the mind that has issued forth toward the objective plane (bhūmi); and for this reason, it is the cutter of the bonds of worldly existence (bhavapāśa). [This is so] because it is experienced by the mind.
Having abandoned that [world], one should enter the supreme abode with one's own mind;
this is called *pratyāhāra*, which severs the bonds of worldly existence.
Having transcended the qualities of the intellect (*dhī*), and having pacified the qualities of the buddhi such as existence (*sattva*) through absorption,
one perceives that which is to be meditated upon as having emerged from the objects of meditation— namely, forms such as determination (*niyati*) and activity (*ākṛti*).

That which has emerged from these, the all-pervasive (*vibhu*), omnipresent (*vyāpaka*), imperishable (*avyaya*), eternal (*nitya*), self-cognizable (*svasaṃvedya*), and self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*) Lord.

That which is to be meditated upon (*dhyeya*) is worthy of meditation; furthermore, it is that which is to be studied (*adhyeya*), to be investigated (*vimraṣṭavya*), and to be remembered (*smartavya*).

That is to say, having meditated upon and investigated the Supreme Lord—who is a mass of consciousness and bliss—the knowers of reality understand that very investigation of Him to be meditation through an uninterrupted lineage; and the particle *ca* (and) is used here in the sense of emphasis.
Having meditated upon the supreme,
all-pervading object of meditation, which is to be realized through one's own direct experience— that, the wise know, is true meditation.

Dhāraṇā: For that yogin who always maintains the state of the Supreme Self (paramātmatva) as consciousness through immersion, his dhāraṇā—which is a mental modification (vṛtti) consisting of the reflective awareness of consciousness—is the cause for the destruction of the bondage of worldly existence; this dhāraṇā is specified as being distinct from other forms of dhāraṇā. And furthermore:

That *dhāraṇā* is the abundant intensification of the manifestation of the Supreme Self, which is a mass of consciousness and bliss; it is not the experience of the specific forms—such as triangles or squares—of the various elements within their respective substrates.
By means of this, the state of the Supreme Self is maintained at all times.
That is designated as dhāraṇā, which wards off the bonds of worldly existence.

"Having an equal mind toward all beings, whether situated in oneself or others, in this world— 'I am Śiva, I am non-dual'— this is remembered as the supreme samādhi. This consists of a firm conviction arising from pure knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*), characterized by the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of "I-ness" and "this-ness."
Concentration.
Thus, according to the system set forth by the venerable Lord Mṛtyujit, through practices such as *dhāraṇā* (concentration) and others,
there occurs only immersion into the Supreme Reality (*paratattva-samāveśa*), and not limited supernatural powers (*mitasiddhi*).
Thus it is said:
"From the victory over delusion and from infinite enjoyment, the innate..."
Victory through knowledge. || 7 ||
From the victory—that is, the overcoming—of Māyā, which consists of delusion (moha) and has as its nature the fetter (pāśa) culminating in non-apprehension (akhyāti).
Of what kind [is it]? It is such that its extent (ābhoga), or expansion, reaches to the end of the subsiding of latent impressions (saṃskāra).
Through such passages as "of the phenomenon that is beginningless sensation...

and so forth, there occurs the victory—that is, the attainment—of innate gnosis (*sahajavidyā*), whose nature has been thus defined. This is because it has been stated that even the individual means (*āṇavopāya*) culminates in the empowered means (*śāktopāya*); [therefore, the individual meditative absorption (*samādhāna*) which is conducive to meditation...]

The meaning is: because of resting completely within the *śākta* [power], which is the means (*upāya*) consisting of pure conceptualization (*vikalpa*). And likewise, in the venerable *Svacchanda*, up to the level of *samanā*, the elevenfold *māntra* resonance (*dhvani*) is as follows: the vowel *a*, the vowel *u*, and the consonant *m*.

The Bindu, Ardhacandra, Nirodhī, Nāda, Nādānta, Śakti, Vyāpinī, and Samanā—this group of six, together with their cause, consists of the manifestation of duality and is like a web of fetters; therefore, it is to be abandoned. Beyond this, because it consists of non-dual awareness (*abheda-vimarśa*), it is to be accepted. "O Varārohā" means one whose ascent (*āroha*) is excellent (*vara*) and supreme.
[The vocative address "O Varārohā" refers to her whose rest is in the twelve-finger space (dvādaśānta) of power. Having begun with: "O Varārohā, the endless web of bonds...
[the text continues].

87) The "contemplation of the bonds" (*pāśāvalokana*)— the contemplation of the bonds ending with *samanā*, the conceiving of them as one's own self, and the essential nature which is pure consciousness transcending the bonds— this constitutes the extent of the pervasiveness of the Self.
For when one abandons the observation of one's own nature, this becomes the pervasion of the self; otherwise, it is the pervasion of Śiva.

When one meditates upon those qualities— such as omniscience and the rest— which are attributes consisting of omniscience, omnipotence, and so forth, and which are "objects" (arthas) because they are sought after as being supremely worthy of attainment; and when one encompasses those all-pervading qualities in their entirety without exception through internal differentiation, then the perfection of that meditation is achieved for oneself.

And that pervasion by Śiva is the cause, in the form of an instrumental factor, for the manifestation [of Śiva] within the consciousness of the practitioner; it is effective precisely through His grace, because of the firm rooting of that contemplation in the pure self. When one contemplates those objects as pervasive, this pervasion by Śiva occurs, appearing as the cause within consciousness.

By this passage, it is stated that through the conquest of delusion—which culminates in the pervasion of the self—one attains the innate wisdom (*sahajavidyā*), which consists of the pervasion of Unmanā-Śiva. As it is said in that very same [text]: "Having then abandoned the principle of the self (*ātmatattva*), one should apply oneself to the principle of wisdom (*vidyātattva*)."
That state is to be known as *unmanā*; "mind" (*manaḥ*) is said to be volitional construction (*saṃkalpa*).

"From *saṃkalpa* (volition), knowledge arises sequentially; the *unmana* state stands simultaneously. [The word "one should unite the self" is to be supplied. That is *vidyā*; *saṃkalpa* is desire (*icchā*), and because it consists in the threading together of the sequence of the universe that is to be governed by the Lord, it is said to be "knowledge arising sequentially. It is *unmana*.

The state where the mind has transcended (*utkrānta*) and reached its highest excellence (*utkarṣa*) is *unmana*. This occurs simultaneously because even the universe—which is divided into hundreds of infinite branches such as its initial projection (*āsūtraṇa*), manifestation (*avabhāsana*), and construction (*nirmāṇa*)—abides here as the very self of the radiance of the power of absolute freedom (*svātantrya-śakti*), which is a mass of eternally arisen bliss. Therefore, it is of such a nature.
Unmanā is indeed knowledge itself; she is the power Unmanā. Therefore, she is the supreme Vidyā, because no other exists beyond her.
Because it brings about the realization that the nature of phenomena such as sensation is the supreme self,
and because it leads to the abandonment of what is not the supreme self, it is therefore called "knowledge" (vidyā).
Abiding there—abiding in the Vidyā—he should recognize his own nature as that of the uncontracted Supreme Śiva;
he should manifest that supreme light, the ultimate cause.
Thus [ends verse 7].
Thus, having attained innate gnosis (sahajavidyā), he is the one who possesses a second hand [of power] while awake. || 8 ||

Even having attained pure knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*), while remaining vigilant in its singular pervasion— that is, while maintaining one-pointedness toward that knowledge— whatever second object of awareness characterized by "this-ness" (*idantā*) exists in relation to one's own "I-ness" (*ahantā*) which consists of full self-reflection, [that is what is meant].

[In relation to the light of one's own self-experience, there is a second form consisting of power. The world, whose nature is the manifestation of the object of cognition, becomes such that its rays are His hands; the meaning is that the universe flashes forth as if it were His own radiance. As it has been said in the *Śrīvijñānabhairava*:

Wherever— in the case of blue, pleasure, and so forth— the consciousness (*caitanya*), which is the light of awareness (*cit-prakāśa*) of the all-pervasive Self, the Supreme Bhairava, is manifested and vibrates through the path of the senses, that is, the hollow channels of the eyes and other organs, that object such as "blue" possesses that [consciousness] alone as its essential nature (*tanmātra-dharmitva*); for were it separate from consciousness, it would necessarily follow that it lacks the status of being an object of cognition (*cetyatva*).

Having contemplated that its essential nature is pure consciousness, like the various reflections appearing in a mere mirror, he who dissolves into that very Consciousness which serves as the foundation of the universe attains the state of Supreme Bhairava; just as light itself, when condensed,
becomes the solar orb, so too is Consciousness itself, when congealed, the world.

The sacred tradition states: "It shines. Wherever the consciousness of the All-pervasive Lord is manifested through the path of the senses, because that [consciousness] possesses that [organ] as its sole attribute, there arises the state of being a full self through absorption into consciousness (cillaya).
Thus it is said. Also, in the *Śrīsarvamaṅgalā*, it is stated:
"Power (*śakti*) and the possessor of power (*śaktimān*) are declared to be the two fundamental categories (*padārtha*)."
The entire universe is his power, while Maheśvara is the possessor of that power.
Thus [ends the eighth].
And such is this Self, always permeated by the reflective awareness of its own essential nature—a dancer. (9)

It dances, its root being the support of its own concealed essential nature, manifesting as the manifold expansion of various stages such as waking and so forth (the term "and so forth" including dreaming and deep sleep as objects of perception);
preceded by the unfolding of the powers of will and the rest, it produces these various stages without any collection of material causes or instrumental factors.
The meaning is that He causes [the universe] to unfold upon the very wall of consciousness. By the mere play of His own vibration, He manifests [it] upon His own wall;
thus, the Self is a dancer. This has been stated in the seventh chapter of the *Śrīnaiśvāsadevīmaheśvaranartaka*, in the hymn composed by the Goddess:

You are the inner self (antarātmā) by virtue of one part; being bound by auspicious and inauspicious latent impressions (vāsanās) through its connection with the subtle body of eight constituents (puryaṣṭaka), it wanders from womb to womb. Because it dwells within both the self and the non-self, it is to be known as the "inner self" (antarātmā), like a guardian of a storehouse.
The meaning is: one who protects his own essential nature as the Supreme Self; he is a dancer and a protector of the treasure-house.
Thus it is said. Bhaṭṭa Śrī Nārāyaṇa also [describes it as] "containing within its womb all the seeds of the existent" (*visṛṣṭāśeṣasadbījagarbham*);

that is, that in whose womb (*garbha*) all the seeds (*bīja*) of the existents (*satām bhāvānām*), such as *māyā*, *prakṛti*, and so forth, have been emitted (*visṛṣṭa*). In the context of drama, these are known by terms such as *bīja* (the seed).

Apart from you, what other poet—author—is capable of composing this *Trailokya-nāṭaka* (the drama of the three worlds), which is well-known according to that [dramaturgical] treatise, to be introduced for the sake of its destruction and pacification through the *mukha-sandhi* (opening juncture), and to be brought to its conclusion through the *nirvahaṇa-sandhi* (concluding juncture)? The meaning is: none at all. [The *Trailokya-nāṭaka*.]
Having introduced the subject, who other than you is capable of destroying it? O Hara! Who else is a true poet (kavi) able to do so?
Thus it is said in the *Śrīpratyabhijñā*, the secret essence (*upaniṣad*) of all scriptures:
"The director of the drama of transmigratory existence, who remains awake while the world sleeps."
The Supreme Lord is indeed one alone.
Thus [ends the ninth].
The inner self is the stage for this dancer of the world's drama who assumes such various roles. 10.

It is called the *raṅga* (the stage) because the Self takes delight therein with the intention of displaying the drama of the world-play; it is the locus for assuming various roles, the inner self (*antarātmā*) whose true nature is the manifestation of contraction, and which—
predominantly consisting of either the void (*śūnya*) or the vital breath (*prāṇa*)— is of the form of the *puryaṣṭaka* (the eightfold city), situated within relative to the body.

The individual soul (*jīva*) is constrained by the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*), for within the state of being a living soul, the vital breath and the subtle body are primary. In that state, this [soul] has established its footing through the sequence of the vibration of its own instruments; it is the internal vibration of the senses, which consists of the manifestation of the power of innate sovereignty.
It manifests the drama of the universe. And it is said in the *Śrī-svacchanda* (p.
"He who, having entered the *puryaṣṭaka*, wanders through all wombs, possesses a body consisting of nothing but the *kañcukas*."

The self that is dissolved in primordial nature (prakṛti)— meaning, due to its connection with the constituent elements that initiate this very subtle internal body and being impelled by latent impressions (vāsanā), it goes to another womb—
should be known as the inner self (antarātmā).
Thus [ends the tenth].
Thus, the senses are the spectators of this [Self] as it dances upon the stage of the inner self. || 11 ||

For the yogin’s senses, such as the eyes and so forth, inwardly realize their own true nature— which is filled with the joy of manifesting the drama of saṃsāra— and through the deepening of that performance, they bring about a state of fullness of the aesthetic flavor of wonder, in which all divisions have dissolved.

The meaning is that, through the firmness of cultivating the wonder (*camatkāra*) of the "I-ness" (*ahantā*), one experiences wonder while cognizing one's own self as "I am Śiva," free from the distinction of "I am this [world]" (*aham idam*). As the Śruti says:
A certain wise man, having turned his gaze inward, beheld the inner Self, attaining immortality.
(Kaṭhopaniṣad, Chapter 2, Section 4, Verse 1).
Thus [ends the section]. || 11 ||
And for this [entity], the establishment of its existence is through the power of cognition. (12)
*dhīḥ* is the intellect (*dhiṣaṇā*) expert in discerning the true nature [of reality];
by virtue of that, there arises the subtle internal vibration of the *sattva*, which is of the nature of radiance. (p. 92)

Success is manifestation. And in drama, the success of the *sāttvika* expression (*abhinaya*) arises precisely from skill of intellect—the grammatical connection being that "the success of the *sāttvika* form of expression" [is achieved thus]. *Sāttvika* refers to the imitation of the states of persons such as Sītā, Rāma, and Yudhiṣṭhira, characterized by paralysis, perspiration, and so forth. The term *sāttvika* is also indicative of the *vācika* (verbal) and other forms of expression.

Thus, precisely because of the attainment of being whose essence is vibration—[the meaning is: because of the acquisition of being whose nature is the manifestation of the power of absolute freedom]—this yogi’s independent state is established. || 13 ||

The perfected one (*siddha*) is one who has attained an independent state (*svatantrabhāva*), which is the sovereignty that brings the entire universe under its control, consisting of innate knowledge and agency. As it was said by the venerable Śrīnātha: "One should take refuge in the power of sovereignty; they call that the immortal digit within the sixteen-fold person."

The power of absolute freedom (*svātantrya-śakti*), whose nature has been thus described, impels, reflects upon, casts forth, emits, withdraws, calculates, and knows; she is Kālī, who protects the universe by means of its internal and external forms—thus [it is said]. Also in the *Śrī-svacchanda*:
p.
93) All principles (*tattva*): because all that is knowable shines forth as one with one's own self, which is non-different from Śiva, there is a reflective awareness (*parāmarśana*).

Indeed, the principles consist of the elements such as water and fire; the beings consist of predatory animals and the like; and the phonemes (*varṇa*) reside within the body of the mass of sounds (*śabdarāśi*).
The beings and the mantra-syllables that are remembered always remain under his control;
indeed, they are eternally subject to him through constant meditation on Śiva.
Thus [ends the section]. 13.
This is his state of independence—
just as it is there, so it is elsewhere.
In whatever body the manifestation of the yogin has arisen, that [manifestation] occurs for him everywhere else as well, provided he remains constantly attentive.

[The meaning is that for the attentive yogin, there is the emergence of sovereignty even in the transition to another body, in the act of departing from the body, and so forth. As it is said in the venerable *Svacchanda*:

"Free-willed indeed, free-willed, one should always wander free-willed. This means that due to the excellence of yoga, he remains constantly vibrating as this very Śrī Svacchandabhairava at the beginning, middle, and end.
Thus it is stated in the *Śrī Spanda* as well:

Through that effort, one attains this intention: that very reality, by the power of contact with which even this ordinary, insentient wheel of external and internal sense organs becomes capable of conscious activities such as engagement, is clearly manifested as the Self.
Just as there is independence in bringing about the consciousness of the senses, it is indeed capable of attaining independence with respect to all objects;

therefore, one must diligently examine that reality by which, when independence is manifested even at the stage of practice, such play as entering the bodies of others becomes possible. One must examine that reality with earnestness.
For this independence of his is everywhere uncreated.
Thus [ends the section]. 14.
(94) Even so, he should not remain indifferent; rather—there must be attention to the seed. 15.
The word "must be performed" is the ellipsis. The seed is the cause of the universe, the supreme power whose nature is vibration (*sphurattā*). As it is said in the venerable *Mṛtyujidbhaṭṭāraka*:
"She is the womb of all the gods and of the powers in their manifold forms."
The womb consists of Agni and Soma; from that [arise] dissolution and creation, means of knowledge and objects of knowledge, and so forth.
In this regard, one should repeatedly apply the mind—that is, fix the consciousness—upon the seed which is the nature of the Supreme Power. 15.
This being so, that yogi, remaining seated, joyfully sinks into the lake. || 16 ||
*Āsana* is that in which one sits (*āsya-te*) eternally and remains in a state of absolute unity; it is the supreme *śākta* power.
He who abides therein has abandoned all effort associated with activities such as meditation (*dhyāna*) and concentration (*dhāraṇā*) regarding the higher and lower levels.
(Śākta, p. 95)

He who, through constant inward-turnedness, reflects upon that very [reality], experiences bliss effortlessly— that [reality] which is the cause for the flow of the universal stream into the lake, and which possesses clarity,
effervescence, and so forth; [in this context, "clarity" (*svacchatā*) is the capacity to receive the reflection of the universe.]

The state of surging forth (*ucchalattā*) is the capacity to manifest as this or that objective form, independent of the collection of causes consisting of place, time, shape, and material substrate; it plunges into the ocean of supreme nectar (*parāmṛta*) and becomes one with it through the crushing of the latent impressions of contraction such as the body and so forth. As it has been said:
Meditation on the venerable Śrī Mṛtyujit Bhaṭṭāraka himself— not only above [at the *dvādaśānta*], nor below [at the *kanda* and so forth], but also in the middle [at the heart and so forth],
in front, behind, and on both sides, in the form of Tatpuruṣa, Sadyojāta, and the others.
One should not apply it below, nor in the middle;
neither in front, nor behind, nor on either side, nor even on both sides at once.
It does not abide within the body. [Regarding "not within the body":

one should contemplate that [light], which, from its base, consists of a radiance like rays, subtler than the subtle, until it reaches the end of the twelve [finger-breadths] and subsides; this is the arising of Bhairava.]
Thus it is said: "It is not external"—when another object is being cognized, there is emptiness regarding all objects of cognition.
Meditating upon that very [emptiness] with the mind, one attains peace even while [the world] is known.
Thus it is said: "Not as space"—
when the sky is variegated by light from the sun, a lamp, or other sources,
one should fix the gaze upon that very [light], and therein one's own self-nature shines forth.
Thus it is said:
by standing in a great pit such as a well and looking upward,
for one whose mind is free from conceptual construction, the dissolution of the mind occurs clearly and immediately and perfectly.
As it has been said: "But one should not meditate on anything external;
one should not fix the focal point in space, nor should one cast the gaze downward."
p.
96) It is not the closing of the eyes; [it is not the closing of the eyes—just so, having closed the eyes and so forth, one sees a blackish appearance before oneself].
Having expanded his form into that of Bhairava, he should contemplate it and become absorbed in that state.
Thus it is said: "The binding of the gaze"—one should cast the gaze upon a place such as one devoid of trees, mountains, or walls.
When the mental state has dissolved, one becomes one whose mental fluctuations have ceased.
Thus it is said: that which is relied upon is the "support" (avalamba), namely the aspect of the object of meditation.
When that [reliance] is abandoned in terms of its objective state, consciousness itself, being ceased, does not proceed toward another state of being;
then, by means of abiding in the midst of that, the supreme cultivation blossoms.
Thus it is said: "Without support" means that, having understood both states through knowledge, one should take recourse in the middle;
and by simultaneously abandoning the two, reality shines forth in the middle.

Thus it is said: "That which exists together with an object is 'with an object' (sālamba); one should fix the mind upon the knowledge that possesses a form (sākārajñāna), whether through desire or once that knowledge has arisen.
Therein, with a mind undistracted by intellect, from that [state] there will be the vision of the Self."
Thus it is said: "Nothing whatsoever is a bond of views;
one should not cultivate anything as having a support, as being without support, or even as having a support."

Not the senses—not the senses means that, according to the principle stated in the chapter on *dhāraṇā*, having abandoned everything, one who is established in *samādhi* is intent upon the contemplation of his own true nature by virtue of not thinking of anything;
he is absorbed in that, merged in the state of bliss, and consists of the knowledge of the single flavor (*samarasa*). Not the elements.
Having thus abandoned sound, touch, taste, and the rest, one established in samādhi should become solely absorbed in that [reality].
p.
97) That state—which is such a condition—is the Śiva-state, the state of liberation;
it is the stage where the manifestation of objects of knowledge (*vedya-ullāsa*) never again appears, and thus one turns back and abandons the worldly condition.
This is the meaning: [it is said that] the supreme state of Śiva, the Supreme Self, is the state beyond all appearance (nirābhāsa); having attained that, one does not return.
Thus [ends the section]. || 16 ||
Thus,

the yogi— whose nature is pure *vidyā* emerging from the conquest of delusion attained through the sequence of the *āṇava* means beginning with the withdrawal of the channels (*nāḍī-saṃhāra*)— [proceeds].
He brings about the manifestation of his own measure. || 17 ||

The *mātrā*—that is, a portion consisting of the solidification of the essence of consciousness (*cidrasa*)—belonging to one's own consciousness, brings about a manifestation whose nature consists in the appearance of the desired object and subject; it displays [this] as something created.
As it is said in the venerable *Svacchanda*:

That very [reality]—because the venerable Lord Svatantra-natha, who is Svacchanda-bhairava and whose essence is Great Light, manifests through his own sovereignty as a gross appearance—is itself conditioned by the manifestation of diverse objects of cognition.
For the all-pervasive Light manifests as the pervaded; indeed, that which is called "the pervaded" is not distinct from it.
Therefore, the meaning is that this limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is not distinct from the essence of consciousness (*cittattva*). O Beloved, by virtue of its gross limiting adjunct, it becomes gross;
yet that single reality remains established through the distinction between the gross and the subtle.
Thus, even in recognition (pratyabhijñā),
by virtue of such pure sovereignty (śuddhasvātantrya), the Self is not at that time separate from it.

One understands an object that has attained stability; however, by virtue of its unconditioned power, it makes even the unknowable Self an object of knowledge (*jñeya*). The intended meaning is that if [the Self] were dependent on a separate object of knowledge, its status as the agent of cognition (*jñāna-kartṛtā*) would fade away and its nature as the Knower (*jñātṛtva*) would be lost.
Thus, this [Self] may indeed make [itself] an object of knowledge while remaining in a state of distinctness.
The object of knowledge is not, however, .......................................... ||
Thus, it is stated even in the Āgama:

"Just as there is the absence of the essence of water and its solidification in the case of water and ice, so too, in the case of Śiva and the world which consists of His power, there is the absence of the essence of consciousness and its solidification, due to the perception thereof."

For those whose hearts are purified by the expansion of the Supreme Śakti, there is no further subsequent birth; for even while remaining in this present life as one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), the body will cease once the experience of *ārabdha-karma* is exhausted.
And he who knows the "Him" from the oral tradition of the Guru, O Dear One—
For him there is indeed nothing further to be done; he possesses his final birth.
It was stated with this very intention:
"He whose consciousness perceives this entire world as play—he, seeing thus, is constantly disciplined and is liberated while living; of this there is no doubt."
Thus, this has been established in the Spanda [Kārikās]. || 17 ||
And it is not thus that for him who possesses a body composed of both *bhūta* (elements) and *bhāva* (mental states), fashioned by his own power— [for his body is twofold,
consisting of the elemental and the mental]— there occurs, at the moment of perceiving an object, a forgetting of his true nature due to the overwhelming majesty of the power of *māyā*.
This individual soul (*jīva*), its power contracted through a lack of awareness of its own true nature (*svarūpa*), perceives that which is the locus of the limited ego (*avacchinna-ahaṃkāra*)—

namely, the body possessed of a head, hands, and so forth— as being composed of the elements (*bhūtātmaka*), because it consists of the products of creation and the like. However, that which it perceives as distinct, by way of objects such as sound and the rest, is [of a different nature].

[It is of the nature of existence. But when the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) is investigated, these two are indeed distinct from themselves, because there is no difference in their being perceived as having a body. [Regarding this, he says that some form of bondage, such as birth and so forth—p. 99)]—he says:
With the destruction of ignorance comes the destruction of birth. || 18 ||

When there is the non-destruction—that is, the constant manifestation—of the aforementioned innate wisdom (*sahajavidyā*), there occurs the cessation of birth, which has ignorance as its cause and karma as its auxiliary cause [the word "ignorance" here means *apūrṇamanyatā* (the sense of being incomplete);
"auxiliary" means that which supports or strengthens]; and the cessation of the aggregate consisting of the body, senses, and so forth, which is composed of suffering.
Destruction—that is, utter dissolution—has indeed been accomplished. As it is stated in the *Śrīkaṇṭhī*:
"Having abandoned the world of manifestation characterized by what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted, as well as grass and the like, leaves, stones, and all that is moving and unmoving."

From Śiva down to the earth, everything augmented by existence and non-existence is composed of Śiva. The very abandonment of the inclination toward the expansion of objects of knowledge (*prameya*) is the process of making the universe—
which prior to creation was merely the unmanifested Śiva— consist of the unsurpassed Śiva who is identical with the universe.
The meaning is: because of abiding in identity with the very nature of the essence of consciousness; having meditated thus, one shall not undergo birth again.
Thus, in the *Śrī-svacchanda*, it is said:

"One's own nirvāṇa is the path to liberation because it consists of the supreme non-duality; for this very reason, it is supremely pure, more excellent even than the states of Sadāśiva and others who are both pure and impure, and belongs to the Gurus."

"Tradition" (*pārampara*) means that which has come down through a lineage (*pāramparya*), beginning from Supreme Bhairava and His Power, through Sadāśiva, Īśāna, and so forth, until it reaches the disciple.
One who is liberated [from the bonds] shall, at the end of the body, go and attain identity with That. "Supreme" (*para*) means pure, having come down through the succession of gurus.
Having known that, one is liberated; having gone there, one is not born again.
Thus, in the *Śrīmṛtyujit* as well (p.
it is said that [the reality] is free from the three principles (*tattva*)— namely, those called Nara, Śakti, and Śiva.

Having directly realized— by means of the divine path of yoga, through the method of relying on non-conceptual awareness that dawns upon the abandonment of conceptual construction— that which is eternal, irreversible, immovable, unchanging, stable, and constant, like the doctrine of *vivarta* (illusory manifestation) yet not grasping at other forms as distinct from the unreal, one attains freedom from rebirth.
[He] does not return; [that state is] eternal, immovable, and constant.
Having seen it by means of the divine path of yoga, one is not born again.
Thus [ends the section]. 18.

But when his true nature as Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā) sinks away, then— within the groups of consonants beginning with *ka*— reside Māheśvarī and the others, the Mothers of the bound souls (paśu). || 19 ||

The intended meaning is that even though they have ascended to the abode of the supreme reality (*paratattva*), the Mātṛkās— possessing sovereignty over those bound souls (*paśu*) who, despite being established there, fall into negligence—

delude them by generating verbal cognitions consisting of the "supreme-non-supreme" (*parāpara*) nature, thereby causing them to never rest in their own supreme essence. The word "they become" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.

That power which consists of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), which is inherent (*samavāyinī*) because it is inseparable from the supreme subject and is thus identical with his very self— by virtue of its nature as an initial surging forth and its inherent desire to manifest externally,
it attains the state of Will (*icchā*). This power is declared to be the inherent cause of the universe.
O Goddess, that [will] becomes the desire of Him who wishes to create;
hear how, though being one, it attains multiplicity.

"It must be known that this is so, and not otherwise"—this is well-ascertained. Because it makes known [the object] here in the world as distinct from the subject (pramātṛ), such as the imagined void (śūnya) belonging to māyā, it is called the power of knowledge (jñānaśakti). [The phrase "this is that" refers to: because it makes known [the object] as distinct from the subject (pramātṛ) such as the imagined void (śūnya) belonging to māyā, it is called the power of knowledge (jñānaśakti).
Furthermore, when one thinks, "May this thing become such as it is," and it has indeed come to be so,
the activity performed at that very moment is what is called "action" (kriyā) in this context.

This sovereign power of absolute freedom (*svātantrya-śakti*) of the Supreme Lord— which unfolds the manifold expansion of various diverse stages rooted in the concealment of His own essential nature— is that very power which constitutes each respective subject.
Thus, although it possesses these two forms, it again attains infinity through its further divisions.
By the power of the adjunct of her purpose, she has become like a wish-fulfilling gem, the Sovereign Lady.

In that regard, first, she who has entered the state of being a Mother (mātṛbhāva) is distinguished as twofold and ninefold, because she gives birth to the world consisting of the signified and the signifier; and [she is so called] because even the seed-syllable (kūṭabīja) is accepted as having the nature of other groups [of phonemes].
Mālinī consists of nine elements and likewise fifty elements.

Due to the division into the nature of seed (bīja) and womb (yoni), there are two types; the vowels are considered the seed, while the consonants beginning with *ka* are remembered as the womb, which is ninefold according to the division of the classes (*varga*).
In this context, Śiva is designated as the seed (bīja) and Śakti as the womb (yoni);
through the division of the eight groups of letters, there is the group of eight beginning with Māheśvarī.

Distinguished by the differentiation of each individual phoneme, she blazes with fifty rays; [the term "fifty" refers to her radiance as the fifty Śaktis, established as the designators of the fifty Rudras who constitute the designated.]
She is established as the designator of the Rudras, corresponding in number to them.

Thus, according to the principle established in the *Śrīmālinīvijaya*, the supreme speech (*parāvāk*) of the Supreme Lord, as it unfolds, assumes the nature of the *mātṛkā*— consisting of the forms from 'a' to 'kṣa' which denote [the powers] such as Will, Knowledge, Action, Śiva, Śakti, and Māheśvarī—
and becomes non-conceptual within all subjects.

102) In the states of various cognitions accompanied by conceptualization (*savikalpaka*), [the powers] perform the interpenetration of gross and subtle sounds through the nature of internal reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), thereby establishing the categories.

Veiling its own nature as the uncontracted, independent mass of consciousness (*ciddhana*), it brings about the state of being composed of the contracted, dependent body and so forth. This has also been stated in the *Śrītimirodghāṭa*:
"Residing within the space of consciousness (the void called Brahman) situated in the center of the consciousness within the cavity of the heart..."
The Mothers of the bound souls (paśu-mātaraḥ), beginning with Māheśvarī, are designated as "most terrible" (ghorataryaḥ) because they are intent on manifesting knowledge characterized by duality;
they cause the bound soul to fall downward by relying upon the Brahma-knot, which is difficult to sever. As it has been said:
Those [powers] which, embracing the rudra-aṇus, cause the atoms who are completely absorbed in sense objects to fall lower and lower,
are known as the "more terrible" (ghoratara) others.
Thus:
"Ghora" refers to that which is called the net of bonds (*pāśajāla*), joined with evil and terrifying.
And: "Those who hang from the bonds of Brahmā."
The mistresses of the seats, most terrible, delude [beings] again and again.

This was previously stated as well. It was said in general that "Mātṛkā is the locus of knowledge" (1.4); however, this [statement] is made with the intention that even one who has attained reality may be deluded by Māheśī and the others—who, though they are the presiding deities over bound souls (paśu)—through the medium of the permeation of sound, should he become negligent.
The distinction. || 19 ||

Since this is so, he says that the yogi must remain vigilant in all states so that the nature of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*), even though attained through the aforementioned arguments, does not perish: (p. 103) ...therefore, the yogi must be attentive at all times so that [the nature of Pure Knowledge], although attained by the aforementioned methods of reasoning, does not perish. Thus he says:
The fourth [element] should be poured like oil into the three.

In the three states beginning with waking, the fourth state— which is of the nature of the light of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*) and consists of the essence of the bliss of *turya*— should be poured like oil; just as oil, spreading more and more gradually, pervades its receptacle, so too should it be infused into all three states.

By means of the surging *turya-rasa* (the essence of the fourth state) that vibrates at the two extremities— the beginning and the end— which consist of the cessation of *unmeṣa* (expansion), one should pervade even the intermediate state through the method of firm support (*avaṣṭambha-yukti*), whereby one may attain the state of *tamayī-bhāva* (the nature of darkness/absorption).
This applies to the *unmeṣa* characterized by the manifestation of the creation of the universe, as well as to the states of waking and so forth.

Because of the subsiding [of all else] at the initial and final limits, the essence of the pervasive fourth light (*turyaprakāśa*) alone is tasted; therefore, even the unfolding of the form of emanation (*sṛṣṭirūponmeṣa*) must be made to consist of the essence of the fourth through firm practice of focused attention upon that—this is the meaning. Thus, the full enjoyment of the fourth state arises within waking, dreaming, and deep sleep.

(1–7) By this, the state of pure existence (*sattāmātra*) of the Fourth (*turya*) has been described for one who maintains the support of the contemplation of the wheel of power (*śakticakra*) through exertion, even in states such as waking which flow forth by their own inherent nature. (1–11) "The Lord of Heroes (*vīreśa*) is the enjoyer of the triad. Thus [it is said].
p.

104) By means of the method of "forceful ripening" (haṭhapāka) which is consistent with the Śāmbhava-upāya— [the process of haṭhapāka being that ripening which occurs through force (haṭhena), characterized by the bypassing of stages (kramātikrama), consisting of sudden instruction and so forth, and occurring by way of compulsion].
The realization [of all things] as the fire of consciousness (*cidagni*) and the gradual dissolution of its adjuncts (*upādhi*), such as creation and so forth—this is the method (*yukti*);
the meaning is that it conforms to the specific *śāmbhavopāya*, by virtue of the authority of an extremely intense descent of power (*tīvratara-śaktipāta*).

Thus, the withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) of the waking state and the others has been shown. But by this aphorism, [the process is shown] through the method of firm support (*avaṣṭambha-yukti*) appropriate to the *āṇavopāya*.

The triad beginning with waking, when moistened by the nectar of the Fourth (turya), is to be cultivated; this is what has been stated, and this is the distinction. [The term *dalakalpa* means that just as a scabbard (*dala*) is distinct from the sword, so too [the triad] appears as separate.
This is the specific point.
Regarding this, he states the means: "In this case—[that is, during the waking and other states]—when there is an effusion like oil, one who is submerged should enter by means of one's own mind. (21)

Having abandoned the gross state of the vital breaths and so forth—[the gross being the nature of exhalation, inhalation, and so on; that which follows immediately after it is the subtle, internal form consisting of exhaling and inhaling through the middle path; and that which transcends even that is the vibration whose essence is the prior radiance of consciousness distinct from the vital breath]— [Note: The bracketed portion provides a commentary on the terms *sthūla*, *sūkṣma*, and *tadatīta* as they relate to the states of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).]
Then there is the subtle, and the inner;
from which the supreme vibration, beyond even the subtle, is attained.
Having begun thus...
one should enter that with one's own mind.
Thus, according to the method established by the venerable Lord Mṛtyujit, through *prāṇāyāma*, *dhyāna*, and so forth—

by means of one's own consciousness (*svacittena*), which, having first abandoned the tendency toward the contraction of objects of thought, consists of uncontracted consciousness; this is the meaning.
"Because of the realization of identity through the manifestation of that consciousness"—
thus, according to the perspective of the *Spanda*, having first made the disciple's self one in flavor with one's own self within oneself,
and having transcended up to the level of *Samanā*, one should establish a firm state in the pure Self by means of the nature of awakened consciousness.
By means of non-conceptual awareness (*avikalpasaṃvit*) alone, one should unite with Śiva, beginning with the entry into the power of the Transmental (*unmanāśakti*).

One should enter—that is, fully immerse oneself—into that consciousness by way of its non-conceptual form, which consists of the wonder of inward-turned internal reflective awareness (*antarvimarśa*). Being of what nature? Immersed right there in the state of being a subject (*pramātṛtā*) consisting of the body, vital breath, and so forth.

By immersing oneself in the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) of the wonder of consciousness (*ciccamatkāra*), one pacifies [the mind]; as it is said in the venerable *Svacchanda*: "Having abandoned mental activity, one should unite with the nature of pure awareness;
then, becoming Śiva, the bound soul (*paśu*) is liberated from the ocean of worldly existence."
Thus it is said. Also in the *Śrīvijñānabhaṭṭāraka*:

"O Dear One, when this quartet—the mind (*mānasa*), consciousness (*cetanā*), power (*śakti*), and the self (*ātman*)—is completely dissolved, then that is the body of Bhairava (*bhairava-vapuḥ*). [The mind consists of volition.]
Volition (*cetanā*), intellect (*buddhi*), power (*śakti*), and that which is called vital breath (*prāṇa*)— the self conditioned by these four constitute the limited subject.
When this tetrad is completely dissolved and has attained the state of the wonder of pure consciousness (*ciccamatkāra*), then that aforementioned body of Bhairava manifests.

Thus it is said. In this very *Jñānagarbha-stotra*, having set aside all mental activities, O Mother, [the state] shines forth, being entirely liberated from dependence on the pursuit of the functions of the senses.
By remaining steadfast through your power, men immediately experience that supreme state which flows with the nectar of tireless and incomparable bliss— [a state] mental in nature.
With conceptual thought, memory, and so forth as the instruments—

the instrument known as the "divine instrument" consisting of the binding of mudrās such as the upward *ūrdhvarecaka*— the state of unsurpassed bliss is experienced by yogins thus immersed in the Śāmbhava means.
Thus, this was composed by the great gurus. || 21 ||
And thus, for this one who has entered the supreme state— the solar orb of consciousness which is the abode of emission— it is his very nature,
by virtue of the inherent character of reality, to be intent upon the outward expansion of the multitude of rays whose essence is the desire to sport with the various objects of the universe.
Because its nature is that of the one who reflects back; furthermore, when there is outward expansion, then—there is equal vision in the activity of the vital breath (prāṇa). || 22 ||
Of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) which has been refined by the fragrance of Śakti consisting of the nature of mutual throbbing—

by the power of internal support characterized by the complete unfolding of all knots, wherein all the knots consisting of bonds are assimilated into one's own self— of such an internal essential nature.

By the power of the objective support (*ālambanabala*): "Ā" refers to the slight, slow, and gentle movement or expansion; "sama" refers to the vision or perception which is of a single form due to its nature as a mass of consciousness-bliss (*cidānandaghanātmatā*). This very state of the conscious being, whose essence is life, is itself the universal vibration (*sāmānyaspanda*) that exists even in insentient things such as the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
That which accomplishes the state of being conscious as "I"— consisting of the reflective awareness of the conceptualization "I"—

assumes a fivefold nature through its specific forms such as the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth. Therefore, the states beginning with waking and ending with that which transcends the fourth (*turyātīta*), which exist by depending upon the expansion of the vital breath and so on, would otherwise [not exist].

Since emergence (*vyutthāna*) is impossible in the states of the Fourth (*turya*) and Beyond-the-Fourth (*turyātīta*), the yogis emerge [from those states] precisely because of the existence of the activity of the vital breath (*prāṇavṛtti*).

Therefore, the intended meaning is that in the first three states, which are to be abandoned, the object of knowledge is experienced as being of the nature of consciousness (*cidātmatayā*). That is to say, this occurs for him in all conditions. And it has been said:
In the Śrīmadānandabhairava (p.
Having abandoned worldly conduct, one should take refuge in non-duality, which bestows liberation.

He is equal toward all deities— [meaning he is one who contemplates the identity with the conscious self (cidātman) of the substances belonging to the gods, such as Anāśrita, Sadāśiva, Īśvara, and others, as well as milk, wine, and so forth]— and likewise toward the system of castes, stages of life, and the like.
"One who perceives the equality of all things is liberated from all bonds.
For this very reason, in the *Śrī-Pratyabhijñā*,
it is said that even when the expansion of intellect and vital breath occurs, for those whose contraction has not been induced by the appropriation of external locations and so forth—
"For those who have not contracted [their nature]" means for those who have not performed the concealment of the true nature of consciousness;
it is precisely the attainment of the essential nature of the universal Self.
Thus it has been said. || 22 ||

But when he does not thus enter the state beyond the fourth (*turyātīta*), which is attainable through the excellence of the support provided by inward-turned attention to the fourth state (*turya*), but instead remains satisfied with merely the aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*) of the fourth state experienced at its prior and posterior limits, then for him—
In the middle, there is the production of the inferior. || 23 ||
