For one who tastes the flavor of the Fourth (turya) at both the prior and posterior limits, there occurs in the middle—the intermediate state—a lesser birth, which consists of the manifestation of duality; this happens only in the intermediate state, not everywhere.
"Lesser" means inferior; "birth" refers to emergence (vyutthāna).

(108) A contemptible creation does not arise for the Self; rather, according to the principle of the stated aphorism—"But upon the cessation of knowledge, there is no vision of dreams arising from that"—it means that [the individual] is perpetually deluded. Thus it has been said.
In the *Śrīmālinīvijaya*,

even upon attaining the mere latent impression (*vāsanā*), one who remains vigilant in the savoring of the nectar of his own true nature— which is a mass of consciousness and bliss— possesses the refinement of meditative absorption (*samādhāna-saṃskāra*).

The meaning is that for one who is negligent regarding attainment, because of the seductions of the Siddhas— such as those possessing the powers of Maheśvarī— who create obstacles by means of transient divine enjoyments, one should not direct one's attachment toward them in order to enter the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta). [It does not arise.]
The guides lead them toward those impermanent enjoyments.
Therefore, one should not form attachment to them out of a desire for the highest [state];
this was already stated previously (p. 71). || 23 ||
In the very same way, even when procreation has begun, if one sprinkles the middle state with the support of the nectar of the Fourth (turya-rasa), then—
provided there is no reconnection with the conviction in the measures (mātrās)— that which was lost [is restored].
Re-arising. || 24 ||

Regarding the *mātrās*: they are called *mātrās* because they are measured (*mīyante*). These are the objects such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth; for all worldly entities are fully comprised within these five objects alone. Regarding "the connection of one's own cognition with the objects":
this refers to the connection made by the eye, which is the cognition of form, or that which is made by speech.
Those [objects] such as pleasure and so forth which belong to the forms beginning with the Visionary (paśyantī), or that which is the domain of speech,
those which the mind reflects upon, and that which the intellect determines;

p. 109) Those very things which are characterized by the ego (ahaṅkṛtāni), and that which exists as an object of cognition (vedyatayā)— which, in relation to the imagined subject (kalpitapramātṛ), is animated by a manifestation of difference, serves as the locus of "this-ness" (idantā), and exists as the state of being grasped (grāhyabhāva) by one who takes it as an objective support— that is "it" (sa).

The light of consciousness, Paramaśiva, is to be sought and recognized within this universe composed of existence and non-existence, which shines as one with that very light of consciousness. Just as it is said: "This is that Great Lord, the light of the conscious Self, through non-difference from whose light this entire universe shines; for there is nothing outside of light."

Since the manifestation of anything else is impossible, the intended meaning is this: "I am that very light which, being self-luminous, shines as the nature of the illumination of the entire universe.
And that which does not exist, one must seek it there with effort.
Thus, according to the principle established in the *Śrī Svacchanda*, for one who continuously maintains the realization that "this entire universe is I"— that is,
who persistently contemplates with focused attention due to the presence of repeated immersion (*āveśa*)— the previously mentioned inferior emanations are destroyed.

The meaning is that for the yogin whose very nature consists of the singular, dense wonder of having seized the fourth state (*turya*), there occurs a "re-arising" (*punarutthāna*), which is an emergence—that is, a fulfillment through the attainment of oneness with That. As it is said in the *Śrī-svacchanda*:
"Violently becoming restless, it moves crookedly through the desire for enjoyment; it runs toward the state of emergence (*vyutthāna*) itself."
"Because it does not grasp the desired state, even the mind of yogins [does not grasp it].

Having begun thus, the word "of which" (*yasya*) must be supplied [to the following], as it depends on the preceding verse; [the object] to be known is the supreme reality (*paratattva*), the state of being (*bhāva*).

The intention (*āśaya*) consists of the state that transcends the fourth [state of consciousness]; it is stable, immovable, full, and entirely free from desire. Indeed, even in the sense of "also," the state consisting of the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) is stable, full, and all-pervading.
But his mind does not waver, even when he encounters all possible circumstances.

(p. 110) Wherever the mind [of such a great yogin]— the mind itself, permeated by the meditation on the supreme reality— thinks, it perceives everywhere only the object of knowledge, the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta).
As it has been said by the Great Gurus:

"When the mind, bound by the medicine of the contemplation of Śiva, is cast upon wood, walls, and the like, they attain the state of the gold of Śiva, just like mercury. Thus, the object of knowledge reaches that very state.
One should reflect: "Having moved, where will you go? For everything is composed of Śiva.
Thus.

Regarding all objects— that is, the senses (*indriya*), their objects (*artha*), the sensory purpose (*aindriyika prayojana*), and the enjoyment of those objects— the preeminent yogi who is established therein, when examined and investigated anywhere at all,
has no inauspiciousness; for all this is manifest to him.
And it remains established through its identity with Śiva, who is a mass of light;
wherever one may investigate, nothing exists that is not Śiva.
And thus it is said. || 24 ||
Thus, the yogi who has attained excellence becomes equal to Śiva. || 25 ||
Through the excellence of the repeated cultivation of the fourth state (*turya*)— due to the firmness of the constant awareness of the *turyapada*—
there arises a growth of the wonder of the surging *ahaṃtā* (I-consciousness) within the central channel (*madhyadhāman*). Thus, having attained the state beyond the fourth (*turyātīta*),
he becomes equal to the Lord Śiva, who is a mass of perfectly pure, autonomous, and blissful consciousness, yet remains distinct by virtue of his bodily form.
Because there is no depletion, he becomes equal to that—as in the expression "the moon of his face" [the equality is due to being slightly less than perfect].
By the absence of such depletion, the meaning is that he is Śiva himself in person. And so it is stated in the *Śrīkālikākrama* (p.

Therefore, having understood from the mouth of the Guru the Yoga that is eternal and beyond doubt, one should, through non-conceptualization— by means of the abandonment of conceptual thought (*vikalpa*), by the support of the emerging non-conceptual awareness (*avikalpa-vimarśa*),
and by the state consisting of Śiva— cultivate the state called "beyond the fourth" (*turyātīta*) through the contemplation of the nature of Śiva.
One should contemplate [the deity] with one's being, because of the state of being identical with that, until the limit of attaining identity with the nature of Bhairava.
The Blessed Lord Bhairava said: "Until it attains that state of equality. || 25 ||

Even so, according to the manner stated in such passages as "that by which this [body] exists is indeed for the sake of experience," the maintenance of his body must not be disregarded, as its sole purpose is merely to pass through the experiences that have presented themselves; thus he says: "[Even though] the future and accumulated karmas have been reduced to ashes by the fire of knowledge, [the karma] that has already begun..."

Because it is impossible to destroy [the body] without experiencing its fruits of past actions (*bhoga*), the maintenance of the body for one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) must not be disregarded until the completion of the experiences of *prārabdha* karma; like the whirling of a potter’s wheel, it continues until the momentum is exhausted, since upon the fall of the body there is no returning again.
Vow is the maintenance of the body. || 26 ||

According to the perspective previously stated, for the yogin who is equal to Śiva and abides in the state of "I am Śiva" (śivāhaṃbhāva), whatever constitutes his activity or mode of existence within the body is itself his vow (*vrata*).
For one who is intent upon the ever-arisen supreme worship consisting of the reflective awareness of one's own true nature, this must be performed as a constant discipline (*niyama*).
And likewise, in the Śrī Svacchanda (p.
"When it is well-illumined, [this occurs] due to the appropriateness of the body, mantra, vital breath, self, and the state of Śiva."
The wood, the fire-drill (araṇi), the fire, its crest, and the sky are the illustrative examples. By that analogy,

when the fire has been well-kindled and ignited through the method of churning the fire-drill, just as the crest— the flame— is seen in the sky after burning the fuel, having attained identity with it through dissolution therein, so too is it perceived.

In the same way, through the friction of the divine organ and the mantra as the fire-drill, when the vital breath (*prāṇa*) within the body is thoroughly kindled, it assumes the state of the upward-moving external *udāna* fire. The Self (*ātman*) residing in the body— which is said to be of the nature of pure, isolated consciousness (*śuddhavijñānakevala*)— becomes like a flame of fire, encompassing everything up to the level of *samanā*.
Having burnt the wood of the body, one dissolves into that state beyond the fourth (turyātīta), which is like the sky free from all limiting adjuncts (nirupādhi).
Likewise, even while abiding in the body and vital breath, the Self should dissolve into that state.

By saying this, it is stated that one who is already established within the body, the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and so forth, is indeed possessed by Śiva; however, no vow distinct from his abiding in the body is required for him. As it is said in the *Śrītrikasāra*:
"The wise man who is always sealed by the mudrās arising from the body..."

He is indeed a bearer of the *mudrā* because he is sealed by the *Śāmbhavī-mudrā*, according to the principle stated as "the inner object of focus with the gaze directed outward" (*antarlakṣyabahirdṛṣṭi*), and not because of the physical gesture of the body. This is also stated in the *Śrīkulapañcāśikā*:

Seeing one whose signs are unmanifest, the Marīcīs converse: "All the Śaktis approach and become manifest for one who is marked by the secret Bhairavīya Mudrā; however, this does not happen for one who wears only manifest, gross mudrās, because they do not approach him."
They do not approach one who bears the sectarian mark (liṅgin), because such a person is exceedingly well-guarded.
Thus [ends the section]. || 26 ||
The recitation of the narrative of such a one as this is [the practice]. || 27 ||

"I alone am the supreme *haṃsa*, Śiva, the ultimate cause"— according to this principle established in the venerable *Svacchanda-tantra*, because [the Self] is eternally composed of the supreme state of "I-consciousness" (*parāhaṃbhāvanā*).
Of that God of gods, whose nature is supreme awakening...
Vimarśa is the supreme power; she is all-knowing and endowed with wisdom.
Thus, according to the method established in the *Śrīkālikākrama*,

for one who has ascended to the uncreated self-reflection (*ahaṃvimarśa*) whose nature is the Great Mantra, whatever speech or other activity occurs becomes his recitation (*japa*), consisting of the incessant revolution of the reflection upon one's own Self as the Deity.

Because the yogin possesses unsurpassed knowledge (*anuttarajñāna*), whatever worldly discourse and so forth he engages in according to conventional usage constitutes his *japa*. This is because his primary intent is the contemplation of his own self as the deity, which has the reflective awareness of "I" (*ahaṃparāmarśa*) as its essence.
The meaning is that nothing whatsoever can manifest without being of the nature of the supreme subject whose essence is Light (*prakāśa*).
As it is said in the *Śrīvijñānabhairava*: "That contemplation which is cultivated again and again within the supreme reality is itself the recitation (*japa*) here;
the sound (*nāda*) whose essence is mantra is the object of such recitation. [Because it fills all things, it is the supreme.]

Regarding "bhāve": within one's own essential nature (*svasvabhāve*), that contemplation (*bhāvanā*) or reflection (*vimarśanā*) which takes such forms as "I alone am the supreme *haṃsa*, Śiva, the ultimate cause"—that which is thus cultivated and accomplished is *japa*. The *nāda* (resonance), whose essence is the uncreated reflection of "I" (*akṛtakāhaṃvimarśa*), is what is to be recited (*japyo*).
The Japanese is his own self-deity. As it has been said:
"There is no one to utter this, nor is there any obstructor;
O Goddess, it utters itself, abiding in the chest of living beings."
Thus: (p.
114) "By means of the letter *sa*, one goes out; by means of the letter *ha*, one enters again."
The individual soul constantly recites this mantra: "Haṃsa, haṃsa."
Twenty-one thousand six hundred recitations of the Goddess are prescribed for day and night; they are easily accomplished, yet difficult for the dull-witted to achieve.
Thus [ends the section]. || 27 ||

He describes the conduct of one who observes such a vow of recitation: [Conduct is the state of abiding in the means for the direct realization of one's true nature, or it is that which must be performed.]—Giving is self-knowledge. (28)
The "giving" (*dāna*) of this Self—which is of the nature of consciousness as described—is its direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*).

That which is given is its perfect essential nature (*svarūpa*); the differentiation of the universe (*viśvabheda*)—that is, the differentiation characterized by the thirty-six principles beginning with Earth and ending with Śiva—is cut away (*khaṇḍyate*) and purified (*śodhyate*).
Because by this [means] the nature of Māyā is given (*dīyate*), protected (*rakṣyate*), and the Śiva-nature which has been attained is maintained (*labdhaḥ*), it is so called.
[The roots] *ḍudāñ* (in the sense of giving), *do* (in the sense of cutting off), *dīṅ* (in the sense of protecting), and *daip* (in the sense of purifying)—these are the verbal roots used here.
Furthermore, "it is given" (*dīyate*) means that the gift (*dāna*) is indeed the knowledge of the Self (*ātmajñāna*), and it is given by him to his disciples. As it has been said:
(115) By seeing or even by touching them, the lords of yogis will cause one to cross over the vast ocean of existence— the sight of the lords of yogis, such as the yoginīs, siddhas, and so forth.

The meaning is that they must bestow grace upon those fit for favor who possess an intense descent of power (*tīvra-śaktipāta*). "Established in the conduct of the *kula*s" means they are attentive to the conduct (*ācāra*)— namely, the process of emanation and reabsorption— of the *kula*s, which consist of the body, the senses, the worlds, and so forth.
Thus [ends the section]. || 28 ||
By the method already described, through his constant equality with Śiva due to his steadfastness in vows, recitation, and ritual practice,
he is mounted upon the wheel of his own power (*svaśakticakrārūḍha*)— that is, he dwells within the universe which consists of the unfolding of his own power.
He alone is, in reality, the awakener of those to be instructed (*pratibodhaka*), making them recognize their own true nature (*svasvarūpapratyabhijñāpaka*).
Thus he says:
"That which is present and is the cause of cognition. (29)

Because he protects the sheep (*avīn*), he is called *Avipa*. According to the perspective stated in [the verse] "The Mothers of the Flock (*paśumātaraḥ*) are Māheśvarī and the others among the groups beginning with Ka" (3-19), the wheel of powers (*śakticakra*) beginning with Māheśvarī resides there, because [the Lord], having realized his own majesty, [thinks]: "All this is my own manifestation."
Because his own self-sovereignty has been recognized: he who shines forth by virtue of his lordship is the cause of knowledge (*jñāhetu*).

"Knowledge" (*jñā*) means the power of knowing; he is the cause of that power. This is for the sake of instruction, meaning in order to awaken [the disciple] through the power of knowledge—that is, to cause him to recognize his own self.
[He is] capable. But the other, because he has been brought under the control of the wheel of powers (*śakticakra*), lacks sovereignty over himself;
[having been subjected to dependence by the powers such as Māheśvarī and the rest, he has been reduced to the state of a bound soul (*paśu*).]

How else could one awaken others? Since the word "that" (*tat*) must be supplied here in the sūtra in relation to the word "this" (*yat*), and since the particle "ca" has the sense of "for" (*hi*), it is therefore rightly said that "the gift is self-knowledge," because this [self-knowledge], being present within oneself, is the cause for awakening to knowledge.

Others, however, [argue that] because of the similarity to the syllable *akṣara*— [the word being derived from the root *aś* with the *auṇādika* suffix *saran*, meaning "it pervades (*aśnute*) the Vedāṅgas by illuminating the desired meanings through each word (*pratiśabda*)"]— the etymological derivation (*nirvacana*) should be performed for each word using terms that are consistent with the form of the syllable *akṣara*. This is the meaning.
According to the convention of the *Nirukta*, one should explain it as follows: "yo" refers to the Lord of Yogins; "vi" refers to discernment (*vijñāna*); "pa" refers to the state (*pada*);

"stha" refers to one established in that state (*padastha*), being the final syllable of this word; "jña" refers to the knower; "he" refers to what is to be abandoned (*heya*); "tu" refers to insignificance (*tucchatā*);
and by the *visarjanīya*, there is the power of emission (*visarga-śakti*), which consists of the upward and downward creation. By the letter "ca,"...

Relying on the view that the agent is referred to by the particle *ca* (and) for the purpose of including those not previously mentioned, that lord of yogins who, through the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*), abides in the state of self-knowledge regarding his own essential nature, should be understood as both the knower and the agent;
and at that time, his state of being something to be abandoned, its worthlessness, and its lack of substance— not its worthiness to be accepted— [is to be understood].

(117) Some explain [the term] as "it causes to perish. However, this does not occur to us as plausible, because the connection of the word-meanings is not very elegant, and because such a method of commentary could be shown by the thousands for every single sūtra. || 29 ||
And of this [Lord]:
"The universe is the accumulation of His own powers. (30)
Since he is said to be equal to Śiva, therefore,
just as his entire universe [is composed] of powers (śakti),
so too, according to the perspective of the sacred tradition (āmnāya), the universe of Śiva consists of his own power; likewise, that of this [deity] consists of his own.

The expansion of the power of the conscious Self, which consists of the manifestation of the power of action (the meaning of which is that the power of action is the capacity for the creation of the universe), is the universe.
As it is said in the venerable *Mṛtyuñjaya*:
Since the Supreme Lord, the God who consists of knowledge, is composed of knowledge whose ultimate reality is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*),
and since that knowledge— by virtue of its absolute freedom (*svātantrya*)— manifests contraction in manifold ways and persists by resorting to multiplicity;
therefore, those who partake in this manifestation of contraction are manifested by the Lord as being constrained through the concealment of their true nature.

Thus bound, because the Lord (*deva*) is their protection (*trāṇa*) by means of the various philosophical views and modes of worship which serve as the cause for the manifestation of their own true nature, He is called the "Eye" (*netra*) according to etymological derivation (*nirukti*), and not merely as the physical eyeball. The Lord is knowledge, and He exists in manifold ways.
The protection of those who are restrained and bound is called their leader.
Also in the *Kālikākrama* (p.
"By way of those respective forms—that is, by way of forms such as blue, pleasure, and so forth—[of things] manifesting externally and internally..."

The meaning is that because all entities have manifestation as their essence, they possess no separate existence apart from that [manifestation], since they conform to its presence and absence. Knowledge shines both externally and internally;
apart from knowledge there is no existence of objects; therefore, the world is of the nature of knowledge.
Indeed, entities have never been made objects of experience by anyone apart from cognition;

therefore, it is determined that cognition has attained the nature of those very entities. Whatever is not perceived independently of something else is non-different from it—just as a pot is non-different from the clay [without which it is not perceived]. Therefore, [the world] is nothing but cognition itself.
The meaning is: a final, definitive certainty by virtue of the knowable having the nature of being.
Through the distinction between existence and non-existence, and by means of negation and affirmation,
the nature of consciousness is established as the ground of all objects of knowledge through the power of meditative cultivation.
From simultaneous perception, there is the identity of knowledge and the object of knowledge; for,
due to the power of contemplation and the power of direct realization of one's own nature, entities such as blue, pleasure, and so forth—
whether positive or negative in form— cannot exist if either of the two, knowledge or the object of knowledge, is absent.
The acceptance of uniformity.
Thus [ends the section]. 30.
It is not only during the state of emanation that there is the expansion of His own power into the universe; persistence and dissolution also follow upon its wake. || 31 ||

The phrase "the accumulation of one's own power" (*svaśaktipracayaḥ*) continues [from the previous context]. It refers to that state of consciousness (*cinmātra*)— which is the manifestation of the universe through the power of action (*kriyāśakti*)— that, in relation to various subjects, consists of the appearance of extroversion for a certain period of time.
119) And that dissolution which consists in resting within the subject—both of these are merely the accumulation of His own powers;
for whatever object of knowledge appears and dissolves is indeed of the nature of His own power of self-consciousness.

Otherwise, its perception would be impossible. For the imagined subject—the one who is empty and illusory—the state of the universe consists in the manifestation of externality; however, upon the immersion of that imagined subjectivity, because the manifestation of the universe's externality relative to it ceases, there is a dissolution which is a resting in the nature of pure consciousness for both.

The intended meaning is that because this [reality] consists of the power of self-awareness (*svasaṃvit*), if that were not accepted, the perception of both of these would be impossible. For this very reason, in the *Śrīkālikākrama*, it is said:
"By means of the distinction between existence and non-existence..."

Thus, and so forth, it is stated with reference to maintenance (*sthiti*) and dissolution (*laya*). Likewise, all knowledge (*jñāna*) is pure, without support— meaning it has emerged from the object of support (*ālambana*, i.e., the object of cognition), having embraced the entirety of the knowable, consisting of its own internal conviction, and consisting of its own "I-ness" (*svāhantā*).
He who perceives that which consists of one's own realization is a liberated soul even while living; of this there is no doubt.
Thus [ends the section]. || 31 ||

"Now, one might object: 'In this way, during the states of emission, maintenance, and reabsorption—which consist of the manifestation of mutual difference—does not a change in His essential nature (svarūpa) result? [Change consists in the cessation of the self-reflection of one's own Self when there is an inclination toward the awareness of the object of knowledge.
To pacify such a doubt, he says:"
(120) Even when that [cognition] arises, there is no exclusion [of the object],
because of the existence of the cognizer. || 32 ||

Even when these [states] such as creation and the rest proceed—that is, even when they emerge—for this yogin there is no movement [of the mind] due to his state of being the perceiver (*saṃvettṛ*), which consists of the wonder of the Fourth State (*turya*) and is composed of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), because he is the subject of apprehension (*upalabdhṛ*). In the absence of that movement, nothing at all is manifested. As it has been said in that very same [text]:

Upon the destruction of the phenomenal expansion of ignorance—that is, even when the body, senses, principles, and worlds manifested by *māyā* have dissolved—there is no arising or setting for the nature of consciousness, whose characteristic is an eternally emergent radiance; therefore, it is indestructible.
This is because, even during the state of empirical transaction (*vyavahāra*), destruction and origination appear as manifestations that are non-different from that [consciousness].

The meaning is that [the nature] is metaphorically designated as such because of its resting within the light; the essential nature does not perish, for it is devoid of both arising and destruction; therefore, destruction is not real.
Since [the world] is metaphorically described through the arising and destruction of ignorance,
how can it be said that what is not destroyed by its own nature is destroyed?

Thus it is said. In this very *Spanda*, there is a pair of states: between the objective world (the expansion of *māyā* consisting of the object of enjoyment) which is established in duality, and the subject (the enjoyer), the former dissolves and arises again within the latter.
Since that which consists of consciousness is not delimited by time, there can be no suspicion whatsoever of its dissolution or arising. Furthermore,

what is here designated as "the state of being an agent of action" is such that while the state of being an object (*kāryatā*) is perishable, the state of being an agent (*kartṛtva*) therein is imperishable.
Likewise: (p.
121) Only that effort which is directed toward an effect is here suppressed.
When that [intellect] is dissolved, the ignorant person thinks, "I am dissolved. It is just as when someone like Devadatta, staying at home, is called by someone, "O Devadatta!
and wishing to deny his own existence, replies, "I am not here. When this has been said, on the contrary—

It is established that "I am standing" [is perceived], and not merely "non-proximity"; such is the case regarding the unawakened. Therefore, during states of non-existence or meditative absorption, because there is an absence of activity, the notion that the Self does not exist—arising from the mere cessation of the organs' functions—is nothing but an error; this is the intended meaning.
But as for that inward-turned state which is the locus of the quality of omniscience, its disappearance could never occur, because nothing else is perceived [the meaning is:
if the nature of the inward-turned state were destroyed, the entire universe would become as if colorless and mute].
This has been stated by this [verse]. || 32 ||
For this yogin, there is no external mental perception of pleasure and pain. || 33 ||

The perception and awareness of pleasure and pain—which arise from contact with objects of knowledge—occurs through their manifestation as "this-ness" (*idantā*), as if they were external objects like blue or other colors;

however, this is not like the ordinary worldly experience where they are touched by "I-ness" (*ahantā*). For, according to the principle of the aphorism stated as "His own mass of powers is His universe" (3-30), everything flashes forth as being enveloped by "I-ness," and not otherwise.

This [statement] is intended to mean that pleasure, pain, and so forth are indeed determined; for how could a yogi, whose state as a subject consisting of the eightfold subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*) has been stilled, [experience them]?
One is touched by pleasure and pain; and likewise, in the *Śrī-Pratyabhijñā-sūtra-vimarśinī*:

"Even for those who have transcended the level of the subject (*grāhaka*) and have attained the state of the real knower (*vāstava-pramātṛ*), although there is the direct perception of pleasure and pain presented by their respective specific causes..."
[Various garlands, sandalwood, women, and so forth are causes of pleasure; the approach of an enemy is a cause of pain.

For them, pleasure, pain, and so on do not arise at all, or rather, pleasure and so on do not arise due to the deficiency of their causes [because the causes of pleasure and so on are submerged within the light of consciousness and, being sublimated, are absent].
At that time, there shall be the manifestation of innate bliss (sahajānanda).
Thus it has been said: "Therefore,
that wherein there is neither suffering nor happiness, neither the grasped nor the grasper,
and even no state of delusion— that exists from the perspective of ultimate reality."

Since the reality of consciousness (*saṃvittattva*), which is untouched by the two states of existence— the substrata of pleasure, pain, and so forth— which are of a perishable nature, does not perceive them, the existence of the cognizer is nevertheless admitted therein, because even the state of deep sleep (*sauṣuptapada*) is an object of experience; otherwise, the recollection occurring at a later time would be untenable.
Thus it has been established in the Spanda [Kārikās]. || 33 ||

And because the yogin, whose state as a subject consisting of the eightfold body has transcended, has no internal contact with pleasure or pain, for that very reason he is "liberated from that [body] and solitary" (tadvimuktastu kevalī). || 34 ||
Completely liberated from those two, pleasure and pain, and internally untouched even by mere mental formations (*saṃskāra*), he is the *kevalin*.

That whose nature consists solely of the subjectivity of pure consciousness alone. As it is said in the *Śrīkālikākrama*: "Having pierced through the great delusion of duality—which is fashioned by the manifold conceptualizations of the cognitions of pleasure, pain, and so forth—the yogi shall obtain the fruit of yoga."

Thus [ends the commentary]. The word "tu" (but/however) indicates a distinction in view of what is to be stated hereafter; likewise, that occurring in the subsequent sūtra indicates a distinction in view of this present sūtra. || 34 ||
As it is said: "But the self, when bound by delusion, [performs] karma. (35)

One who is constricted by delusion—that is, by ignorance—and is thus made into a single solid mass, becomes for that very reason the locus of pleasure and pain; he is the "karmic self," eternally stained by auspicious and inauspicious [actions]. As it has been said in that very same work:
"Because of being shrouded by ignorance, through the application of the process of conceptualization..."
One does not suddenly manifest all [the deities], beginning with Śiva.
Consequently, auspicious and inauspicious states are perceived because of being under their influence;

and from inauspicious states, supreme suffering arises for the ignorant person who remains established in the conceptualization of a web of various mental constructs, such as pots, cloths, and so forth, regarding the principles (tattvas) beginning with Śiva.

Because one fails to grasp the nature of the unsurpassed mass of consciousness (*cidghana*), one falls into the impurity of the veil of illusion (*māyīyamala*) and experiences the suffering arising from the stains of auspicious and inauspicious karma. However, for the knower of that [reality], who discerns within the canvas of all phenomena that "this is the play of one's own Self," there occurs the manifestation of innate bliss (*sahajasukha*).
This is the meaning.
Thus [ends the section]. || 35 ||
p.
124) When even for one such as this, whose nature is bound by karma,
there occurs the union with innate sovereignty that blossoms through the power of the unimpeded descent of Maheśvara’s grace, then for him—
When difference is set aside, it constitutes the activity of another creation. || 36 ||

For the subjects beginning with the *sakala* and *pralayākala*, whose nature consists of the ego-identification (*ahaṃtābhimāna*) with the body, vital breaths, and so forth— [wherein] in the sphere of *māyā*, the *pralayākalas* are of the nature of void-subjectivity (*śūnyapramātṛ*),

and for them the universe of objects of knowledge is as if dissolved according to their own fitness; while the *sakalas* are the individual souls (*kṣetrajña*) from Brahmā down to the smallest insect.

Perceiving the universe as consisting primarily of diverse and distinct entities, for them, the object of knowledge (*prameya*) is likewise [perceived] as entirely divided, limited, and finite. Thus, the meaning is that for subjects (*pramātṛs*), there is the manifestation of difference according to their respective natures.
Even while remaining within the concealment of difference, because of the emergence of the nature of the mass of consciousness (*cidghana*), [the non-dual reality is revealed].

When the [limited] hand is cast aside, there occurs, in due order, the state of being a Mantra, a Mantreśvara, and a Mantramaheśvara, characterized by the power to create whatever one desires. Thus it is said in the venerable *Svacchanda*:
"By means of the three qualities" [the three qualities are indicative of manifold qualities].

Because one is attentive to the self-reflection of one's own essential nature through the state of "I-ness" (ahaṃbhāva), which is complete and consists of the Great Mantra, there is a resemblance to Svacchanda.
Thus, it has been stated that by means of this resemblance to Svacchanda, his [the practitioner's] sense of duality is cast aside through recitation;
having thus described the casting aside of duality by means of resemblance to Svacchanda—

[He is the master] of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and the gods; of the Siddhas, Daityas, and the lords of the Uragas (the term *urageśinaḥ* refers to those such as Śeṣa who rule over the serpents because they possess that nature); and of the Siddhas and others, because he performs acts such as bestowing curses and favors upon them.
The state of being both the giver of fear and the remover of fear.
He may be a giver of fear and a taker away; he may be one who bestows curses or favors.
He takes away even the pride of Time (Kāla) and can cast down even the mountains.
Thus it has been said. || 36 ||
And this is not impossible for it, because:
"The power of the instrument [is known] from its own experience. (37)

From itself—that is, from its own very experience—in cases such as volitional imagination (*saṃkalpa*) and dreaming, the power of the instrument [the power to create the manifold variety of the universe] is already established as belonging to the Self; that is, its status as the creator of various unique objects is proven. With this very intention, it is stated in the *Śrī-Pratyabhijñā*:

For this very reason, because of the manifestation of the representation of whatever is intended— due to the cause of correctly representing and manifesting even those things not previously experienced, since desired objects do not exist externally— the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) consisting of representation belongs to any living being whatsoever, from Brahmā down to a worm.
And it is established that the power of knowledge is essentially luminous and innate; therefore,
even on the level of the imagined subject,
it does not depend upon a prior creation fashioned by a separate Lord.
Since there is an absence of any possibility for activities such as the mental representation of desired objects,
the sovereignty characterized by knowledge and action must necessarily be clearly recognized;
for knowledge and action are indeed clearly established in every living being.
Thus it has been said. Because such a thing is impossible,
if one reflects upon this with intense conviction, then— by virtue of the excellence of that reflection— it becomes common to all.
The meaning is that its creation can be seen by all people, like the well-known accounts of the new creation of heaven composed by sages such as Viśvāmitra and others.
Furthermore, it possesses the quality of being a creator of desired objects; as it is said in the *Tattvagarbha*:
When those yogis clearly possess their own powers of knowledge and action, then, in the creation of desired objects, their lack of firmness and instability— however great it may have been—
is soon and not far off shattered and broken, and their resolve becomes like that of the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpataru).

The meaning is: because they have not yet fulfilled their intended purpose. However, when those [powers] also become radiant with the quality of their own clearly manifested capacity, and when there arises a state of firmness that has torn asunder the distance [between them and the goal], then their resolve shall attain the status of the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpapādapa).
Thus [ends the section]. 37.

And because the fourth nature (*turyātman*), which is the power of absolute freedom (*svātantrya-śakti*) alone, is the essence of the cognizer whose form is consciousness— as expressed by the term "power of instrument" (*karaṇa-śakti*)— otherwise, in the absence of freedom as its essence, the light of consciousness, being devoid of self-reflective awareness (*nirvimarśa*), would fall into insentience (*jāḍya*), like a crystal and the like, even though it reflects the entire multitude of objects.
The meaning is that there would be a total collapse of all worldly transactions.
Therefore, for the purpose of reviving its true nature which has been eclipsed by the power of *māyā*, there is the "animation by the three steps and so forth" (tripadādyanuprāṇanam). || 38 ||

Of these three—consisting of the orientation toward existence, attachment to it, and the inward-turning state [of consciousness]—which are designated by the terms emission, maintenance, and withdrawal;

Among the various states of giving (*dāna*), that which is the primordial and preeminent— dense with bliss, known as the Fourth (*turya*) state, and characterized by a threefold wonder— is, although veiled by the power of *māyā*, manifested like a flash of lightning during the occasions of enjoying various objects; by means of that [bliss], there occurs an enlivening (*anuprāṇana*) even for a mere moment arising at those respective occasions.

One should effect the vitalization of the self by means of that very life-force which follows along with the varying degrees of abiding in the inward-turned reflective awareness of that [consciousness];

and one should effect the stimulation of life itself by that same life. Even the state of the Fourth (turyapada), in which the perception of other objects of knowledge has dissolved during the enjoyment of sense-objects such as women, though it may arise for ordinary people—
Direct perception perceives that which is veiled by objects such as the triad [of states]; however, when free from obscuration, it is perceived by those who are attentive.
By this, the meaning is that through the fourth state (turya) of the living self, there is the focusing and stimulation of the Self in its very nature as the living one.
As it has been said in the *Śrīvijñānabhairava*:

Within, her nature is the bliss of self-experience—that is, she whose form is the self-luminous bliss of self-experience within the fullness of the I-consciousness (*pūrṇāhaṃtā*). She consists of the state of not thinking of anything; she is the power inseparable from me, the Self who is Bhairava in form, and her state is filled with the wonder of non-duality with the entire universe.

That whose form (*ākāra*) is its own essential nature (*svarūpa*) is such; and that very [nature], in reality and from the perspective of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), is the stainless body (*vapuḥ*)—the essential nature (*svarūpa*) which, by its own wall, manifests the world, is unobscured, fills the universe, and illuminates everything without exception.
It should be known as not consisting of the elements (*bhūtamaya*). Its sphere of experience is free from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
Whatever state is full in form belongs to Bhairava, whose nature is Bhairava.
"His body should be known in its true nature as stainless and filling the universe," beginning with these words (p.

The emergence of bliss that occurs at the conclusion of the immersion into power (*śaktyāveśa*) when one is agitated by the union with power (*śaktisaṃgama*)— even without the actual union with a manifest woman,
but solely through the recollection of the state of bliss produced by that union— is to be understood as one's own innate bliss of Brahman (*brahmānanda*). As it has been said:
Embraced by his wife, he perceives neither the external nor the internal;
the Śruti provides this illustration, yet the fool considers it a mandatory injunction.
Creation is not born from the male organ, nor from the female organ, nor from semen;
rather, the power surging forth from bliss creates itself by means of itself.
According to such statements, at the conclusion of absorption into the power of bliss (*ānanda-śakti*) manifested through union with a woman,

one should contemplate that which pertains to Brahman alone, established solely in one's own self due to the absence of contact with women and the like; or else, [one should contemplate] that which exists within the power of consciousness (*cic-chakti*) when it is agitated by union with the power of the manifestation of the universe.
At the conclusion of that absorption, there arises the bliss of one's own true nature;
that bliss which belongs to the reality of Brahman is called the bliss of the Self.

Through licking, churning, and striking— where "licking" is the tasting of the nectar of the lips, "churning" is the stirring of the principal organ or embracing, and "striking" is the impact or scratching with the nails—
and through such excitants (*uddīpana-vibhāva*) and others, there arises an intense recollection of bliss that has been ignited.

One's own self alone, consisting of radiant bliss, should be contemplated. O Mistress of the Gods, through the recollection of the intensity of sexual pleasure, a flood of bliss may arise even in the absence of the [physical] power.
When great joy is attained upon seeing a long-lost kinsman,
one should meditate on that surging joy and become absorbed in it, becoming one with it.
Through the expansion of the bliss of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) arising from the joy produced by eating and drinking,
one should contemplate the state of Bhairava, which consists of great bliss (*mahānanda*).
[This refers to] the excellence of bliss manifested through the tasting of flavors such as the consumption of delicious food and the drinking of milk.
For one who contemplates the state filled with bliss through single-minded devotion, the attainment of unsurpassed happiness shall occur.
p.

129) For one whose self is unified with the incomparable bliss produced by the aesthetic wonder (*camatkaraṇa*) of objects such as song— where "song" is the first among objects like the resonant sounds of flutes, lutes, and soft voices— [the state of being a knower of the Self arises].

For one whose mind is concentrated, the attainment of the bliss of Brahman occurs through the penetration of the touch of Śakti; for the yogi, by becoming absorbed in that, there arises identification with it through its ascent into the mind.

This has been elaborated through the demonstration of such means as these. And this [is further explained] by the phrase "extremely enraged" (*atikruddhaḥ*), which refers to the activity of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) consisting of the grasping of objects characterized by suffering, pleasure, and delusion, through three modes such as excessive anger and so forth.
Furthermore, other such diverse states belonging to the waking condition— characterized by the activity of the organs of action, such as the sound of running— are to be included. Thus,
in whatever stage the mind may abide during these various states while its mental fluctuations are without external support, one should remain in that state.

The meaning is the perception of that which has its support in pure self-nature alone, whose wheel of all particular powers has subsided, whose supreme nature is the attribute of the Self, and whose vibration is firmly established; [or, one who is] either overjoyed or reflecting, "What shall I do?"
Or, whatever step one takes while running, therein vibration is established.
By these and other such [means]...
he shall become awakened and unobscured.

This has been demonstrated by the preceding [text]. This [work], *Spandanirṇaya*, has been determined by me alone to be complete in itself, because there is no possibility of a desire for further inquiry regarding the subject matter once it has been ascertained beyond doubt. By the aphorism, "The fourth among the three... (3.20), it is stated that the fourth state (*turya*) underlies the waking state and the others.

The distinction here is that [the reality] has been described by this method— which pervades all states and is defined by emission, maintenance, and withdrawal— at the beginning, middle, and end; for even though the unity of meaning between these two previously mentioned sūtras is accepted according to their sequence, there exists a difference in the composition of their meanings as general and specific.
[The resolution of the objections regarding tautology and contradiction. || 38 ||
And one should not be satisfied merely by attaining this vitalization of the three steps and so forth during the state of inward-turnedness and firm support; rather—
As with the stability of the mind, so too [is there stability] regarding the body, its instruments, and external objects. || 39 ||

This is precisely what is meant by "vitalizing the three steps and so forth. Just as one should perform vitalization through the fourth state (*turya*) during the inward-turned state of consciousness (*cittasthiti*), so too, even in the outward-turned state consisting of the body, the organs, and external appearances, one should gradually [vitalize them] by means of the power of support from internal reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).
One should perform the vitalization by means of that [consciousness] which possesses degrees of intensity;

having attained the wonder of the Fourth State (turya), which lasts for only a moment— like a flash of lightning in a state characterized by occasional repose in one's own nature— one should experience satisfaction through being filled with bliss.

Thus, even when directed toward external objects, because there is a continuous sprinkling of the nectar-essence of the ultimate reality consisting of bliss, the intended meaning is that there is a blossoming through the bliss of its reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). As it is said in the *Śrīvijñānabhairava*:
"One should contemplate the entire universe or one's own body as filled with one's own bliss."

Simultaneously, by means of one's own nectar alone, one becomes composed of supreme bliss. This means that for a person who contemplates the state of Śiva as completely full— because every object in the external world considered "other" is permeated by a drop of the dense essence of the bliss of consciousness—
there occurs an immersion into one's own nature, which consists of unsurpassed bliss.
Thus, indeed, the blissful Self, whose power is absolute freedom, having become manifest in all states, becomes the agent of creation according to its will. || 39 ||

But when he does not contemplate this very internal fourth state— the state consisting of unsurpassed bliss— as his own self, then, due to the absence of the subjectivity of the body and so forth, [he enters the supreme state].
The outward movement of that which is to be carried [the mind] arises from desire, which consists of the *āṇava-mala* characterized by the sense of being incomplete. (40)

The *saṃvāhya*— the bound soul (*paśu*) whose nature consists of karma— is that which is "carried along," meaning it is led from one womb to another, together with the coverings (*kañcuka*), the internal organs, the external organs, the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), and the gross elements, as well as with *kalā*, *vidyā*, and the rest, accompanied by *māyā*, all of which are presided over by the wheel of powers (*śakticakra*). Of him...

...desire (*abhilāṣaḥ*)—which consists of the sense of being incomplete and takes the form of longing, rather than the thought "may something be mine"—because the principle of attachment (*rāgatattva*) has such a nature. The meaning here is that upon this *āṇava* impurity (*mala*), which serves as the foundation, the other two impurities are supported. As for the impurity here:

Thus, according to the principle stated in the *Śrī Svacchanda*, due to the cause known as the impurity of *āṇava-mala*— which consists of the ignorance characterized by the sense of being incomplete (*apūrṇamanyatā*)— there occurs an outward movement, which is precisely the orientation toward external objects, and never the state of being attentive to the inward-facing form. As it is said in the *Kālikākrama*:
Because it is obscured by ignorance and due to its association with the process of conceptual construction,
one does not immediately manifest the entirety [of reality], beginning with Śiva.
Consequently, auspicious and inauspicious states are perceived because of being under their control;
and from inauspicious states, supreme suffering arises for the beast shrouded in ignorance,
who does not realize the true nature of consciousness due to the constant agitation of natural conceptual constructions that flow forth spontaneously.
Because it is touched by the stain of merit and demerit, it results in various inferior and evil fruits.
Having formed an unreal conceptualization, they are cooked in the hells and other realms;
they are consumed by their own arisen faults, just as bamboos are burned by fire.
Those people who always enjoy ignorance through entities consisting of illusion take on illusory bodies; they become vessels for affliction,
like a bamboo stalk consumed by fire produced from its own internal friction through false conceptualization.

The intention is as follows: after experiencing the torments of hell due to the defects such as desire produced within oneself, one again takes up a physical body for the sake of enjoying objects that are like illusions; thus, from affliction to another affliction, this transition continues incessantly until the attainment of the unsurpassed knowledge of Śiva.
Thus [ends the section]. 40.

But when one contemplates one's own true nature, which has blossomed through the power of the descent of the Supreme Lord's grace (*pārameśa-śaktipāta*), then, due to the absence of desire, there is no outward movement for him; rather, there is only delight in the Self (*ātmārāmatā*).
[For one whose disposition is possessed by desire, which consists of the *āṇavamala* characterized by a sense of incompleteness, there is both an internal and external state.]

For one who perceives their own nature as a mass of consciousness and bliss, there is the self-delighting act of producing the wonder of the manifestation of the state of being a conscious subject; thus [the author] says it is "eternal" (p.
Through the destruction of that [ignorance], the cognition based upon it is destroyed, and consequently, there is the dissolution of the individual soul (jīva). || 41 ||

The word "that" (tat) refers to the consciousness (*saṃvit*) of that yogin who has ascended to the fourth state (*turyapada*), the self which is the previously mentioned subject, and who is intent upon the reflective awareness (*vimarśana*) of it. Because of the cessation of desire, "that" refers to the dissolution and pacification of the transmigrating individual soul—
the state of being a limited subject consisting of the eightfold city (*puryaṣṭaka*)— which then shines forth as nothing other than the pure conscious subject.
This is the meaning. As it is stated in that very same place:

"Just as one who has awakened [perceives] objects experienced in a dream—such as various groves, rivers, mountains, cities, and so forth, which were experienced during the state of sleep within the heart, in an extremely small space."

In reality, there are no manifestations occurring at that very moment; rather, the awakened person simply recognizes them as the play of the sovereignty of the conscious Self (cidātman). Thus, even in the waking state, because the expansion of sovereignty does not appear as something separate from consciousness, the entire universe is non-different from consciousness and consists entirely of Śiva.

For the yogin who reflects through the perfection of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), the vision of saṃsāra is destroyed. It is said that consciousness (*saṃvit*), by its own will to manifest the manifold variety of the universe, assumes the state of the grasper and flashes forth in the form of the grasped;
thus, the vision of saṃsāra arises from a perverted meditation upon this very flashing forth of consciousness, whereas [liberation] arises from non-perversion.

The meaning is that through the excellence of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), once that [duality] has perished, there occurs again the wondrous power of one's own self-sovereignty (*svātmaiśvarya*). Thus, by such cultivation, the yogi does not perceive saṃsāra at all.
Thus,
having cast aside the conduct of both being and non-being, and having resorted to another state,
one abandons the web of conceptual constructions through non-duality, which is both supreme and non-supreme.
The yogi who is eternally devoted to his own self, who is solely intent on swallowing time,
and who possesses the fortune of the state of absolute liberation (kaivalya), shall attain the state of nirvāṇa.

Having first dispelled the expansion of the various lower and higher conceptualizations— which consist of the functions of existence and non-existence regarding the self such as blue, pleasure, and so forth— by means of non-conceptual reflective awareness (*avikalpa-parāmarśa*), and having firmly grasped the state of full I-consciousness (*pūrṇāhaṃtā*) through the excellence of beholding one's own Self, one begins with the "digit" (*kalā*), thinking: "I live by means of this digit which consists of conceptualization."

The meaning is that for one who has reached the end of the earth— that is, for the gross time— the attainment of the state of Nirvāṇa occurs because of the density [of consciousness], which is inclined toward devouring [time].
Thus: "partaking of the state of isolation" means not being carried away by the senses or their subtle elements (tanmātras). || 41 ||

An objection is raised: "If the destruction of the *jīva* occurs in this way, does it not follow that the fall of the body must happen? Yet, even for one who is perfectly awakened (*suprabuddha*), such a thing is not observed to occur immediately. Therefore, how can he possess the realization attained at that time? [The meaning is: because the existence of the body contradicts the ascent to the fourth state (*turyapada*). Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Then, liberated from the sheath of the elements, he becomes once more the supreme one, equal to the Lord.
Thus, through the exhaustion of desire and the dissolution of the individual soul (*jīva*), when the conceit of being the subject consisting of the "eightfold city" (*puryaṣṭaka*) has fallen away,

this one who possesses the sheath of elements (*bhūtakañcukī*)— the elements that initiate the body— is like a sheath, a distinct covering, and not [identical with] the locus of the "I-sense" (*ahantā*).
p. 135) [The meaning is:
because the limited sense of "I" has dissolved within the body—such as the imagined *puryaṣṭaka*—just like that of an ordinary bound soul. Being thus, he is liberated.
Since he partakes of Nirvāṇa, being for the most part equal to the Lord (*pati*),

having entered into the essential nature of the Supreme Lord which is a mass of consciousness (*cidghana*), he is therefore supreme and full. According to the principle of the meaning of the sūtra stated as "the bodily activity is the vow" (3-26), he is like a petal— [where *dala* means a withered slough].

This is the intended meaning: just as when a snake's skin has been shed, there is no longer any grasping at the conceit of "I-ness" (ahantābhimāna), so too, through the practice of the knowledge of Śiva, there is an absence of the conceit of being a cognizer (pramātṛtābhimāna) regarding the body and so forth once they have been perceived as distinct [from the Self]. Or else, it is like a sheath for a sword.
Just as [the sword] is distinct from the scabbard, so too, even while residing within the body—which is distinct [from him]—he is not touched by the state of being its subject (*pramātṛ*).
Although situated in the body and so forth, he is not touched even by the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of being its subject. As it is said in the *Śrīkularatnamālā*:
When the excellent guru explains it correctly, there is no doubt;
at that very moment one is liberated, and only the machine remains.

Furthermore, what need is there to mention that wise yogi who, with one-pointed concentration— meaning whose mental activity is directed exclusively toward nothing else— is established for even a single moment in the supreme Brahman? Such a liberated one shall liberate all beings.
Thus it is said: even in the *Śrīmṛtyujit*,
it is stated that if the reality is perceived for even the duration of a single blink of an eye,
then indeed he is liberated at that very moment and shall not undergo rebirth again.
Thus [it is said]. Also in the *Kulasāra* (p.
"O beautiful one, oh, the majesty of reality, which is realized merely by being known!"
But when it reaches another ear, one is liberated at that very moment.
Thus [ends the section]. 42.
One might ask: "Why does his state of being encased in the sheath of the elements not cease at that very moment? To this he says:
"The connection with the vital breath (prāṇa) is innate. (43)
The innate connection with the vital breath (*prāṇa*) arises from its own nature, which is by definition freedom.

Indeed, the Blessed Consciousness, desiring to manifest the manifold variety of the universe, first assumes the appearance of limitation; having taken recourse to the stage of the perceiver, whose form consists of the throbbing of the entire contracted universe in the guise of the vital breath.

It flashes forth as the appearance of the world in the form of the graspable; thus, through her innate sovereignty, this connection with the vital breath (prāṇa) is first manifested. Due to this innate connection with the vital breath, the persistence of the sheaths (kañcukas) lasts as long as that [connection] endures; there is a constant concomitance between the two.

It is dependent upon the bonds of karma produced by the limited subject. Consequently, the body—the locus of experience—which arises from previously accumulated mixed karma, is exhausted only through the enjoyment of the objects of experience presented by what has already begun (*prārabdha*), and not otherwise; therefore, [this applies] to the body of the knower of reality.
The meaning is that its state is like the whirling of a wheel, with the purpose of carrying through the enjoyment that has been undertaken. And so it is said in the Śrī Vājasaneyī:
"That power which is supreme, subtle, all-pervasive, stainless, and auspicious..."
She is the mother of the wheel of powers (śakticakra), whose essence is the nectar of supreme bliss (parānanda).
Mahāghoreśvarī is the fierce one who effects both emanation and withdrawal;
she forcibly draws forth Time— which flows in three ways, is of three kinds, and resides in the three— [she who is the transformation of the vital breath and whose nature is life].

The Supreme Power (parā śakti) is "terrible" (ghorā) because she gives birth to the circle of powers beginning with the "extremely terrible" (atighorā), and she is "fierce" (caṇḍarūpā) because she is intent upon concealing her own essential nature. Her status as the creator and destroyer [of the universe] arises from her drawing forth time, measured by the powers beginning with the *truṭi*, up to its full extent. She is called "flowing through three" (*trivaha*) because she flows through the three paths of the *iḍā*, *piṅgalā*, and *suṣumnā*.
It is threefold, consisting of the forms of the Moon, Sun, and Fire, and is situated in the three states, abiding within the past and so forth.

Thus, it has been stated that the Blessed Consciousness itself, through the process of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), effects the manifestation and dissolution of external time—consisting of the past, future, and present—which exists in the form of the moon, sun, and fire flowing through the three channels (*nāḍī*). [Manifestation is emission to the outside; dissolution is [withdrawal] within.]
[The withdrawal. This is also stated in the *Svacchanda*: "The letter *ha* is remembered as the vital breath (*prāṇa*).

That which is called the vital breath—consisting of the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) that is devoid of the distinction between the signified and the signifier, and having the form of a consonant (*hal*)—is indeed that very same [vital breath].

That universal vital breath (*prāṇa*), whose essential nature consists of the process of descent preceded by the manifestation of contraction through its own sovereignty, proceeds toward the filling of emission (*visarga*) through all its hollow parts;
for the sake of the emission consisting of the creation of the manifestation of various external objects, it acts preceded by that manifestation.

The meaning is that it is the *prāṇa* because of its entry (*praveśa*), its drawing forth (*āharaṇa*), and its intense inhalation (*prakarṣeṇa ānamana*) for the sake of internal filling; it is so called because of the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) appropriate to the state of desiring, grasping, and resting within the object, which results from sounding (*dhvanana*). He clarifies this very point with the word "eternal" (*nityam*): although this [prāṇa] resides in all bodies, it is [located] in the chest of living beings.

The connection with what follows is as follows: existing as something clearly perceived and constantly filling [the body], it brings about a life consisting of reflective awareness (*vimarśamaya*) for living beings and their objects through inhalation and exhalation;
this is the vital breath (*prāṇa*) consisting of breath (*prāṇamaya*), directed toward emission and filling.
Abiding in the chest of living beings, this [breath] constantly fills them.
Thus: the letter *ha* of *prāṇa* (p. 138)—that which has the form of *hal*—is without vowel (*anacka*), consisting of the sound of the unstruck resonance (*anāhatadhvani*).
"O Goddess, abiding in the chest of living beings, it vibrates by itself"— according to this principle, that which is the supreme seed called *nāda* arises spontaneously.

Thus, according to the position stated in other tantras, this very *prāṇa*— which is synonymous with *prāṇana* (vitalization) and known as *jīva* (the living principle)— is taught through the unbroken lineage of the gurus as that which vibrates by itself within all things.
Furthermore, according to the classification of the "dust" (*dhūli*), it takes the form of the letter *ha*, encompassing the entire universe within its womb.

The form of Kuṇḍalinī, resembling a sleeping serpent, having spontaneously arisen, remains having submerged itself into the nature of the awareness of *nāda* and entered the form consisting of the vital breath (*prāṇa*); for the supreme power of the Lord called Consciousness, being the Supreme Kuṇḍalikā, exists having internalized the entire universe.

The traditional teaching (āmnāya) is that [the breath] shines as the nature of resonance (nāda), as the nature of the phonemes (varṇa), and as the nature of the coiled energy (kuṇḍalikā). And thus, the vital breath (prāṇa), whose form has been explained in this way, is indeed remembered as the *haṃsa*, because it flows upward and downward by its own natural impulse,
manifesting through the reflective awareness (vimarśa) of the letters *ha* and *sa*, which possess the characteristics of abandoning (*hāna*) and taking up (*samādāna*).

According to the principle stated as "the vital breath (prāṇa) is well-functioning and shaped like a plow," because [the Self] consists of the vital breath whose form is the venerable Lord Svacchanda-bhaṭṭāraka,
its capacity to effect emission and withdrawal through the fullness of the Visarga has been declared; thus, it is rightly said that the connection with the vital breath is innate (naisargika).

Thus it is said. For this very reason, the venerable Bhaṭṭakallaṭa stated in the *Tattvārthacintāmaṇi*: "First, consciousness, having become transformed into the vital breath (prāṇa), [becomes] the firmness of the instrumental cause called prāṇa. || 43 ||

And therefore, even though the natural connection with the vital breath (*prāṇa*) remains, he who dwells while contemplating the internal *kalā*— [the phrase "mounted upon that" means having resorted to the stage of the perceiver whose form is the act of breathing]— is indeed transcendent; thus he says:
(139) By means of restraint upon the center within the nose, what need is there here for the left, the right, or the *suṣumṇā*? (44)

Within the right, left, and central channels—the primary forms of the entire network of channels (nāḍīcakra)—there is that which is called the "nose" (*nāsikā*) because it "breathes" (*nasate*), meaning it flows with curvature; thus, it is the vital energy (*prāṇaśakti*) that flows crookedly. That which is "internal" (*āntarī*) is the consciousness (*saṃvit*) within that [energy], and the "middle" (*madhya*) is even the center of that [consciousness].
It is the primary [power] because it is the most internal of all.
Of that God of gods, whose nature is supreme consciousness,
reflective awareness (vimarśa) is the supreme power, omniscient and endowed with knowledge.

Thus, according to the principle taught in the *Śrīkālikākrama*, that form which consists of reflective awareness (*vimarśamaya*), through *saṃyama*— that is, through the excellence of internal contemplation [due to repeated, firm, and attentive focus upon the inward-turned nature; for "contemplation" (*nibhālana*) means the fixing of the mind, according to the root-meaning of the verbal root *bhal* in the sense of "fixing"]— what is there [to be attained]?
It is said: for this is the supreme samādhi, which shines intensely in all states and is free from emergence.
As it is stated in the venerable Vijñānabhairava:
"The consciousness of the grasped and the grasper is common to all embodied beings."

However, this is the distinction for yogins regarding the connection: attentiveness toward the movement of prāṇa and apāna. While the consciousness of the self as grasper and grasped is common to all subjects, for yogins, in the shifting of that [consciousness], there is the state of being intent upon entering into another subject.
Thus [ends the verse]. 44.
140) Thus, demonstrating the fruit of such yoga, he concludes the treatise:
"Furthermore" [the word *bhūyaḥ* has a dual sense of frequency and repetition; its redundancy is thus resolved].
There may be a closing together. || 45 ||

For one who is intent upon supreme yoga, there occurs once again the closing of this universe— which had arisen from the essential nature of consciousness— toward that very consciousness; this closing consists of the dissolution of the latent impressions of duality and, for the most part, the re-emergence of one's own essential nature, which is consciousness itself.
It belongs to the yogin. As it is stated in the *Śrīsvacchanda*:

"Beyond Unmanā [that is, beyond the power of Samanā], that which is the union of the Self with the power of Unmanā is of the nature of identity (*tādātmya*). In that state of Aunmanasa, the abode of Paramaśiva, even non-conceptual reflective awareness (*nirvikalpa-vimarśa*) does not exist."

Because of the absence of objectivity (*vedyatva*). Since objectivity, which extends up to the level of *Samanā*, consists of the net of bonds (*pāśajāla*) and is thus of a conceptual nature (*savikalparūpa*), O Goddess, one should fix the self there. For when the self is joined to that, it becomes identical with it.
Thus it is said: "And so,
once awakened, just as a fire that has become utterly pure and intensely radiant would not enter the wood again,
so too the Self [of the sixfold path] does not re-enter the path."
The meaning is "from the net of snares"; [it has been] extracted.
By means of the impurities, karmas, kalās, and so forth, one becomes stainless and free from fatigue;
even while situated therein, one is not afflicted, because one is exceedingly pure.
(141) Thus it is said.

The intention of one who says "it would become more" is this: that the state of Śiva belonging to this yogin is not something new, but rather his very own nature (*svabhāva*), which [appears otherwise] solely due to the wickedness of his own conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) instigated by the power of *māyā*.
Although that [reality] is manifest, one is not capable of reflecting upon it;
thus, by means of the sequence for demonstrating the aforementioned method, that very reality is made manifest—may there be auspiciousness! 45.
This commentary on the meaning of the *Śivasūtras*, beautiful through its union with the vibration of scriptural corroboration, has thus been presented. || 1 ||

May those of meritorious deeds taste the overflowing essence of ever-new nectar, intense with its flavor, which flows from the revelation of the *Śivarahasya*, for the sake of severing worldly existence.
This *Śivasūtravimarśinī* is clearly [composed]. || 2 ||
This [treatise] increases the appetite of those who suffer from a loss of relish;
it brings about the supreme maturation of the intellect,
like a flood of nectar by the mere act of tasting it.
It removes the fear of death, old age, birth, and so forth. || 3 ||
Enveloped by limited forms of egoity such as the body, vital breath, and pleasure, people do not perceive their own vast and supreme nature as the Great Lord; instead,
they see the entire universe surrounding the ocean of the nectar of consciousness as if it were a mass of foam in its midst.
He who perceives [the Self] through instruction as it has been described is that one Śiva himself in person. || 4 ||
Cross quickly over the ocean of saṃsāra; place your feet firmly upon the supreme state, which is overflowing with eternal light and bliss.
Reflect upon this aphorism proclaimed by Śiva, which is radiant with secrets and,
through its spontaneously manifesting and immediate reasoning, causes one to leap up within.

Thus ends the third unfolding (unmeṣa) of the *Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikāvṛtti*, composed by the illustrious Abhinavagupta, who lives upon the lotus feet of the most eminent teacher of the Great Maheśvara, the venerable Kṣemarāja. 3.
And thus this Śivasūtravimarśinī is completed.
This *Śivasūtravimarśinī*, composed by the venerable Kṣemarāja for the sake of realizing the identity of Śiva with one's own self, may it lead to the welfare of those who possess discernment.
